en: The Words and Phrases of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Volume One.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty;
recorded by his disciple Guanding.
This four-fascicle text contains eighteen chapters in total; traditionally, there have been various discrepancies in how they were divided.

The masters of the north of the River regarded the first chapter as the "Introduction," the sections from the "Life Span" (*Nyorai-juryō*) down to the "Sacrifice of the Body" (*Shashin*) as the "Main Body," and the "Praise of the Buddha" (*Sanbutsu*) as the "Circulation."
The main text further consists of three parts:

from the "Life Span" chapter downward is the formal exposition; from the "Four Kings" chapter downward is the great vow to protect the sutra; and from the "Curing Illness" chapter downward is the great compassion that receives and guides sentient beings.

The masters of Jiangnan regard the first chapter as the introduction, the sections from "Life Span" (*Nirdeśa-parivarta*) downward as the main body, and the thirteen chapters from "The Four Heavenly Kings" (*Caturmahārājika-parivarta*) downward as the dissemination.

The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha divided the new text into twenty-two chapters: the first chapter serves as the introduction; nineteen chapters, from "Life Span" down to "Relinquishing the Body," constitute the main body; and the final two chapters comprise the dissemination.

The *Zhendi* commentary states: "The 'Chapter on Lifespan' clarifies the fruit of the Master; the two chapters on 'Repentance' and 'Praise' clarify the causes of the Disciples; the 'Chapter on Prediction' is the fruit of the Disciples; the 'Chapter on Removing Illness' is the cause of the Master; and from the 'Chapter on the Four Kings' onwards, the actual power and function are discussed."

"If the former master’s position that the effect is primary and the cause secondary is already correct, how could the latter master’s position that the cause is primary and the effect secondary be considered a valid transmission?
The present master says:
"The division of the text is merely a matter of human sentiment."
People generally say:
"The Preface does not yet distinguish the Way; it concerns the transmission of the final dregs, and thus one cannot discuss the causal relationship between teacher and disciple.

This interpretation is incorrect. Indeed, the three sections [of the scripture] must not be treated as disconnected or severed; the Preface fundamentally introduces the Main Text and the Transmission, and the Preface itself possesses three meanings.
The "Correcting the Root" (zhèngběn) rectifies the "Preface and General Introduction" (xùtōng), and "rectifying" also carries three meanings;
the "General Introduction" (tōngběn) penetrates the "Preface and General Introduction" (zhèngxùtōng), and "penetrating" also carries three meanings,
because the words of the superior, middle, and inferior [sections] are all excellent.

Furthermore, since the spiritual capacities of sentient beings for attaining the Way are not fixed, how could it be permissible to claim that [this teaching] lacks flavor or that its transmission has reached its end?
Since it has not reached its end, what harm is there in speaking of the causal relationship between teacher and disciple?
As stated correctly in the introduction, this too should present no hindrance.

Within the section on circulation, there is a correct intention; it serves all the more to urge and encourage the proclamation and practice [of the teaching], and thus does not deviate from the meaning of the sutra.

Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that the seer Asita was the cause as a teacher, while the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions" (*Dhāraṇī-paṭala*) granted the fruit of prediction to his disciples; all masters unanimously judge this to be the section on propagation.
There are precedents for this, and it does not contradict the meaning.
Whether one grants or denies [this interpretation] depends on the person; there is no need for stubborn adherence.
Now, from "Thus have I heard" up until the assembly of devas and nāgas at the chamber of the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa constitutes the introductory section.
From "At that time, the four Buddhas" downwards, ending with the "Chapter on Emptiness," is the section of the main exposition;
from the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" downwards, until the end of the sutra, is the section of the dissemination.
The "Preface" (xu) means to introduce that which is about to provide benefit.
The "Correct" (zheng) means to correctly discern the Way according to the capacity of the recipient.

"Circulation" (liutong) means that "flowing" (liu) refers to pouring downward, and "penetration" (tong) refers to being unobstructed; it is intended to cause the water of the True Dharma to pour forth from now on into the present, so that the fish-trap of the Holy Teachings shall not be blocked in future generations.
The Sūtra states, "Words of superior, middling, and inferior quality are all excellent," which refers to this very meaning.
A doubter asks:
How can the introductory section (nidāna) be included within the main body of the teaching (bhāṣya)?
This is the pattern seen in many sutras.
For instance, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* lacks a formal "Introductory Chapter" (*nidāna-parivarta*), as its introduction is contained within the main discourse;
whereas in the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the main discourse is contained within the introductory chapter.
The introductory section (*nidāna*) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is included within the "Authentic" (*bhūta*) portion.
This is the case for all scriptures; there is no reason to doubt it, so why should this alone be an exception?

This was the intention of the compilers of the scripture: to resolve the doubts of the four Buddhas by setting forth this passage in isolation, with its prose rendered exceptionally sublime, and to cite the introductory section and place it within the "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) chapter.
Now, following the convenience of the context, we shall not divide this into equal sections.
The preface has three meanings:
first, sequence; second, narration; and third, initiation.
Regarding "sequence" (*cixù*): it occupies the beginning of a single section and stands at the head of all expositions; hence it is called "sequence. Regarding "narration" (*xùshù*):
it introduces what is about to unfold and recounts what is to be beneficial; hence it is called "narration."
"Initiation" (pratimokṣa) refers to the arousal of faith and the commencement of the teaching.
Since this section of the sūtra contains these three meanings, it is titled the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta).
Regarding "chapter" (parivarta), the Sanskrit term is *varga*, which here means a chapter; "chapter" carries the sense of a category or class.
In this text, phrases and passages that follow one another by way of similar categories are divided into *vagga* (sections).
This is, for example, like the *varga* and *skandhaka* in the Vinaya, or the *kanda* in the Abhidharma.
From "Thus" (*evam*) onwards is the transition;
from "At that time, the Tathāgata" onwards is the narrative;
from "The room spontaneously became vast, spacious, and magnificently adorned" onwards is the introduction.
Regarding the sequence of the introductory sections, the old tradition speaks of five matters;
by adding the "Earth" and "Person" chapters to open the way for the Buddha, they become six matters.

In this sutra, the devas and nāgas gathered in the Hall of Faithful Signs (Xinxiang-shi); since they did not hear the preceding introduction nor the subsequent dream, they may be considered both fellow-hearers and non-hearers.
"The assembly that heard it together was small and not in proper order," and so forth.
These five or six lines are also called the "Seal of Certainty" (yin-ding xu), because the sūtras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time invariably begin with the words "Thus" (evam).
It is also called the "General Preface" (tōjū), as it is common to all sūtras.
It is also termed a "general title," because it serves as the foundation.
It is also called the "Postscript to the Sūtra" (kyōgojū), because it was placed there by the compilers.
It is also called the "Preface Prior to the Sūtra," because it was left as an instruction for its placement at the beginning.
It is also called the "Preface Refuting the Erroneous," because it refutes the *āgama* (scriptures) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
It is also called the "Preface of Verified Faith," because it causes those who hear it to have no doubts.
The Master of Tiantai said:
"Taken together, these six explanations all embody the intent of the four *siddhāntas*.
That the various Buddhas and various sutras are the same is the *loka-siddhānta*."
That which precedes and follows the sutra for the benefit of future generations constitutes the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint of benefit for people);
that which refutes non-Buddhist paths constitutes the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment);
and that which is believed and followed without doubt constitutes the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).
The ancient interpretation holds that "as" (ru) means not differing from the name; this is called "non-erroneous.
The phrases transmitted by Ānanda are like pouring water from one vessel into another, identical to those of the Buddha; therefore, they are called "as" because they do not differ.
The principles underlying the text are correct and unerring; therefore, being non-erroneous, they are called "is" (shi).
To speak briefly, the words are such as the principle is.
Master Zhao said:
"‘Thus’ (rúshì) is a term for faith and compliance."
"Through faith, the principles one has heard are integrated; through compliance, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"The term 'thus' (evam) signifies certainty."
There is determination of number and determination of principle.

The Buddha taught that this sutra contains a specific number of phrases; if there were more, it would constitute the slander of exaggeration, and if there were fewer, it would constitute the slander of diminution. Ānanda transmitted it like pouring water from one vessel to another—neither more nor less—and thus the number is determined.

The Buddha taught that the principle of signlessness is neither existent nor non-existent; for if it were existent, one would fall into the extreme of increase, and if it were non-existent, one would fall into the extreme of decrease. Ānanda transmitted this without increase or decrease, and thus the principle is definitive.
Nāgārjuna’s explanation of "thus" (evam) refers to words of faith and compliance.
One who has faith says, "This matter is thus"; one who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus."
These four interpretations each rely on the intent of a single *siddhānta*.

The traditional explanations are general and do not clarify which principle is designated as "suchness" (*tathatā*) by the text, nor which principle is actually being expounded by the text. Which of these is correct?
Since it is not explicitly manifest, it is merely the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint);
Master Zhao bases his "faithful compliance" on the *pudgala-viniścaya* (the standpoint for guiding individuals);
and the textual principles of the Tripiṭaka are definitive as the *pratipakṣa* (standpoint of remediation).
"Nāgārjuna believed and followed this as the primary meaning," and so forth.
Now, I shall provide two explanations: the general and the specific.
The Buddha taught according to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and Ānanda transmitted it according to the manner in which he heard it; therefore, it is called "according to" (*yathā*).
The Buddha understands according to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), while Ānanda receives them like the vastness of the ocean;

therefore, it is said that "this is so," and so forth. Regarding the separate explanation: *Ā* (阿) is called "auspicious" (*kalyāṇa*). Since the text deviates from its underlying principle, it is not "as it is" (*tathatā*); since the principle differs from the text, it is not "so. One cannot see *Ā* at the beginning while the middle and end are all auspicious.
Because the expression accords with the principle, it is said to be "as it is" (yathābhūta); because the principle accords with the expression, it is said to be "thus" (evam).
Now I say:
at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka sūtras, the term "thus" (evam) is used; however, because the two truths are distinct, it is not "as it is," and because the principle is shallow, it is not "thus."
In the Mahāyāna, because the two truths are mutually identical, it is called "thus" (ru); because the principle is profound, it is called "is" (shi).
Now, I say that since the three types of people hear this together yet each understands it differently, it is not "thus"; and because their levels of realization and entry differ, it is not "is."
Only that which is heard by Bodhisattvas is "as-it-is" (tathatā); only that which is reached by Bodhisattvas is "that-which-is" (bhūta).
Now, it is said that a text clarifying the "middle" while departing from extremes is not "as-it-is," and that a middle way existing outside of the two truths is not "that-which-is."
The very nature of being free from words is itself suchness; therefore, it is called "suchness. That all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma is what is termed "this.
First, by refuting the heterodox to clarify the orthodox, this is precisely how the Tripitaka Sūtras function.
Next, by refuting difference to clarify identity, the sutras of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) are thus explained.
Next, by refuting the shallow to clarify the profound, the sutras of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) are thus explained.
Next, by refuting departure to clarify the Middle, the sutras of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are thus explained.
Since this sutra is of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) class, it universally addresses various capacities and dispositions; thus, there is no fault in its manifold explanations.

For one who understands through the contemplation of the mind: because contemplation merges with the object, it is "as-it-is" (ru); because the object is itself right contemplation, it is "thus" (shi).
The meaning is as stated in the Sūtra: "To view it in this way is right view; to view it otherwise is called wrong view.
Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), the traditional explanation is as follows:
Ānanda did not rely on his own mind but personally received the Buddha’s instructions; therefore, he said, "Thus have I heard.
Zhen Di stated:
"The character 'I' (wo) has the meaning of a vessel."
First, the distracted mind is called a "covered vessel," because it lacks the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Second, the forgetful mind is called a "leaking vessel," because although one may acquire [knowledge], one loses it, due to the absence of the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Third, the inverted mind is called a "defiled vessel," because one takes what is not so to be so, due to the absence of the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Ānanda was free from the three faults and was a vessel of pure excellence; because he personally received [the teaching], it is said, "I heard.

The *Śāstra* states: "When the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and one applies the mind to listen attentively—through the convergence of these causes and conditions, it is called 'hearing.'"
Ānanda recounted the Buddha’s final instructions to the assembly, stating that he had personally received them without error; therefore, he said, “Thus have I heard.

The Master explained that there are four meanings of "I": namely, the "I" of self, the "I" of non-self, the "non-I" of self, and the non-dual true "I" which is neither self nor non-self—these meanings correspond respectively to the four types of root-nature individuals, and so forth.

Hearing also has four meanings: hearing what is heard, hearing what is not heard, not hearing what is heard, and not hearing what is not heard; these are applied to the four methods of teaching, as explained at length.
There are four kinds of Ānanda: namely, Ānanda of Joy, Ānanda the Worthy, Ānanda the Keeper of the Treasury, and Ānanda the Ocean; these four names were established based on four distinct conditions.

"Rejoicing, Ānanda, it is 'I' and 'I' who have heard and heard; having personally attended upon the Buddha of the sixteen-foot body and upheld the Dharma of the Tripiṭaka, I therefore say, 'I, I, have heard and heard.'"

Worthy Ānanda, my "self" is non-self; whether I hear or do not hear, I have personally received from the Buddha of the sixteen-foot *vaimātra* body, who possesses the unified body of all Buddhas. Because I uphold the Dharma of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), I say that my self is non-self, and whether I hear or do not hear.

The Elder Ānanda is without self and without "I," yet he does not fail to hear what is heard; having personally received the Buddha’s sublime physical form and upheld the distinct Dharma, he therefore says, "I am without self and I do not hear what is heard."

"O Ānanda, 'self' and 'non-self' are non-dual; through their non-dual functioning, one neither hears nor does not hear. Having personally received the Dharma-body Buddha and upheld the Perfect Dharma, I therefore say that 'self' and 'non-self' are non-dual, functioning through neither hearing nor not hearing."

This sutra teaches universally for the three vehicles; since listeners each understand according to their own capacity upon hearing a single sound, it is necessary to make such distinctions, and so forth.
As for the contemplative understanding: if one practices the contemplation of aspiring upward and loathing downward, this constitutes "I" and "I hear hearing."
If one practices either of the two types of contemplation—analyzing the substance or entering emptiness from the conventional—these are both cases of "I" and "non-I," "hearing" and "not hearing.
If one practices the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional, this is "non-I" and "I," "not hearing" and "hearing."
If one practices the contemplation of the Middle Way, this is the true self that neither hears nor does not hear.
Regarding "at one time," Master Zao said:
"It is the time of the auspicious assembly when the Dharma King inaugurates his mandate."
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"Whether at a high pitch or a low pitch, both are acceptable; however, if it is too fast or too slow, one is unfit to hear the Dharma.
Only when it is at a moderate pitch is it truly 'one time'."
I say: when one is high, the mind of pride does not arise; when one is low, one does not indulge in the five desires; this state of neither indulgence nor pride is the "ordinary" state.
The Master explains:

Sentient beings respond to the Dharma and the Buddha’s compassion responds to their instruction; this is the moment of the meeting between capacity and response. It is also the moment of awakening to the true realization of the Truths (satyadarśana). It is also the moment when the Dharma-eye becomes clear and illuminates the world. It is also the moment when the Buddha-eye shines upon all, and so forth.
As for saying "one": if there is prior thought and subsequent awakening, these two are not one;
it is said to be "one time" because at the moment of sudden, expansive awakening, both thought and awakening are falsely severed.

Regarding "liberation through contemplation" (*guan-jie*): entering from the conventional into emptiness is simultaneous with the ultimate truth; entering from emptiness into the conventional is simultaneous with the capacities of sentient beings; and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way is simultaneous with the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and so forth.
Regarding the term "Buddha," Paramārtha states:
"The Buddha has three meanings:

omniscience distinguishes him from non-Buddhists; compassion distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles; and equanimity distinguishes him from lesser bodhisattvas—these qualities do not exist in others."

The *Śāstra* clarifies that "Buddha" is the ninth title. "Buddha" means "Awakened"; because he has attained clear and great enlightenment regarding the mundane and supramundane, the permanent and the impermanent, the numerical and the non-numerical, and so forth, he is called a Buddha.
The Master of Tiantai said:

"As for the Buddha, there is the Buddha of one zhang and six chi based on the knowledge of all (sarvajñā); there is the Honored One of Distinct Excellence (vairocana) of one zhang and six chi based on the knowledge of the paths and their seeds (mārgajñatā); and there is the Dharmakāya Buddha based on the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)."
The three Buddhas are neither identical nor different; yet, while they are neither identical nor different, they are both identical and different. Regarding contemplative understanding:

through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one realizes that all phenomena have a single characteristic; through the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*), one realizes that all phenomena have manifold characteristics; and through the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), one realizes that all phenomena possess neither a single nor a manifold characteristic, yet simultaneously possess both a single and a manifold characteristic, and so forth.
Regarding "abiding" (sthiti): the Buddha is that which abides, and Rājagṛha is the place where he abides.
According to the *Satyārtha-śāstra*, there are eight ways in which the dharma of abiding is elucidated:
first, abiding within the great trichiliocosm; [and so forth].
The second abiding is the place of reliance, which is the royal city;
the third abiding is the fivefold Dharma-body, whose lifespan is present;
the fourth abiding is majestic deportment that benefits sentient beings.
The five divine abodes consist in dwelling in meditative concentration;
the six Brahma abodes consist in dwelling in the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
and the seven noble abodes consist in dwelling in the three samādhis.
The abiding in the eight great stations is the abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The *Śāstra* explains that the four stations subsume the eight: the celestial station (*devasthāna*) and the Brahma station (*brahmasthāna*) subsume the celestial station and the concentration station (*samādhisthāna*);
the noble station (*āryasthāna*) subsumes the fivefold life-sustaining station (*pañcavidhajīvitasthāna*).
The Buddha abides by means of the "abiding that encompasses the great spheres";
furthermore, there is the "abiding with traces" at Rājagṛha, which encompasses the three types of abiding: the sphere within, the reliance, and the deportment.
The Master of Tiantai said:
The Buddha with a body sixteen feet tall dwells in the ultimate truth;
the Buddha with a combined body of both the sixteen-foot form and the special marks dwells in the union of the ultimate and the conventional;
the Buddha with only the special marks dwells in the union of the conventional.
The Dharmakāya Buddha abides in the Middle Way.

Regarding contemplative understanding: through the contemplation of emptiness one abides in the True, through the contemplation of the conventional one abides in the Worldly, and through the contemplation of the ultimate meaning one abides in the Middle.
As for "Rājagṛha," the *Śāstra* provides an extensive account of its causal origins.
Originally, among the five mountains, seven times it was burned and seven times it was rebuilt; because the king came to dwell here, it is called Rājagṛha (King’s House).
It is also said: "When other houses were burned, the King’s House was not burned."
Later, they all cleared away [the debris] and declared it to be Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence), whereupon they were immediately spared from being burned.
From that time onward, it has been called Rājagṛha.

Regarding the contemplative interpretation: the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute the residence, and the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) dwells therein; therefore, it is called the Royal Residence.
Regarding "Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata," the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) translates it as "Vulture Peak.

Paramārtha states: "The Mountain of Curved Birds lies to the southeast of Rājagṛha; Mount Vipula lies to the southwest; the Mountain of the Rishis lies to the northwest; the Mountain of Black Soil lies to the northeast; and the Mountain of White Soil lies in the center."
"The center, three *yojanas* square and level, is the royal city.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the "mountain" refers to the numinous, which is spiritual wisdom; this is *prajñā*.
The vulture represents the ten thousand virtues; this is liberation.
The mountain represents immovability; this is the Dharma-body.
Being constantly observed by the mind-king, it is the dwelling place of contemplation, wherein all mental factors are made to enter together.

Regarding the absence of a list of the assembly of listeners in this sutra: there were five different times and four different locations. The assembly on Mount Vulture Peak did not hear what was spoken in the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa; the assembly in the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa did not hear what was spoken in the dream; and the assembly within the dream did not hear what was spoken after waking from the dream. Because the assemblies were not gathered in a single session, they are not listed as the "listeners together."
If that were so, Ānanda should not have said, "Thus have I heard.
However, although he did not hear it [directly], the Buddha spoke it for him once more.
Furthermore, because he had attained the Buddha’s awakening-samādhi and was able to realize it for himself, he was entitled to say, "Thus have I heard."
The section beginning with "At that time, the Tathāgata" constitutes the introductory narrative (*nidāna*), as it introduces the subsequent seventeen chapters.
It is also called the "distinctive introduction" (*pratyeka-nidāna*); it is termed "distinctive" because it differentiates this sutra from others and serves as the basis for its specific title.
There are seven distinct categories:
first, from "At that time, the Tathāgata" for one and a half lines, this is the distinction of entering meditative absorption;
second, from "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*" down to the twenty-seventh verse, this is the distinction of the narrative exposition.
Third, from the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) onwards is the section distinguishing the doubts;
fourth, from "The Great Being was thus... onwards is the section distinguishing the auspicious omens;
fifth, from "Śraddhālakṣaṇa saw the Buddha... onwards is the section distinguishing the articulation of those doubts.
Sixth, from "The Four Buddhas said" onwards is the section distinguishing the cessation of doubt;
seventh, from "The devas of the desire and form realms" onwards is the section on the assembly of the multitude.

Regarding the sequence of development: although the Buddha is constantly in meditative concentration, when the various sentient beings (the *jī* or capacities) strike upon him, the Buddha desires to respond to them, and thus he manifests the formal ritual procedures (*vidhi*).

The Tathāgata is eternally quiescent and yet still delights in meditative concentration; he enters the Dharma-nature and emerges to expound the King of Sutras. When Śraddhālinga heard this profound Dharma, he doubted that if the Dharma is eternal, how could the human lifespan be so short?
For this reason, they harbored doubts.

Through the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit, these doubts were able to evoke a response; because of that response, the four Buddhas appeared. As the Buddhas appeared, the doubts were dispelled; as the doubts were dispelled, the Buddhas ceased [the manifestation]. Since the rain of Dharma was about to fall, the great assembly gathered like clouds.
The seven matters differ from other sūtras; therefore, they are called "distinct.
The explanation of the seven distinctions is complete.
At times, they are arranged as three distinctions:
First, from "At that time" onwards is called the Narrative Introduction;
second, from the "Chapter on Lifespan" onwards is called the Introduction of Manifesting Auspicious Omens;
third, from "Then the four Tathāgatas" onwards is the Introduction of the Assembly of the Multitude, and so forth.
Regarding the statement "narrating the introduction," this refers to the narration of the subsequent seventeen chapters.
The first five lines narrate the *Jiuliang pin* (Chapter on the Lifespan) in three parts:
the first two lines narrate the fruit-virtue; the next one line narrates the arising of doubt; and the final two lines narrate the severing of doubt. These may be sought in detail.
The following one and a half lines describe the intent of the "Chapter on Repentance" (*Chānhuǐpǐn*) regarding the destruction of evil and the generation of goodness, and so forth.
The subsequent one and a half lines describe the "Chapter on Praise" (*Zàntànpǐn*) regarding the generation of goodness and the destruction of evil, and so forth.
The following six lines describe the refutation of the three obstacles among the refutations of evil in the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-parivarta*), and so forth.
From the section beginning with "The Four World-Protecting Kings" (*Lokapāla-caturmahārāja*) onwards is the description; this chapter is easy to understand.
"Mahāprajñā" (Great Eloquence) refers to its chapter; "Nirgranthī Mātṛ" (Mother of the Nirgrantha Ghosts) refers to the "Chapter on Guṇakaraṇḍavyūha," as both are female deities.
"Earth Deity" refers to its chapter; "Mahābrahmā and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" refers to the "Chapter on Saṃjñeya."
Vajrapāṇi is the general and Brahmā and Śakra are the lords; by mentioning the lords, one thereby includes their ministers and generals.
The kiṃnaras and others are those under their command; by mentioning those under command, one thereby includes their subordinates.

Regarding the phrase "The secrets of all Buddhas that I now proclaim," this refers to the two chapters, "The Right Discourse" (Zhenglun) and "The Well-Assembled" (Shanji). It explains that worldly secrets can be used to govern a state, while supramundane secrets can lead one to the Path; thus, it is known that these two chapters are being referred to.
"If one is able to hear this sutra" introduces the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits.
Within the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits," it is explained exclusively that the merit of hearing the Dharma consists in being protected by the eight classes of beings, and so forth.
The two lines beginning with "Donning pure garments" describe the "Chapter on Prophecy.
Because the three great bodhisattvas and ten thousand devas possessed minds of profound sincerity and purity as vast as space, they received their prophecies.

It is not that the principle illuminated by the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*) of those of the Two Vehicles constitutes the *dharmatā*.
Because the *dharmatā* of the Two Vehicles is shallow, it is not profound;

The principle illuminated by the present *yathābhūta-jñāna* (knowledge of reality as it is) encompasses the dharma-realm horizontally and penetrates the three truths vertically; therefore, it is said to be "immeasurable" and "profound.
Furthermore, regarding "immeasurable," there is no separate dharma that exists independently named "the immeasurable."

Vairocana pervades all places; all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, and because they are all the Buddha-dharma, they are all the dharma-nature (dharmatā). Since the Buddhas traverse them all, it is said to be immeasurable.
Furthermore, there is no separate dharma that can be called "profound.

Reality is present within phenomena themselves; nothing is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way. Because they are all the Middle Way, they are profound.

For example, the *Vyākhyā* (Śāstra) explains the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) as follows: "Taking sentient beings of the eastern direction as its object is called 'vast' (*vipula*); taking those of the four cardinal directions as its object is called 'great' (*mahat*); and taking those of the four intermediate directions, above, and below as its object is called 'immeasurable' (*apramāṇa*)."

According to this principle, that which takes the dharma-nature of ultimate truth as its object is called "vast" (prthu); that which takes the dharma-nature of conventional truth as its object is called "great" (mahat); and that which takes the dharma-nature of the Middle Way as its object is called "immeasurable" (apramāṇa).

If one takes the Middle Way as the object of cognition, this is precisely the three knowledges taking their objects within a single moment of mind; it is the three truths as one truth. This realm is immeasurable, and only the immeasurable wisdom of a Buddha can take it as its object, like a box and its lid fitting perfectly together.
The two vehicles and those of the lower stages cannot fathom its limits or depths.
Regarding the phrase "the sphere of action of all Buddhas," this precisely reveals that the Buddha's wisdom is immeasurable and profoundly deep.

Because the Buddha's wisdom is immeasurable and profound, his sphere of action is likewise immeasurable and profound; because his sphere of action is immeasurable and profound, the Buddha's wisdom is also immeasurable and profound.
Raising the box reveals the lid; raising the lid reveals the box—this is precisely what is meant here.

Because Bodhisattvas dwell on a stage not yet reached and their practice of wisdom is not yet profound or vast.

"If one enters the ninth stage of the pure-pure dhyāna (*śuddha-śuddha-dhyāna*), all afflictions—both the universal and the particular, as well as their active manifestations (*vāsanā*) and residual habits—are entirely exhausted; therefore, it is called the pure-pure dhyāna.
From the stages below this, there remain residual habits; the Buddha abides at the summit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi-śikhara*), and if he enters this dhyāna, he transcends all bodhisattvas.

The section beginning with "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*... is the preface.

The first twelve and a half lines describe the name, essence, principle, and function; the subsequent fourteen and a half lines describe the circulation and wide propagation of this scripture, which constitutes the exposition of the doctrinal characteristics.

As for the "King of Sutras," it has already been explained above; now it is restated once more.

"The present sutra is universally intended for people of eight stages; therefore, it is called a 'king' [of sutras].

Since the assembly listening to this Dharma are not beings subject to birth and death, how could it merely be intended to dispel the attachments of ordinary worldlings?

To make such a partial interpretation would cause those without wisdom to give rise to contempt for the various sūtras, which is an unacceptable position.
Now, regarding what is called the "King of Sutras": if one takes the words as the sutra, it constitutes the three kinds of conventional truth;
if one takes the principle as the sutra, it constitutes the three kinds of ultimate truth;
if one takes the union of words and principle as the sutra, it constitutes the three kinds of the Middle Way.
If it speaks of other truths, it is a sūtra but not a king;
if it speaks of the Middle Way, it is both a sūtra and a king, attaining sovereignty among the nine types of sūtras.
However, while this King of Sutras is one, its names differ according to the conditions for which the teachings were established.

The *Avataṃsaka* calls it the Dharma-body; the Vaipulya sutras refer to it as the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); the *Prajñāpāramitā* titles it the Mother of Buddhas; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* regards it as the crest-jewel; and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* names it the Teacher of Buddhas. These are all alternative names for the Dharma-nature, serving collectively as the essence of all sutras.

For example, just as various dynasties arise in succession, with dragon-kings, sages, and bird-officials each establishing their hegemony in turn according to the times— though the hundred generations differ, the sovereign who rules remains one—
so too is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
It is fitting that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Mother of Buddhas, should be the sovereign, while other names are set aside.
It is fitting that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Precious Place, should be the sovereign, while other names are set aside.
The Dharma-nature as the King of the Golden Light is likewise so.
If one understands it in this way, above, it does not fail to capture the intent of the King of the Buddha’s sutras; below, it does not increase the conceit of sentient beings.
Regarding the term "subtle and wondrous" (*sūkṣma-udāra*): other commentators explain that the cause is subtle and the fruit is wondrous.
