Within the cause, the intrinsic qualities (*dharmatā-guṇa*) are profound and difficult to perceive, which is termed "subtle"; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, which is termed "wondrous. The cultivated qualities (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) within the fruit are likewise so.
Regarding "the four Buddhas of the four directions provide protection and support": the "four directions" refers to the four gates.
The "four Buddhas" refers to the awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*) manifested upon the fruition at each of the four gates.

The awakened wisdom of Śākyamuni is identical to that of the four Buddhas; the resultant wisdom of all Buddhas merges with the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and when this dharma-nature is made manifest, it is called the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
That the Dharma-body is immovable is what is termed "sustaining" (dhṛti).

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternal, all Buddhas are also eternal. Since the Dharma is eternal and the Buddha is eternal, his lifespan is also eternal; being eternal, it is immeasurable.
Xinxiang (Belief in Signs) inferred from the traces or the source; the four Buddhas caused him to penetrate the source and awaken to the traces, which is termed "protection" (*hù*).

This single phrase contains manifold meanings: the four gates of the dharma-nature and the four virtues of the dharma-nature constitute the meaning of its essence (*tī*); the manifestation of the essence through resultant wisdom constitutes the meaning of its thesis (*zōng*); and being mindful of [the practitioner], the signs of faith, and the severing of doubt constitute the meaning of its function (*yòng*). However, the exposition of the thesis is intended as the primary purport.
Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the four directions are the Four Noble Truths, and the four Buddhas are the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths.
The east is the beginning of the directions, just as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya*) is the cause of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, in the east, the months of Jia and Yi represent spring and birth; this "birth" is precisely the Truth of Origination.

From the east, one proceeds next to the south; this is like birth followed by growth, where spring comes first and summer follows. Therefore, the south represents the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
After growth comes the autumn harvest, and furthermore, the White Emperor belongs to Metal; since Metal is capable of decisive judgment, the west represents the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
From the autumn harvest until the winter storage, all activities come to rest; the northern direction is like the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The causes and effects of suffering and its origin have both faded away and are no longer functional.

By contemplating these Four Truths, one gives rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening; because one maintains the principle without loss and guards against the arising of perversions, it is called "guarding and maintaining" (*ārakṣā*).

Furthermore, one contemplates the four directions as the four virtues: contemplating permanence in the east is for the purpose of destroying impermanence; contemplating impermanence is for the purpose of destroying permanence; and contemplating that which is neither permanent nor impermanent is for the purpose of destroying both permanence and impermanence. This applies likewise up to the north, where contemplating non-self is for the purpose of destroying self.
Because this contemplation maintains virtue without loss and guards against the arising of perversions, it is called "guarding and maintaining" (huchí).
Because one contemplates that the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) in the eastern direction is neither permanent nor impermanent, and is immovable, it is named Akṣobhya.

Contemplating the southern direction, one observes the Truth of Suffering as the blissful reality of phenomena, which neither comes nor goes; because this true mark (dharmatā-lakṣaṇa) is most noble, it is called the "Treasure Mark" (Ratnalakṣaṇa).
Contemplating the western direction, one observes the Truth of the Path as ultimately pure; because the life-span of its dharmatā is equal to space, it is called "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus).

"Contemplating the northern direction as the extinction-truth (nirodha-satya) of eternal stillness, I enter the secret treasury; because it is the secret treasury, it is called the Sublime Sound," and so forth.
The nine lines of verse beginning with "I shall now speak" constitute the section on application.
The text consists of four parts:

the first three lines clarify the superior dharma that can destroy [the afflictions]; the next three and a half lines clarify the evil transgressions to be destroyed; the next one and a half lines set forth the method of practice and exhortation to cultivate it; and the final line provides the conclusion.
The first three lines clarify the supreme dharmas capable of destruction: the dharma of the object refers to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
the dharma of practice refers to repentance and praise;
and the dharma of guidance refers to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Therefore, when we speak of practices such as repentance (*pratikramana*), we know that they are not of a single kind.

If we discuss them in terms of mutual support: practice supports wisdom; wisdom reveals the principle (*tattva*); because the principle is revealed, one is able to exhaust all suffering; because suffering is exhausted, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is manifested; because wisdom is perfected, the Reward-body (*sambhogakāya*) is manifested; and because merit is unsurpassed, the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is manifested.

If one speaks according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), the three dharmas are cultivated neither vertically nor horizontally, and the three bodies (trikāya) likewise manifest neither vertically nor horizontally.
Although there is a distinction between the Perfect and the Separate Teachings, both are supreme dharmas capable of shattering [delusion].

Observing that the language of the old text was abbreviated, the new version contains the full account of the three cycles of teaching: the four Buddhas preach the fruit of permanence, whereby those of superior faculties benefit;
the Brahmin preaches that the Dharma-body has no *śarīra*, whereby those of middling faculties benefit;
and the Buddha distinguishes the three bodies, whereby those of inferior faculties benefit.
The current preface states, "I shall now expound the dharmas of repentance and so forth," which refers to the methods of the subsequent three assemblies that are capable of destroying evil.
Next, from the passage beginning with "those with impaired faculties," the *Śūnyatā-parivarta* (Chapter on Emptiness) is introduced.
The text consists of two parts:
the first three and a half lines clarify the evil that is to be destroyed, and the subsequent two and a half lines clarify the method by which it is destroyed.
The first part is further divided into three sections:

The phrase "deficiency of the sense faculties" below refutes the obstacle of retribution; the single phrase "grief and anxiety" refutes the obstacle of affliction; and the section beginning with "malevolent stars and calamitous anomalies" refutes the obstacle of karma.

Other sutras state regarding conditions that the obstacle of retribution (vipāka-āvaraṇa) is difficult to transform; it may be remedied during the causal stage, but once the fruit has manifested, there is nothing that can be done.
This sutra, however, states that all three obstacles can be transformed.
To explain these three obstacles briefly: they arise from the violation of the five precepts.

Violating the five precepts constitutes the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*); receiving rebirth in the three miserable realms or as a human or celestial being constitutes the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*); and afflictions (*kleśa*) as the root constitute the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Now, to clarify directly within the context of the human realm the retribution for violating the five precepts: externally, one’s sensory faculties are deficient; internally, one’s lifespan is cut short.
These two phrases refer to the retribution for killing: having harmed another's body in the past, one's own faculties are now impaired;
having severed another's life in the past, one's own lifespan is now diminished.
The Sūtra states: "By the causes and conditions of killing, one receives two kinds of retributive fruits: much illness and a short life.
This refers precisely to such matters.
If one suffers from poverty and hardship, this constitutes the external lack of supportive retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
The various devas abandon him; this indicates an internal lack of merit.
These two phrases refer to the violation of the precept against stealing.
The Sūtra says: "There are devas and nāgas born together with him and sharing his name who assist him, and the goddess Guṇakārandhāvatī makes a vow to benefit him."
"A thief does not do such a thing.
Furthermore, one who was formerly wealthy but later becomes poor must surely have been abandoned by the *nāgas* and forsaken by the gods.
If there is internal strife among close kin and external pressure from royal law—these two conditions constitute a violation of the precept against sexual misconduct."
The Sūtra says: "If one protects a person, that person will become resentful; if one protects the Dharma, the Dharma will be destroyed.
In the past, one encroached upon another's person, and now their own flesh and bone fight and litigate;
in the past, one defiled another's Dharma, and now the royal law is brought against them."
This refers precisely to that matter.
Each person becomes angry and quarrels; this should consist of two phrases, though perhaps they were omitted by the translator or were simply abbreviated.
Internally, each person quarrels; externally, everyone lacks faith—this pair constitutes the offense of lying.
In the past, one deceived others with falsehoods; now, one is constantly deceived and provoked to anger.
In the past, one’s speech lacked substance; now, no one places trust in one.
To squander wealth and property externally, and to fail in propriety and decorum internally—this is the retribution for drinking alcohol.
In the past, you were arrogant and squandered your days; now, much has been wasted.
Formerly, you lacked moderation; now, you have fallen into deafness and stupidity.
As the Sūtra says, "The fierce winds of resentment and hatred blow upon the fire of the sinful mind, constantly causing it to blaze," this is precisely what that refers to.
Question:
When explaining Mahāyāna sūtras, why can the five precepts be used as a point of correspondence?
Answer:
The opening and closing of the five precepts are of great significance. The *Tiwèi jīng* states:

"The five precepts are the great prohibitions of heaven and earth; above they correspond to the five stars, below they are matched with the five sacred peaks, and in the middle they constitute the five viscera."
"Those who violate these offend Heaven and provoke Earth, thereby destroying their own persons. Furthermore, in relation to the Five Constant Virtues:

not killing corresponds to benevolence (ren); not stealing corresponds to righteousness (yi); not committing sexual misconduct corresponds to propriety (li); not drinking alcohol corresponds to wisdom (zhi); and not speaking falsely corresponds to trustworthiness (xin).

Furthermore, in relation to the Five Classics: abstaining from killing corresponds to the *Shangshu*; abstaining from stealing corresponds to the *Chunqiu*; abstaining from sexual misconduct corresponds to the *Liji*; abstaining from false speech corresponds to the *Shijing*; and abstaining from drinking alcohol corresponds to the *Yijing*.

Furthermore, in relation to the ten wholesome actions, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three of the body; false speech subsumes the four of the mouth; and drinking alcohol subsumes the three of the mind.
Since laypeople are unable to guard their speech fully, they are briefly restricted to the single precept of not engaging in false speech.
The *Śāstra* states: "To speak with emphasis constitutes false speech," which already subsumes three [of the precepts].
Drinking alcohol constitutes wrong livelihood for one's own sustenance, and it increases hatred and delusion.

Transcendence takes wisdom as its foremost element, while birth and death take the three poisons as their root; if one can abstain from alcohol, this prevents the three poisons of the mental ground and nurtures transcendental wisdom.
This constitutes the opening of the five precepts to reveal the ten wholesome actions.

These ten wholesome actions were employed by the ancient Wheel-Turning Kings; they are also termed natural offenses and natural virtues, and together they constitute the very root of all transgressions.

Furthermore, the five precepts correspond to the five aggregates (*skandhas*): non-killing corresponds to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); non-stealing corresponds to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); non-sexual misconduct corresponds to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); non-lying corresponds to the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and non-drinking of intoxicants corresponds to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

The five aggregates open the way to the four foundations of mindfulness; the foundations of mindfulness open the way to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the thirty-seven factors open the way to the three gates of liberation; and the three gates of liberation open the way to nirvana. Therefore, it is said that form can give rise to precepts, sensation receives meditative concentration, perception awakens to wisdom and its pervasive penetration, volitional formations give rise to liberation, and consciousness is itself knowledge and vision.
One should know that the five precepts can accomplish the fivefold Dharma-body and bring about the dharmas of the Two Vehicles.

Furthermore, the five precepts are also a Mahāyāna gateway; the *Tiwai jing* states, "The five precepts are the talisman for longevity and the seal of immortality," which refers to the constant virtue (*nitya-dharma*).
"Entering and exiting without confusion, coming and going without interval" refers to the virtue of purity (*śubha*).
"Governing the single body" refers to the virtue of self (*ātman*).
"Thereby establishing the root of the Way" refers to the virtue of bliss (*sukha*).
These five precepts correspond to the four virtues.

When the five precepts are condensed into the three karmas, they correspond to such infinite triads of dharmas as the three absences of error, the three absences of need for protection, the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels, the three secrets, the three tracks, the three bodies, the three Buddha-natures, the three types of prajñā, the three nirvāṇas, the three knowledges, and the three virtues. These are boundless both horizontally and vertically, equal to empty space and the dharma-realm; they are also the dharma-gate of the inexhaustible treasury and the samādhi of immeasurable meanings.
To state it briefly, this is precisely all the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, "harming" refers to the activity of killing, while "not harming" refers to the activity of not killing.
Regarding the interpretation of the Dharma-gate: analyzing phenomena is termed the principle of killing, while embodying phenomena is termed the principle of non-killing.
One should know that the precept against killing has various different forms, and its retributive fruits likewise differ.

If one maintains protection through conscious intent—like a horse wearing a bridle or a cowherd holding a staff—the retribution is a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years within the human realm; however, one obtains only the fleshly eye and not the four eyes.

If one’s spontaneous nature is such that it flows like a river into the ocean, the retribution is rebirth in the six heavens; at the longest, for nine hundred twenty-six billion seven hundred million years, during which one attains only the divine eye but not the three eyes.

If one further cultivates the guest precepts and the wisdom of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth, the retribution will be in the realm of transformation, with a lifespan of seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas; yet one will only attain the eye of wisdom and not yet the two eyes.

If one further cultivates wisdom regarding the permanent and the impermanent, the retribution will be rebirth in the Lotus Treasury Ocean to receive the Dharma-nature body, partially attaining the five eyes and partially attaining eternal life.
Compared to the Buddha, even these [bodhisattvas] still possess incomplete faculties and diminished lifespans; how much more so was this the case for those of former times?

As for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), they uphold the conventional precept against killing and also uphold the ultimate precept against killing. They do not destroy the body while conforming to the single mark (ekalakṣaṇa); they do not sever delusion and craving, yet they give rise to illumination and liberation. They realize that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are beyond injury or harm; whether as cause or as fruit, they are neither born nor extinguished. Having perfected wisdom, they dwell in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, where their lifespan is eternally profound and their five eyes are fully possessed. They attain mastery over the faculties, such that the ears see and the eyes hear; they attain mastery over life, freely determining its length. This is called the ultimate upholding of the precepts, wherein all faculties are complete and the lifespan is undiminished.

Furthermore, for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), how could it be that upholding this constitutes precept-keeping solely through physical killing and physical compassion? They also practice "killing according to phenomena" (shisha) and "killing according to principle" (lisha).
For example, when King Xianyu killed five hundred Brahmins, he bestowed upon them the eye to see the Buddha and granted them a lifespan of ten kalpas.

Furthermore, as for "killing" through the Dharma-gate, it means to dismantle and wash away accumulated attachments, thereby purifying all afflictions; it is like a tree spirit breaking off a branch so that the resentful bird no longer dwells there, or like a kalpa-fire burning wood until both ash and charcoal have vanished.

Therefore, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states: "I vow to sever the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*, *āyatanāni*), yet I cannot maintain the precept against killing.

All afflictions (*kleśa*) are the seeds of the Tathāgata; when these seeds are completely severed, one is called a Buddha, having accomplished the subtle and wondrous Vajra-Dharmakāya, which responds to all things with profound stillness.

Manifesting only through killing or only through compassion, he assumes forms within the nine realms of existence; according to what is appropriate for each, he displays long or short lifespans, and in accordance with their various perceptions, he employs deficient or complete faculties to transform and deliver them.
The various precepts and practices mentioned previously were shallow, limited, and obstructed; they were not the universal path.
Perfect precepts are vast and far-reaching, their direct route differing yet ultimately converging with others; therefore, this is called the ultimate observance of the precept against killing.

Regarding the precept against killing, from the realms of humans and devas up to the ultimate state of Buddhahood, its vast and all-encompassing significance is such as this; how, then, can it be called a teaching of the Lesser Vehicle?
Furthermore, taking what is not given is theft; taking what is given is not theft.
Regarding the explanation of this dharma-gate, as the Buddha said:
"Do not take the property of others; this is called the dharma-gate of non-theft."
"To take awakening when there is no one who bestows it upon one—this is called 'stealing the Dharma-gate. The precepts against stealing differ in their various forms;

yet if one observes the precepts and performs actions seeking agreeable fruits, those agreeable fruits are impermanent and quickly decay, being entirely the property of others. They are as foul-smelling as dung-fruit and as harmful as poisoned food; they are not things that a person of wisdom should seek. Even if one were to obtain them, the mind would find no pleasure in them. Why then should one diligently drink bitterness and eat poison, thereby bringing harm and injury upon oneself?
The poverty of the four castes is precisely the suffering of the swirling currents within these three realms; how could it exceed the flow of existence?
These three obstacles obstruct the Buddha and are abandoned by the Heaven of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*); this is what is called "theft," and not non-theft.

Furthermore, when those of the Two Vehicles contemplate the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena through the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, they come to loathe birth and death and long for Nirvana. When this mind for Nirvana arises—whether for oneself, for others, for both, or without cause—the mere stirring of such a thought constitutes taking another's property; it is taking at an improper time.
Realization does not depend on verbal explanation that "burnt seeds do not sprout.
To perceive suffering, abandon its origin, cultivate the path, and achieve exhaustion is not the seeking of the Dharma;
rather, it is called having a view of nirvāṇa because one conceptualizes the existence of nirvāṇa.

If there are those who cling to emptiness, they are not delivered by the Buddhas; though their bodies are three hundred yojanas tall, they lack two wings. They fall into the pit of the three unconditioned states and undergo suffering like that of death or equal to death.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Starving, emaciated, and with sores and scabs breaking out on the body"—is this not the suffering of poverty?

The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Not seeing the Buddha, not hearing the Dharma, and not being included among the ranks of the assembly"—is this not the transcendence of the ultimate heaven (*paramārtha-deva*)?
This is still called stealing; it is not non-stealing.

If a Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching follows the gradual practice, gradual study, and gradual path, abandoning one thing while grasping another from the shallow to the deep—coming again after having come, and going again after having gone—all this is to humiliate the characteristics of coming and going, and it is likewise taking what is not given.
To take and then discard is also poverty.
To discard and then take again—this repeated cycle of taking and discarding is suffering and affliction.
Not being in accord with the primary truth (paramārtha) is itself separation.
This is still called stealing; it is not non-stealing.

A person of perfect realization contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena: they neither accept nor do they not accept; they neither accept nor do they not accept; they neither both accept and not accept nor do they not accept; and they neither accept nor do they not accept—yet even this they do not accept.
Neither receiving nor not receiving—this non-grasping is bodhi, for it obstructs all vows.
This Dharma is equal, without high or low; because it is not high, one does not grasp, and because it is not low, one does not abandon.

One who contemplates in this manner perceives the Tathāgatagarbha as complete and without deficiency; it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel that produces treasures at will, or like a cīṇāra lute that emits sounds according to one's desire—it is indeed great wealth.

Because of great wealth, there is no grasping; because there is no grasping, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); because it is the ultimate truth, the heavens do not distance themselves from one. This is called the ultimate observance of the precept against stealing.

The person of perfect enlightenment further possesses the dharma-gate of "stealing": although there is no one to bestow it upon him, he takes up bodhi. Like the ocean swallowing all streams without distinguishing between ten thousand tributaries, and like the earth bearing its fourfold burden, he delivers all sentient beings, severs all afflictions, fully knows all dharma-gates, and completely accomplishes the Buddha-way; this meaning may be understood, though it cannot be explained at length.
The various precepts and practices mentioned previously are shallow and obstructed; they do not constitute the universal path.

The perfect precepts (pariśuddha-śīla) are vast and far-reaching, their direct route differing yet ultimately converging with others; therefore, they are called the ultimate observance of the precept against stealing.
Furthermore, the physical union of male and female bodies is called sexual misconduct; their non-union is called non-sexual misconduct.
Regarding the interpretation of the Dharma-gate: if the mind is defiled by dharmas, it is called sexual misconduct; if the mind is not defiled by dharmas, it is called non-sexual misconduct.

The precepts against sexual misconduct vary in their specific formulations. If one strictly prohibits the seven branches [of misconduct] like a monkey bound by chains, or carries a bowl of oil through a great assembly, or renounces tactile pleasure to seek pure sensual desires in the future—like the method of bartering in a marketplace where one exchanges copper coins for gold coins—this merely increases the affairs of desire; it is not the absence of desire.

If one observes the precepts for the sake of rebirth in heaven, it is like two rams butting heads: as they advance, they retreat again. Śakra, together with eighty billion nayutas of celestial maidens, indulges in unrestrained play;

looking east, he forgets the west, yet his desire remains insatiable. He transforms himself into the aged asura Nala-kūbara to cause the gods to lose their bodies and heads; furthermore, seeing a rishi enter meditative absorption, he defiles and mocks his daughter. When the rishi emerges from concentration, Śakra is ashamed and transforms himself into a ram. The rishi casts a spell upon him, and a thousand horns grow upon his body that cannot be removed. Later, after he repents and apologizes, they transform into a thousand eyes. This, too, is an increase of desire, not a lack thereof.

If one cuts off the coarse and base desires of the desire realm but becomes stained by attachment to the bliss of meditative concentration in the form and formless realms—like a fish in ice or a hibernating insect falling into the Heaven of Long Life—this is the first difficulty.
To be greedily attached to the flavor of meditative absorption is called a great bondage; it is a dharma of defiled desire, not the absence of desire.

If one loathes birth and death as one would an enemy or a serpent, cherishing *nirvāṇa* as a kinsman or a treasure, and casting them aside to go directly forward on the path without turning back, then all forms and sounds will be unable to defile or subdue one, just as the winds from the eight directions cannot move Mount Sumeru.
If one hears of the sublime and wondrous merits of a bodhisattva, it is like the sound of the kiṃnara lute, causing Kāśyapa to rise and dance, unable to restrain himself;
or like the Sārathi wind arriving, which shatters Mount Sumeru like rotten grass—this is the nature of defiled desire, not the absence of defilement.

If a bodhisattva loathes saṃsāra as if it were excrement and loathes nirvāṇa as if it were a predatory bird, abandoning both extremes and setting his will upon the Middle Way, yet gives rise to a craving for dharmas that accord with the Path, this is called "falling from the summit" (mūrdha-pāta); such a person is a *caṇḍāla* among bodhisattvas.

Since there is no skillful means, this wisdom is bound and cannot overcome the enemy; what one has cultivated and refined thus lacks the benefit of wisdom, being a dharma of defiled desire rather than a state free from desire.
The person of perfect capacity contemplates the three truths within one mind as being simultaneously empty, simultaneously provisional, and simultaneously the Middle.
Being simultaneously empty, what is there to be defiled?
Being simultaneously provisional, what is there to be purified?
What "middle" could there be within that?
Since it is emptiness and it is the provisional, what "middle" could there be?

Because it is emptiness, there is no attachment to self, person, the sixteen views, or the environment and its inhabitants; because it is the provisional, there is no attachment to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and so forth; because it is the middle, there is no attachment to the Buddha, Bodhi, turning the wheel of Dharma, or saving sentient beings. The purity of these three truths is called ultimate purity; this purity is itself pure.
The Sūtra states: "Only the Buddha alone possesses pure precepts; all others are called those who defile the precepts.
When one of the Perfect Person (yuanren) practices within the Buddha-dharma, this is precisely the ultimate observance of the precept against sexual misconduct.

The person of perfect capacity (*yuanren*) also possesses dharma-gates of passionate attachment. For example, regarding the woman Vāsavadattā: when humans see her, they see a human woman; when devas see her, they see a celestial woman. Those who see her attain the samādhi of seeing all Buddhas; those who hold her hand attain the samādhi of reaching Buddha-lands; those who kiss her attain the samādhi of ultimate love; and those who embrace her attain the samādhi of profound darkness. Each and every one of them attains a dharma-gate.

It is also like the Bodhisattva *Māragocarānupaliptaśīla*, who transforms himself into immeasurable bodies and engages with immeasurable celestial maidens, causing them all to resolve upon *bodhicitta*.
Just as when Vimalakīrti enters the inner palace, he transforms the principal ladies of the harem.

First, he draws them in with the hook of desire, and afterwards leads them into the Buddha-way. This is indeed the "desire of non-desire," using desire to cease desire—just as one uses grit to remove grit, or uses sound to silence sound.
The aforementioned various practices are superficial and obstructed; they do not constitute the universal path.
Perfect precepts are vast and far-reaching, their direct route differing yet ultimately converging with the assembly; this is called the ultimate observance of the precept against sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, to say one has seen what one has not seen, or to say one has not seen what one has seen, is called lying regarding facts.
Regarding the understanding of the Dharma-gate, to claim one has attained what one has not attained, or to claim one has realized what one has not realized, is called lying.

Lying is of many kinds: when one seeks sensual desires, there is suffering; when one obtains them, there is much fear; when one loses them, one harbors grief and affliction. There is never a time when sensual desires bring joy.

Yet foolish worldlings, amidst this base suffering, perversely give rise to the notion of pleasure; they erect the banner of *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am") and beat the drum of self-aggrandizement, saying, "Form is the self, the self is form; the self is within form, form is within the self. Clinging to existence, they fight with non-existence; clinging to non-existence, they fight with existence. Relying on the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, they give rise to the sixty-two types of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), destroying the eye of wisdom so that they do not see reality. Their views increase and their various errors grow; the poison of the ego is most virulent, and they are fully equipped with the four faults of speech. This is a brief indication of lying.

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three perceive the yellow leaves of birth and death as being true gold; those in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, possessing the subtle afflictions of their own stage, mistakenly reckon it to be nirvana. This is not a false statement—what, then, would be a false statement?

The followers of the Two Vehicles vie with one another to grasp at tiles and pebbles, joyfully carrying them out and conceiving the thought that they have attained nirvana; yet their births are not yet exhausted—how could they have attained nirvana?
They conceive the thought of peace and security, but what remains to be accomplished has not been finished—how could they have attained peace and security?

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "For those with overweening pride, the Buddha teaches that being free from lust, anger, and delusion is called liberation; yet in reality, they have not attained complete liberation."
"To claim what has not been attained as having been attained—is this not false speech?

The Buddha, for the sake of instructing people through distinct approaches, taught the true reality (*tathatā*) by means of four gates; yet some cling to "existence" alone, thereby obstructing the other three gates, even to the point of clinging to "neither existence nor non-existence" while obstructing both existence and non-existence.
Now, as for true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases; how can one use words to designate that which is wordless?
How can one use numbers to count that which is numberless?
Is this not false speech?
One of perfect realization observes according to reality and speaks according to reality.

As for observing according to reality: this liberation is not attained through internal observation, nor through external observation, nor through both internal and external observation, nor by being apart from internal and external observation; furthermore, it is not attained through non-observation.
To speak according to reality: all is real, all is unreal, all is both real and unreal, and all is neither real nor unreal; such as these are called the true mark of all dharmas.
The Sūtra says: "All Buddhas speak only truth; the Buddha’s words are real and not false.
With a single sublime voice, he fills the trichiliocosm; wherever it reaches according to his will, it is understood by each and every class of sentient beings."
This is precisely using the sound of the Buddha-way to cause all to hear.

Even for those of perfect capacity (*yuanren*), there is a dharma-gate of false speech: one speaks of a chariot where there is no chariot to entice and play with a young child, or speaks of joy where there is no joy to stop a crying infant.
If there are sentient beings who derive benefit from false speech, the Buddha also speaks falsely.
As the Sūtra says: "I am the Śrī of lust, I am the Śrī of hatred, and I am the Śrī of delusion; yet in reality, this is not so."
"I am a deva, I am a human; yet in truth, I am neither deva nor human.
I am a nāga, I am a ghost; yet in truth, I am neither nāga nor ghost.
By means of the void, I bring forth the void, so that there may be that which is not void."
The preceding practices were shallow, limited, and obstructed;

the perfect practice is profound and far-reaching, level and unimpeded. Because it passes through differences to achieve harmony, it is able to be thus; this is called the ultimate observance of the precept against false speech.
Furthermore, if grain or grass causes the mind to become clouded and disoriented, it is called "substantial alcohol" (*vastu-madya*).
For one who understands the Dharma-gate, delusion and inverted views are what are termed "alcohol."

Perverted views are manifold; indeed, alcohol is the root of all that is unwholesome and evil, capable of producing thirty-six kinds of faults. It brings about the loss of hands for five hundred lifetimes, incurs legal punishment, causes the loss of propriety, and brings forth hidden vices. One may fall asleep amidst filth, or stumble into fire and water. Such are its calamities and afflictions, yet people still indulge in it.

In the Jin dynasty, those who could draw their bows to the full were celebrated for their skill; in the Wei court, those who drank clear or turbid wine were deemed sages or worthies. Bi Zhuo styled himself a "drunken companion," and Zheng Quan vowed to become a "wine jar. These matters are recorded on bamboo and silk and sung of by people past and present. To compose such works when one ought not to, and to sing such songs when one ought not to—were these not simply the acts of those intoxicated with wine? What else could they have been?
The *Śāstra* states: "There was a Dharma Master who explained the offenses and blessings of the five precepts to a king.
The king raised an objection, saying:
'Drinking alcohol invites madness, yet those who drink are very numerous; why is it that those who become mad are so few?'"
The Dharma Master merely raised his hand toward the various non-Buddhists and said nothing further.
The non-Buddhists, acting with arrogance, declared:
"The King’s question was most profound; this bald man on his high seat cannot answer it."
The King said, "The Dharma Master has finished his reply.
There are not few who are mad; I am pointing you all out as such."
"This is simply because you do not manifest the protection [of the mind]. This is precisely the intoxication of worldly people.

Furthermore, greed is like the ocean that receives all streams yet never reaches fullness; hatred is like fire to which fuel is added, growing ever more intense; and delusion is like sticky glue, congealing like ice upon water. The eighty thousand afflictions of *kleśa* never allow the mind to rest for even a moment; like the flickering tongue of a lightning-serpent or a leaping monkey, the five desires stir the mind so that there is no time when one is not intoxicated.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "From time immemorial, we have been constantly intoxicated by sounds and forms, wandering through birth and death.
This intoxication is common to all beings within the three realms, including humans and devas.

If those of the Two Vehicles, although they have severed the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) and the four abiding afflictions (*catur-vāsana*), have not yet expelled ignorance, they are like a person suffering from half-remitted malaria.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* cites the analogy of a person returning home while intoxicated.

The world is impermanent and lacks bliss, yet they claim it is self and pure; the Tathāgata is truly self and pure, yet they claim he is impermanent and lacks bliss—this is the intoxication of those of the Two Vehicles, like that man who, being drunk, sees the sun and moon revolving.

For a bodhisattva, because ignorance has not been exhausted, they do not see with perfect clarity; because they are practicing the path of a bodhisattva, their vision is not fully clear—just as one sees a large ship from afar, or gazes at geese and swans from a distance, or views a painted image at night, or looks at a person crossing a bridge from afar, or like a drunkard seeing the road through a blur.
Through such immeasurable parables as these, it is revealed that the Bodhisattva had not yet attained clear understanding.
Therefore, Kāśyapa said:
"From this point onward, we were all known as people of false views."
"This bodhisattva is intoxicated.

One who practices the path of the Perfect Man (yuanren) follows the conduct of the Tathāgata; though possessing the nature of afflictions, they are able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. Although they possess the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye; that which can be seen by it is such that there is nothing further to be seen."
Therefore, the text says: "Entering the profound Dharma-nature, one shall behold me, Śākyamuni, within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "One clearly perceives the Buddha-nature, just as [the Bodhisattvas] such as Samantabhadra do."
"Thus, the five abodes and their residual habits are simultaneously eliminated without remainder.
Once the nature of alcohol is removed, what is there to intoxicate?
This is the ultimate observance of the precept against drinking alcohol."

Even for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanren), there is a dharma-gate of drinking alcohol; the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "Holding the flask of true emptiness and filling it with the wine of real marks, one manifests transformations throughout the five realms of existence to proclaim the great roar."
King Prasenajit was intoxicated, yet his favor increased all the more.
When Queen Mallikā drank, the Buddha said she maintained the precepts.
She entered the wine shops, establishing her own resolve and establishing the resolve of others as well.
Those who find the gate find that both the contrary and the compliant are appropriate; those who lose the handle find their hands wounded by the blade.

Previous practices were shallow, narrow, and obstructed, whereas the perfect practice is vast and far-reaching, its path distinct yet its convergence identical. It is because of this that one can achieve such a state, which is called the ultimate realization that intoxication and sobriety are non-dual.
The wisdom that contemplates the Four Truths above is called the four Buddhas.
How does one contemplate the five Buddhas?
One contemplates the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the five precepts; when awakening-wisdom is pure, this is precisely contemplating the five Buddhas within the mind.
Next, the destruction of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to the phrase "sorrow, anxiety, and fear.

While the preceding matters were discussed either in relation to the internal body or external retribution—conforming to the context of the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*)—this single phrase specifically clarifies the mind as the obstacle of afflictions.

Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty.
The disciple Guanding recorded the obstacles to retribution as explained above; this may be understood accordingly.
What, then, are the afflictions and karma?
Some say: "That which arises frequently but is light is called affliction (*kleśa*); that which arises frequently and is heavy is called karma.
Master Tiantai said:
Spontaneous and constant afflictions are *kleśa*. That which suddenly arises as a resolute mind, inciting body and speech, and necessarily drags one toward retribution, is *karman*.
If that is so, since malevolent stars and calamitous anomalies do not concern the mind at all, how can they be considered *karmāvaraṇa*?

This refers to the external signs of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) about to arise; these are the signs by which karma is held accountable for its retribution, and thus one incurs this karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*).
If afflictions and karma are transformed, retribution is not necessarily transformed;
however, if retribution is transformed, afflictions and karma must necessarily be transformed.
In general discussion, both the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and the afflictions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) involve sorrow, anxiety, and fear;
in specific discussion, sorrow and anxiety belong to the afflictions of views, while fear belongs to the afflictions of craving.
The details are not fully recorded here and so forth.
Third, regarding the destruction of karmic obstacles: this refers to the section beginning with "evil stars and calamitous anomalies.

Since karma is about to manifest its retribution, its signs appear beforehand; the meaning of "signs" (*xiàng*) is that they reveal and manifest [the nature of the karma], which is the intended point here.
As for "malevolent stars," there are additionally the guest stars (atithi-nakṣatra).
Furthermore, regarding the five planets and the twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatra), there are seven in each quarter; four times seven makes twenty-eight.
If it deviates from its proper dimensions and loses its assigned sector;
or if Venus moves erratically, or a comet suddenly appears—
these are guest stars.
Calamities and anomalies refer to such things as wind, rain, snow, and frost occurring out of their proper seasons.
There are three kinds of malevolent influences:
human malevolence, ghostly malevolence, and doctrinal malevolence.
"Parasite paths" refers to poisonous ghosts.
It is also said that the three poisons are parasites.
"Transformations and monstrosities" refers to the grotesque and strange; this means the ugly forms, sounds, and so forth of birds and beasts.
As for "bad dreams," this refers to when the mind is in a state of profound secrecy and karma manifests within it, such that one sees unpleasant events in a dream.

Now, the manifestations and retributions of all karmas do not exceed the five transgressions. If an evil star portends the loss of the body or the forfeiture of life, it is the karmic sign of killing;
if an evil star portends the abandonment by deities or falling into poverty and destitution, it is the karmic sign of theft.
Malevolent stars indicating separation from kinsmen and suffering in obscurity are the karmic signs of the offense of sexual misconduct;
malevolent stars indicating false accusations, calumny, and slander are the karmic signs of the offense of lying;
and malevolent stars indicating the loss of property are the karmic signs of the offense of drinking intoxicants.

As for other calamities, anomalies, strange birds, evil dreams, and the like, each has its own symbolic significance according to the season; if one examines them with a discerning mind, they do not fall outside the retribution for the five sins.
The practitioner who understands and investigates this—why must they break bamboo splints and consult the tortoise shell, seeking answers from Guan Gongming?
From the passage "One should bathe and purify oneself" onwards, section two presents the method by which one can empty oneself of evil.
The signs of past karma manifest externally, and their retribution will arrive before long;
yet if one lacks internal methods, how can one avert it?
By applying the three karmas as a means to cultivate the three virtues, one uses phenomena to express the underlying principle.
Washing the foul body is intended for the realization of the Dharma-body;
sealing the lips and restraining the ears is intended for hearing the Prajñāpāramitā;
and a sincere, pure mind is intended for the realization of liberation.
First, he was ordered to bathe his inner body; later, he was further exhorted to cleanse his outer garments—thus, the internal and external were brought into harmony.
First, he was merely told to listen; later, he was cautioned to listen with single-minded attention—thus, he was solemnly enjoined to maintain silence.
The former instructs one to cultivate a sincere mind, while the latter demonstrates the realm of that sincerity; such is the completion of its method.
Indeed, the human body is fundamentally impure, just as the lotus flower originates from the mud; it is like sandalwood growing from *eranda* grass, as is clearly seen in the world.
Now, as the immediate cause for the regulations of the three karmas and the remote fulfillment of the wondrous meaning of the three virtues, how could one not believe this?

Bathing the Dharma-body can ward off the obstacle of retribution; listening attentively and maintaining silence can ward off the obstacle of afflictions; and a sincere heart can ward off the obstacle of karma, and so forth.
From the passage "The majestic power of this sutra" onwards is the fourth section, the conclusion.
"Able to completely eliminate" clarifies the transformation of the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*).
"Now they are in quiescent extinction" signifies the perfection of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Quiescence is simply *nirvāṇa*, and *nirvāṇa* is simply the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
Once the methods of the preceding three karmas have been perfected, it follows as a matter of principle that the three obstructions (*tri-āvaraṇa*) must be transformed.

Since the three obstructions have already been transformed, they naturally result in the three virtues: the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) is transformed into the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*); the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is transformed into the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*); and the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) is transformed into the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*).
The preceding section on the characteristics of phenomena uses the shallow to represent the profound;
the subsequent clarification of quiescent extinction uses the profound to conclude the shallow.
The sutra’s text is as intricate as embroidery, and those who perceive it are few indeed. So it is said.
Below "The Four World-Protecting Kings," the chapter on the circulation [of the text] is narrated, all as explained above.

Regarding the "Explanation of the Lifespan Chapter": the Buddha fundamentally has no body, no lifespan, and no measure; yet, in accordance with the world, he speaks of the three bodies, and in accordance with the world, he speaks of the three lifespans.
As for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), it takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as its model and takes that very nature of phenomena as its body.

This body is neither material substance nor mental consciousness; it is not comprised within the aggregates, elements, or sense bases. It is merely by designating the nature of phenomena that one refers to it as the Dharma-body.

Regarding the "life-span of the dharma-nature," it is not a life-faculty obtained through karmic retribution, nor is there any continuity or maintenance; rather, one forcibly designates that which is non-transmigrating and unchanging as "life-span.

This life-span is neither of long measure nor short measure; it is without extension or contraction, and one forcibly designates its measure as being identical to that of the dharma-realm and empty space.
This is precisely the body of that which has no body, the life-span of that which has no life-span, and the measure of that which has no measure.
As for the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), it is that which is evoked by spiritual practice.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states, "That which is obtained through long-cultivated karma," and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Because Great Parinirvāṇa is attained through the cultivation of the path; thus, the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) illumines the realm of suchness, and bodhi-wisdom is in resonance and union with the dharma-nature."
"Correspondence" is like the fitting of a box and its lid.
"Merging of characteristics" is like water and milk merging together.

The Dharma-body is neither body nor non-body; since wisdom likewise corresponds and merges, it is also neither body nor non-body, yet this wisdom is conventionally designated as the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya).

The Dharma-life is neither eternal nor impermanent; since wisdom corresponds to the profound mystery, it is likewise neither eternal nor impermanent—it is merely designated by the provisional name "eternal" as "life.

The Dharma is neither finite nor infinite; since wisdom corresponds to the profound mystery, it is likewise neither finite nor infinite—it is merely designated by the provisional name "infinite" as "the finite."

The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) means that it responds by conforming to the bodies of beings as its own body; it responds by conforming to their continuity of existence as its own life-span; and it responds by conforming to their dimensions of length and brevity as its own measure.
Wisdom is merged with the essence, enabling the arising of great function, just as mercury mixed with pure gold can coat all manner of forms and images.
The merit and the Dharmakāya manifest and appear everywhere; they can manifest as a body or as a non-body, as eternal life or as impermanent life, and as the immeasurable or as the measurable.
There are two meanings of "measurable" (*sānta*):
first, it is the measure of the immeasurable; second, it is the measure of the measurable.
For instance, [the numbers] such as seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya*s and eighty are examples of the measure of the measurable.
The weight of Mount Sumeru and the number of drops in the ocean truly have their limits, yet these are unknown to ordinary beings;
likewise, although Amitābha truly has a limit to his lifespan, humans and devas cannot calculate it—this is the immeasurable within the measurable.
The response-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddhas are all measured in two ways; they follow things and accord with conditions, appearing in varying lengths and durations.
However, these three bodies, three lifespans, and three measures cannot be treated as either identical or distinct; to do so would deviate from the essence of the Dharma.
Only by realizing that they are three while being one, and one while being three, does one truly comprehend the profound meaning of the scriptures.

Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Just as with the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one may see me, Śākyamuni, within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*"; this is precisely its meaning.

However, while Śraddhālakṣaṇa was particularly suspicious that the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) had limits, the four Buddhas specifically cited the immeasurability of the response-Buddha to sever his notion of limitation. Once his doubts regarding the traces were removed, he deeply penetrated the dharma of the recompense-body (saṃbhogakāya).
If one were to resolve doubts based on the perspective of Śraddhālinga, one should say that the lifespan is finite;
if one were to resolve doubts based on the explanations of the four Buddhas, one should say that the lifespan is infinite.

Yet, here, neither saying "the lifespan is finite" nor "the lifespan is infinite," he speaks directly of "lifespan" (āyus-pramāṇa). This is because his intention is to provide a comprehensive discussion of the lifespans of the three Buddhas; therefore, he does not take a partial title but explains by grasping the underlying meaning.
If we follow the logical convenience of the context, this is precisely the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Why is this taken?

Because the *saṃbhogakāya* "harmonizes with the above" and "responds to those below": harmonizing with the *dharmatā* above, it is neither measurable nor immeasurable; responding to the conditions of sentient beings below, it is both measurable and immeasurable.
The measure of doubt leads to an immeasurable response, which immediately reaches the Perfect [Teaching].
The compiler of the sutra titled this chapter according to the arising of that perfect understanding, citing one instance to encompass all others.
For this reason, the title is given as "Chapter on the Lifespan.
Furthermore, when explained again at another time, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" is also divided into three parts:
first, the Profound Meaning; second, the Citation of Evidence; and third, the Return to the Source.

Regarding the term "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*): "Life" (*āyu*) refers to vitality; it means that the life-faculty obtained as karmic retribution, which maintains continuity without interruption, is called "life. The duration of its period, whether extended or shortened, is called "measure" (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is termed "Life Span."
This explanation concerns the lifespan resulting from the causes and conditions of a Buddha.
Furthermore, "lifespan" (āyus) means "reception" (vedanā). It refers to the mutual containment and reception through the union of object and wisdom:

non-conceptual wisdom receives the non-conceptual object, and the non-conceptual object receives non-conceptual wisdom. This is like a large box and a large lid fitting together; thus, "lifespan" carries the meaning of "reception."
"Measure" (*pramāṇa*) means correspondence; because the object and the wisdom correspond, it is called "measure.
This explains the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha.
Furthermore, "lifespan" (*āyus*) means "long"; that which is eternal and unchanging is designated as "long."

"Measure" (*liang*) means to weigh and evaluate. A lifespan of eternal duration is neither a great number nor a small number; it is not something that can be fully known through correspondence, nor is it something that cannot be fully known through correspondence. It is neither expressible nor inexpressible; there is no name by which to designate it, yet we forcibly employ the term "measure" to describe its longevity.
This explains the lifespan of the Dharmakāya.
The first section consists of two parts:
first, the measurable limit.
The lifespan of Śākyamuni, for instance, is precisely eighty years.
Regarding "measurable and immeasurable":
the lifespan of Amitābha is in fact measurable, yet because it cannot be fathomed by humans or devas, it is said to be both measurable and immeasurable.
Whether these measures are finite or infinite, they should all be understood as the Buddha’s deeds.
The second section also has two meanings:
the Buddha, by means of the wisdom of suchness, accords with the object of suchness; since the object is without discrimination, the wisdom is likewise without discrimination.
If the object corresponds to the wisdom, then if the wisdom possesses discrimination, the object likewise possesses discrimination.
This knowledge and this non-knowledge are both elucidated by the Nisyanda-buddha (the Reward Buddha).
The third instance also has two meanings:
first, that it is profoundly quiescent and ineffable; second, that through the skillful means of compassion, it can also be spoken.
This state of being both speakable and unspeakable is the dharma of the Dharma-Buddha.
Second, regarding the citation of scriptural evidence: the statement that [the lifespan] lasts for eighty thousand years proves it is finite.

The fact that no beings among the gods, humans, or the eight classes of supernatural beings can conceive of or calculate it—that even the weight of mountains or the drops of the ocean cannot be counted—proves its infinity.
The spatial dimensions of empty space cannot be delimited, for the realized realm is non-conceptual.
Furthermore, it can only be differentiated by the realized wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Moreover, as stated below, that the ocean of wisdom is boundless and fully endowed with the waters of the Dharma is also the realized wisdom.
His lifespan is incalculable; this realization is ineffable.
Yet, were one to proclaim the lifespan attained by Śākyamuni Tathāgata, this realization of compassion may be described.
Furthermore, it is heard that these four Buddhas proclaimed the immeasurable lifespan of the Tathāgata, thereby attesting to the expressibility of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
In the new version, it is clarified that when the brahmin sought Buddha-relics the size of millet seeds and sought the retribution of the six heavens, this immediately attested to its being finite.

The Prince stated that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is inconceivable and difficult to understand, and its meritorious retribution is boundless; that this boundless retribution constitutes immeasurable direct realization (*pramāṇa*), and that being inconceivable and difficult to understand refers to the ineffable nature of the sphere of total realized wisdom (*jñāna*), and so forth.
Third, regarding "returning to the source," it is also called "restoring the fundamental tenet.

Although this exposition of the life-span is presented through the three bodies and six meanings, do not entertain divergent interpretations; it is simply the meaning of the title of the sutra, *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
The first point regarding "measurable" and "immeasurable" merely clarifies the meaning of illumination.

Because it is illumination, all dimensions—large and small, long and short, extended and contracted, and numerical quantity—all manifest within that illumination; this is simply the meaning of illumination itself.

In the second sense, the realm of wisdom and its container correspond through mutual realization; because form is great, so too is Prajñā. Because the Dharma is eternal, all Buddhas are likewise eternal; this is precisely the meaning of "light."

The third aspect concerns what can and cannot be spoken: although permanence, bliss, self, and purity are said to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither benefited nor augmented by them, such that there is not a single word [of addition];
nor is the nature of phenomena diminished by them, for it remains the very meaning of "gold."
Indeed, when one principle is understood, a thousand things follow; when one principle is lost, ten thousand delusions arise—this is precisely the meaning here.
Since these were heard at two different times, they have been recorded together, and so forth.
This chapter is now being formally explained; however, the introductory section is not yet complete, as analyzed above.
From the passage "In the city of Rājagṛha" onwards is the third introductory section concerning doubts.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, identifying the person; second, clarifying the doubt.
Identifying the person consists of four sections:
First, the source; second, the clarification of the stage; third, the emergence of the name; fourth, the praise of virtues.

As for the "source," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the term "Bodhisattva": *bodhi* means the Path (*mārga*) and *sattva* means the mind (*citta*). Because one practices this path oneself and is further able to transform others, one is called a *mahāsattva*; thus, a superior stage is established based on superior practice.

Regarding the "characteristic of faith" (*śraddhā-nimitta*): the characteristic of faith in the household exists within the stage of the semblance path (*pratirūpa-mārga*). According to the distinct classification, it is the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśac-cittotpāda*);

according to the perfect classification, it is the stage of the iron wheel (*ayaścakra-bhūmi*). As the subsequent text states: "One sees a person resembling a *brāhmaṇa* striking a drum with a mallet."
"The drum is the Dharma-body; the striking is the movement of the occasion.
When the occasion arises within a semblance-position, one knows it is not a true strike.
Furthermore, in the positions of the real and the semblance, each stage follows the other; there is no position in which they do not exist."
If Samantabhadra’s cultivation of the practices of Samantabhadra were perfected, his rank would be adjacent to the ultimate supremacy; thus, he would seem superior.
As for Xinxiang, who is said to resemble one on the Path, I do not yet dare to judge their relative status.
The objector says: "If it is identical to Samantabhadra and merely resembles him, why is there doubt?
This is not a hindrance;
it is simply that the Bodhisattva acts as an instigator for those who are in doubt.
Furthermore, as the stage of Buddhahood is not yet fully realized, there is no cause for resentment toward doubt.
Even Maitreya, the successor in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, harbors doubts; likewise, there is the Bodhisattva Saṃśayita in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
Regarding enlightenment, as it has not yet been fully realized, one gives it the name "enlightenment," which is termed "the arising of doubt.
The objector asks: "Since doubt has already been severed upon the realization of the Truths (satyadarśana), how can there still be doubt at the tenth stage?"
He replied:
"The 'universal doubt' is abandoned through the realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya), while the 'specific doubt' exists throughout the ten stages (bhūmi).
As for the contemplative understanding: the mind-king is called the 'king,' and the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are called the 'palace.'"
Contemplate these five aggregates as empty and quiescent; this emptiness and quiescence are themselves nirvana. Because nirvana can ward off wrongs and resist adversaries, it is called a city.
From the initial mind to the final mind, one constantly contemplates nirvana while practicing the Path; therefore, it is the place of dwelling.
The prose extolling his virtues consists of two parts:
external offerings to the Buddhas and internal planting of roots of goodness.

Since this Bodhisattva has planted these roots so deeply that he has encountered many Buddhas and composed expositions on high positions, he should indeed be free from any sense of shame, and so forth.
There are two meanings of making offerings:
first, material offering, which is easy to understand;
second, Dharma offering.
To practice and study according to the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates taught by the Buddha is called the "Dharma-offering.
For one who understands through contemplation of the mind, awakening to the mind in a single thought-moment is called being a Buddha.
The mind of immeasurable merit serves as a support for this awakened mind, causing it to become increasingly bright and pure; this is called making offerings to the Buddha.
Just as oil supports a fire, food benefits the body, and dhyāna gives rise to wisdom, these are all the meanings of "offering."

Regarding the planting of roots of goodness: the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is called "ground"; the wisdom that contemplates the *dharmatā* is called the "seed. Constantly contemplating with contemplation is called "sowing the seed"; long-term practice without regression is called "the seed being long-established"; and the arising of the five roots of goodness is called "growth."
Growth occurs through the movement of wind, the warming of the sun, and the moistening of rain, whereby it gradually increases and becomes lush and beautiful.

Wind is like the Buddha’s wheel of body; the sun is like the Buddha’s wheel of mind; and rain is like the Buddha’s wheel of speech. Encountering these three things of the Buddha can bring about great benefit.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is said: "If prajñā increases, the dharma-nature becomes increasingly manifest;
if the dharma-nature becomes manifest, concentration and wisdom become doubly clear.
Planting the seed and meeting the Buddha—these two meanings mutually support one another. By citing this pair, the virtues of the bodhisattva are extolled.
From the passage beginning with "This mark of faith" (*śraddhā-nimitta*) onwards, the sequence for clarifying doubt is formally explained.
This is further divided into two parts:
first, the cause of the doubt; second, the actual arising of the doubt.

Due to the distinction between the distant and the proximate: the distant refers to the proclamation of entering nirvana three months hence; the proximate refers to the detailed narration. If there are those who hear it, they will be able to contemplate the unsurpassed meaning.
It further states:
"It arises from one's fundamental vow, which strikes and stirs the mind to produce doubt.
As for 'by what cause and by what condition,' generally speaking, all three types [of conditions] are termed causes."

Since this text is concise, it states that the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*) mutually support one another to collectively manifest the Correct [Dharma]. The Correct [Dharma] corresponds to the cause, while the conditions correspond to the conditions themselves; the True Cause is eternal and its lifespan is immeasurable, and because the conditions can manifest the principle, the object is eternal and the wisdom is likewise eternal.
Are these causes and conditions not all the causes and conditions for [attaining] eighty years?
Now that you have just reached eighty, what is the cause and what is the condition?
For this reason, doubt arises.
Regarding the "eighty years": there are three grades of worldly lifespan. The lower realm is forty years, the middle realm is eighty years, and the upper realm is one hundred and twenty years.
The lower realm has too few days; the upper realm is too old; the middle realm represents the constant, being neither too few nor too old.

Furthermore, the eighth link of the twelvefold dependent origination is named *tṛṣṇā* (craving). The "extinction of eighty" signifies that craving has been exhausted, whereby one enters *sa-upadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
The exhaustion of craving and the absence of bondage signify "self," while nirvāṇa signifies "bliss."
Furthermore, the center of the square represents the Middle Way; the Buddha delights in the Middle Way, and the Middle Way represents purity.
For this reason, the period is eighty years.
Since Śraddhālakṣaṇa did not understand it in this way, he gave rise to doubt as to what the cause and what the condition were.
From the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he thought again," there arises a genuine doubt.
Regarding the statement "as the Buddha has taught," this is a doubt concerning the principle based on adherence to the teaching.
The teaching explains that practicing the two virtues of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) results in a long lifespan.

The Buddha’s past cultivation of causes was vast and manifold, yet his present resultant lifespan is exceedingly short; since this contradicts both reason and scripture, one cannot help but be perplexed.
If this principle does not hold, then the scriptures are established in vain;
if it is indeed certain, then where is his long life?
This is to be confused by the teachings while grasping at the principle.
Regarding the "two causes and conditions," this differs from what preceded.

Previously, cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) were combined as being equally dependent on conditions; now, cessation and insight are treated as constituting their own causes and conditions.

Within each of the ten wholesome paths of action, both cessation and cultivation are present: abstaining from killing is the wholesome path of cessation, while releasing living beings is the wholesome path of cultivation; abstaining from stealing is the wholesome path of cessation, while giving food is the wholesome path of cultivation.

In this sutra, the cessation of evil in the family that does not kill and the practice of goodness in the family that does not steal are each cited as one side of the pair, together clarifying both cessation and practice.
If discussed exhaustively, each case possesses both cessation and practice; thus, the distinction between cessation and practice must be clearly understood.
Now, each of these points has its own causes and conditions.
Life is what all sentient beings cherish most; to seize it and harm them is a profound suffering, whereas to pardon and release them is a source of joy.
A compassionate mind is the cause, and not keeping implements for killing is the condition; this constitutes the causes and conditions for the goodness of restraint (*saṃvara-kuśala*).
Now, food is a retributive support (*niśraya-vipāka*); with it, life is preserved, and without it, one’s lifespan perishes.
The intention to give is the cause, and the articles given are the conditions; this constitutes the wholesome causes and conditions of practice.

Just as it is with not killing even a single creature, so it is likewise for everything up to not holding wrong views. In total, there are twenty wholesome practices of abstention and forty such causes and conditions; all these causes and conditions together bring about a long life.
The Buddha’s two virtues of stillness (*śamatha*) and practice (*vipaśyanā*) have accumulated higher than mountains and piled thicker than the earth; how is it that he now ends his life at eighty?

This [previous argument] discussed the two virtues of stillness and practice solely from the perspective of cause and effect, but such an interpretation is not yet fully consistent with the meaning. I shall now explain it further.
The causes for [rebirth as] humans and devas are the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions;
these are called "life. For practitioners of the Three Vehicles, wisdom is their life.

Māra is named the "Slayer"; if he obstructs or seizes these things, it constitutes the severing of human and heavenly life. If he does not obstruct or seize them, it is called "stopping evil"; using skillful means to encourage their cultivation is called "practicing good."

If one destroys the Dharma of the Tripitaka, it is called killing the lives of those of the Two Vehicles; if one does not injure or damage it, it is called ceasing from evil; and if one skillfully encourages its cultivation, it is called practicing good.

If one disparages the practice of giving (*dāna*) up to disparaging worldly knowledge, it is called severing the life-force of a bodhisattva’s six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); if one does not create obstacles, it is called ceasing from non-virtue; and if one skillfully encourages cultivation, it is called practicing virtue.

If one cultivates the dharmas of the essential nature to sever greed, anger, and delusion, this is the life of the Two Vehicles; if one obstructs them so that they cannot be cultivated, it is called "cutting off the life of the Two Vehicles. If one does not obstruct them, it is called "stopping good," and to skillfully encourage their cultivation is called "practicing good."

To deny the emptiness of essence would sever the life-force of a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching; if it does not constitute an obstruction, it is the goodness of cessation, while encouraging its cultivation through skillful means is the goodness of practice.

If one disparages the gradual approach, this severs the life-force of the Bodhisattva of the distinct teaching; conversely, not creating obstacles constitutes the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*), while skillfully encouraging practice constitutes the goodness of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If one slanders this perfect interfusion, one severs the life-force of a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching and also severs the life-force of the Buddha; if one does not create obstacles, this is the good of cessation (*śamatha*), and if one skillfully encourages others to practice, this is the good of cultivation (*samādāna-śīla*).

The person of perfect realization (yuanren) not only follows the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) without destroying phenomena, but even destroys all phenomena to follow that single characteristic. This is like King Xianyu, who killed five hundred short-lived beings to bestow upon them ten kalpas of longevity; or like the Buddha, who severed all afflictions (*kleśa*) and eliminated all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) without remainder. These are cases where the words appear contrary while the principle is harmonious; they are not the conduct of those who practice only minor deeds.

As discussed above, each and every dharma possesses both the two wholesome qualities of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), and each of these wholesome qualities has its own causes and conditions.
If one grasps this principle, then traversing all the various dharma-gates will be as vast and expansive as the ocean.

Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "By practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one attains long life; when a bodhisattva practices giving, they bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings. ... up to ... by practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one attains long life; when a bodhisattva practices wisdom, they bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings."
This is precisely that meaning.
Yet our World-Honored One’s practice was nowhere lacking in perfection and his fruition nowhere incomplete; how is it that today he has reached eighty years?
Next, regarding the provision of food: the hundred flavors, sweet juices, and so forth, are the food of *upabhoga* (retributive support).
The flesh, marrow, and bones of one's body constitute the food of direct retribution;
these are all instances of giving material food.
The Sūtra speaks, however, of the "food of Dharma."
As for the "Dharma-food," it consists of the flavor of worldly dharmas, the flavor of supramundane dharmas, and the flavor of the most supreme supramundane dharmas.

A bodhisattva can act as a great donor for all sentient beings, causing those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment to turn from the heterodox toward the orthodox; for those already established in the orthodox, he causes their sprouts to grow. This is like the nourishment of plants by the yin and yang, or like parents raising a child with many layers of silk and cotton so that the child does not feel pain when falling to the ground, and then bestowing upon them the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.

To those who have already upheld the five precepts, he speaks of how the fires of the three realms are fierce and cause much burning and harm, and he praises the liberation of the three vehicles from all bonds.
To those who have already entered the realization of the path, he disparages the Lesser Vehicle as being like ruined seeds or scorched grain, and he praises the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Providing the royal feast for the people of a famished land, taking afflictions as fuel and wisdom as fire, one thereby produces the food of nirvana, causing all disciples to relish it with delight.
All such dharma-gates as these are called "dharma-food.

Each and every dharma possesses both the excellence of tranquility (śamatha) and the excellence of insight (vipaśyanā); each excellence possesses its causes and conditions, and these various causes and conditions bring about the fruit of long life.
Yet our World-Honored One’s practice is perfectly complete and his fruition is fully realized; why then is he only eighty years old today?
As for observing the mind not to kill: ignorance is the father and craving is the mother; if one were to sever these, it would constitute a parricidal offense.

To contemplate that ignorance is itself clarity and craving is itself purity, and to realize through one's essence that both subject and object are like empty space—this is the excellence of stillness (*śamatha*).
To contemplate all mental factors in the same way is called the excellence of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
One who can contemplate in this manner attains the adamantine, eternally abiding life-span.
Regarding one's own marrow, bones, blood, and flesh: although these are regarded as "one's own body" when compared with another's, when examined through wisdom, they are not one's own body.
As in the cases of the prince who fed the tigress and Śibi who ransomed the dove, they both relinquished their parents’ physical bodies, not their own selves.
Their "own selves" refers to the true mark of the dharma-nature.
The *Śāstra* states: "Precepts are the skin, meditative concentration is the blood, wisdom is the bone, and the subtle, virtuous mind is the marrow.
To preach the precepts for others, one should know that while precepts can obstruct transgressions and cultivate merit, the signless (*animitta*) is supreme.
To neither uphold nor violate the *śīlapāramitā* is to give one's own skin.
