Thus, the superior honors the subordinate.
From the passage beginning with "Because in his dream... onwards is the fourth section, which describes the dream.
From here below, there are one hundred and sixty-two lines of verse, divided into two parts:
first, four and a half lines that explain the dream in general; second, one hundred and fifty-seven and a half lines that explain the dream in detail.
In total, there are two parts:
the first three and a half lines clarify the vision of the golden drum, while the final line clarifies the vision of the drum being struck.
Regarding the vision of the drum, there are again three aspects:
The first line describes seeing the shape of the drum;
the next line describes seeing the light of the drum;

and the subsequent one and a half lines describe the Buddhas within that light—this constitutes the objects of contemplation for the three bodies (*trikāya*) as they enter meditative observation within the prose section.
Next, in the first line, "seeing one beating a drum" refers to personally observing the faculty of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), which strikes the realm of the *dharmakāya*.
"Producing a great sound" has already been explained above; it refers to personally observing the union of that realm and wisdom, which is capable of bringing about manifold benefit.
From the verse beginning with "This great golden drum" down to the one hundred fifty-seven and a half verses, the dream events are explained separately.
The text is divided into two parts:

first, from "This great golden drum" down to "capable of completely extinguishing and eliminating," there are twenty-one lines and three phrases, clarifying that the golden drum possesses the power to extinguish evil and give rise to goodness.

The second section, from "All sufferings have no support and no refuge" down to one hundred and thirty-five lines and three phrases, correctly elucidates the method of teaching and admonishing for repentance.
This passage on the ability to extinguish evil and give rise to good consists of six sections:
first, three lines that extinguish the suffering of worldly causes and effects;
second, three lines that give rise to the bliss of supramundane causes and effects.
The third set of four practices enables sentient beings to fully cultivate both self-practice and the transformation of others;
the fourth set of four practices can eliminate the karmic obstacles of retribution for sentient beings and further give rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives;
the fifth set of four practices enables sentient beings to attain various Dharma gates—starting with a small measure and subsequently attaining a great measure, and so forth.
The six [perfections] each have three practices and three phrases, which can shatter the eight difficulties and the cycle of transmigration for sentient beings.

To explain these six meanings: they all lead gradually from the three miserable realms to the human and celestial realms, as well as to the two vehicles and bodhisattvas; each and every one possesses the power to destroy evil and give rise to goodness.

From the passage beginning with "All sufferings have no support and no refuge," there are one hundred and thirty-five lines and three phrases; this is the second section, clarifying the method of repentance through instruction.
The text consists of five sections:
first, from "All sufferings" downward, there are nineteen lines and one phrase, which instructs on confessing and repenting for one's own transgressions;

second, from "I shall make offerings" downward, there are thirty-five lines, clarifying the practice of repentance through making offerings to all Buddhas and cultivating the transformation of others.
Three: from "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, upon whom I rely" downward, there are twenty-one lines, which clarify the practice of repentance through praise.
Four: from "By virtue of the causes and conditions of my wholesome karma" downward, there are fifty-one and a half lines, which clarify the practice of repentance through the making of vows.
The fifth section consists of nine lines beginning with "If there are those who pay homage and praise the Ten Powers," which concludes the confession.

As for the arising of the five intentions: sentient beings, through the obstacle of perverse inversion, do not recognize the principle of the *dharmatā*; through the obstacle of ignorance, they do not recognize cause and effect; and through the obstacle of evil karma, they do not recognize wholesome dharmas.

The Sage, out of compassion, because of the Great Being’s dream, revealed to him the practice of repentance, revealed the underlying principles, revealed the law of cause and effect, and revealed virtuous conduct; thus he composed this treatise on self-repentance and extended offerings, for his debt of gratitude toward the Buddha’s kindness was profound.
Because one makes offerings without letting their sincerity leak away, one sings praises and offers eulogies.
Offering is the practice; it must be directed toward a vow as its ultimate goal. Once both practice and vow are perfected, they culminate in this expression of praise.
The text for self-confession consists of three parts:
first, one line and one phrase clarify that the Dharmakāya is the basis of reliance;
next, two lines request the Buddhas to provide protection and guardianship.
The subsequent sixteen lines correctly clarify the practice of repentance.

Now, the Dharma-body possesses the three virtues, which constitute the Three Jewels as a single essence: the Dharma-nature is the Jewel of the Dharma; its quiescence yet constant illumination is the Jewel of the Buddha; and its pervasion of all places is the Jewel of the Sangha.
Although ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not understand it, they likewise do not transcend the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
In sum, how could all bodhisattvas ever fail to take this as their refuge? By relying upon this, the foundation is established and the Way arises.
Although the internal foundation may be established, if there is no external empowerment from the Buddha, one will not achieve success;
yet if one receives his protection, evil is severed and goodness arises, with accomplishment occurring in an instant.
Just as sprouts receive rain and grow lush and abundant, for this reason I request the Buddha.
Now that both internal and external conditions are complete, it is precisely the time to perform repentance.
The text for the formal confession consists of two parts:
the first three lines provide a general explanation of repentance;
the subsequent fifteen lines and one phrase provide a specific explanation of repentance.
"General confession" refers to the general confession of the three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
"Fundamental" refers to the fact that afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root of the two obstacles.
"Evil" refers to the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
The unwholesome refers to the obstacle of karma.
These three obstacles obstruct the three bodies, the three Buddhas, and the Three Jewels.
If these three obstacles are transformed, all threefold Dharma-gates become clear; therefore, one performs a general confession.
Regarding "individual repentance," this refers to repenting for the three obstructions.
The text is divided into three parts:
the first line and phrase repent for the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
The next line is the repentance for the obstacle of retribution;
the following thirteen lines are the repentance for the obstacle of karma.
"Before those possessed of the ten powers" refers specifically to the repentance for the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The ignorance that exists independently is a delusion of such extreme severity that one fails to recognize the Buddha of the Dharmakāya.

This Dharmakāya Buddha pervades all places, yet out of the darkness of folly, you remain unaware and openly commit various transgressions before him—like cattle and sheep who do not recognize a sovereign, or like sparrows and finches who do not recognize a statue in its stand, committing offenses right in his presence.
The ignorance that fails to recognize the Dharma-body is likewise so.
Regarding the kindness of parents: skillful means is the father and the perfection of wisdom is the mother; these two dharma-gates are able to give birth to the Dharma-body.
Those who do not recognize this are those who do not know how to repay the Buddha.

Those who do not understand the wholesome dharmas—wholesome dharmas being the practices that assist the Path and which can provide the resources for wisdom to manifest the principle—are likewise ignorant.
Those who do not understand this fail to recognize the Responsive Buddha (Nirmāṇakāya).
Since they cannot comprehend even these three Buddhas, is this not the fault of ignorance (avidyā)?
This is the specific repentance for the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa).
The section beginning with "Pride in one's own lineage" separately addresses the repentance for obstacles to karmic retribution.
Briefly stated, there are three types:
first, being arrogant toward others because of one's clan; second, treating things with contempt because of one's wealth; and third, looking down upon others because of one's youth.
Although retribution includes these three aspects, one should not indulge in self-indulgence.
If one gives rein to such indulgence, this retribution will become an obstacle.
Now, let us further explain this according to the Dharma-gates.
For those who have left the household life, wisdom is their lineage, meditative concentration is their wealth, and ethical discipline is their age.
To be stained by these three dharmas, esteeming oneself and disparaging others, is called being stained by dharmas; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "You are young and vigorous, while I am aged and decrepit. Ordinary people consider the flourishing of the five aggregates to be vigor; those of the Two Vehicles and the Shared Teaching consider emerging from existence through emptiness to be vigor; and Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching consider the Dharma-eye surpassing the Wisdom-eye to be vigor.
Those who are attached to these various dharmas all rely on strength to oppress the weak, thereby creating obstacles to their karmic retribution; all must be repented of.
From the line "Mental thoughts of unwholesomeness" below, there are thirteen lines that separately repent of karmic obstacles (*karmāvaraṇa*).
The text consists of twelve sections.
The first section, comprising one line, concerns the repentance for evil karma created through mind and speech, as well as inciting others to commit evil.
From [the section on] body, speech, and mind onwards, it concerns the evil committed by oneself.
2. One section on repenting for the evil karma created through internal and external causes and conditions;
3. One section on repenting for the evil karma created through the causes and conditions of the five desires;
4. One section on the evil karma created by following and accepting false teachers.
5. One type of action: committing evil deeds by following an evil master.
6. One type of action: committing evil deeds driven by the influence of craving.
7. Two types of action: committing evil deeds for the sake of food, clothing, and female beauty.
The first line of eight refers to creating evil karma regarding the field of merit of reverence during the time of a Buddha.
The first line of nine refers to creating evil karma regarding the field of merit of reverence during a time when no Buddha exists.
The two lines of ten refer to creating evil karma regarding the True Dharma.
Eleven [verses], one line each, concern the commission of evil karma toward the field of gratitude.
Twelve and a half lines, in total, concern the commission of evil karma in all places.
Since the causes and conditions for the commission of karma are extremely numerous and cannot be listed in full, they are here repented collectively.

If one wishes to provide a detailed explanation, beginning from the human realm and proceeding through the practices of the two vehicles, as well as the distinct and common practices of bodhisattvas, each should be treated accordingly;

by this analogy, the meaning should be understood. Thus, the *Fifty-Section Sutra on Examination* states, "From the highest level up to Equal Enlightenment, all must perform repentance"—this is precisely its significance.
From the thirty-five lines beginning with "I now make offerings," the text clarifies the making of offerings to all Buddhas.

The reason for making these offerings is that I was originally ignorant and blind; having been shown the way through the practice of repentance, this kindness is profound and heavy, and thus I have aroused the intent to make offerings.
The text consists of two parts:
the first line clarifies material offerings;
the subsequent thirty-four lines clarify Dharma offerings.
The Dharma-offering is twofold:
the first eight lines and a half clarify the Dharma-offering for transforming others.
To accord with the Tathāgata’s gates of compassion and mercy, thereby rescuing and benefiting sentient beings—this is the cultivation of the Dharma-offering for transforming others.
The subsequent twenty-five lines and a half clarify the practice of self-cultivation as a dharma-offering.
To accord with the Tathāgata’s dharma-gate of wisdom and cultivate the merits of the ten stages constitutes the practice of self-cultivation as a dharma-offering.
Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme; it fully encompasses material offerings and the offering of the Dharma, as well as matters and principles, and self and others.
Regarding the offering of the Dharma for the sake of transforming others, the text is divided into two parts:
the first four lines concern transforming others by causing them to practice.
The final four and a half lines exhort others to practice repentance.
Regarding the initial practitioner: I myself have practiced the ten stages as an offering of Dharma; now, I further transform others to cause them to make offerings of Dharma.
It is like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps; all that was dark becomes bright, yet the light never comes to an end.
This metaphor has four meanings:
first, it clarifies the beginning of transformation, wherein great compassion uproots suffering.
Next, he exhorts [them] toward the true cause, the practices of the ten stages;
next, he exhorts [them] toward the true fruit, the great awakening of Bodhi;
and finally, he exhorts [them] to diligence, urging them to achieve completion swiftly.
Since all sentient beings are equal, their dispositions and desires are likewise equal; thus, when one is skillfully delivered, many are delivered as well.
Without reckoning the toil of accumulating practices and amassing merit, one achieves the great awakening, whereby wisdom and virtue are perfected.
To exhaust all suffering is the fulfillment of the perfection of cessation (*nirodha-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
These words are self-evident and do not require extensive explanation.
As for "contemplating the mind," it means to harmonize the single thought-moment so that true illumination (*bhūta-prakāśa*) arises, spontaneously realizing the true fruit.
The regulation of all mental factors is likewise thus: "The multitude of disciples' afflictions are turned according to the will"—this is precisely that meaning.

The next four and a half lines concern transforming others to practice repentance: "I have received the Buddha’s teaching on repentance, and I in turn teach repentance to others; in this layered manner, I kindle the lamp of the Dharma without end, so that transformation upon transformation never ceases."
The text consists of three parts:
first, the intention to preach the repentance; second, the actual preaching of the repentance; and third, the conclusion after the repentance has been preached.
As for the "thousand kalpas," this is a figurative expression used to demonstrate the great power of repentance through the use of a vast number.

For example, if an evildoer has accumulated mountains of sin, yet can rescue a king from peril, he is still rewarded with half the kingdom; how much less would his prior transgressions be taken into account?

To speak of one who, despite having committed grave offenses over a thousand kalpas—however heavy and profound they may be—is able to rescue the King of Dharmatā and manifest the Dharmakāya from within the Tathāgatagarbha: their Great Enlightenment is brilliantly clear and they have transcended to sovereign freedom. How could they possibly be bound again by the karma of the five ānantarya crimes?
From "I shall establish [myself] in peace" for twenty-five and a half lines below, there is the practice of self-offering to the Dharma.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, five lines on self-cultivation; second, twenty and a half lines on self-cultivation through repentance.
Having already completed the previous confession, why do you now repeat it again?
It is like a goldsmith: from his first apprenticeship until his hair turns white, he repeatedly heats and hammers the metal until the vessel is finished before he finally rests.

Cultivating practice is like burning with wisdom; cultivating repentance is like severing and striking. When wisdom and severance reach their ultimate limit, one then ceases; there is no fault in repeating these teachings.
The former constitutes the gate of personal cultivation, while the present constitutes the gate of Dharma-offering; this is the distinction between them.
Cultivating this for oneself further consists of three parts:
first, the opening phrase that designates the chapter, which is "I shall abide securely";
second, the cultivation of the cause, which refers to the ten stages (daśabhūmi); and [the third part].
Next is the fruition, which is bodhi.
As for "precious jewels," the causes of the ten stages are noble; thus, the various stages themselves are the precious jewels.
As for "feet," the ten stages are the foundation of the fruition, and are therefore called feet.

Furthermore, the ten perfections are the feet of the ten stages; while it is not that other virtues are not cultivated, they are practiced according to one's strength and capacity, yet it is specifically with generosity (*dāna*) as the foot of the first stage.

When the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is fulfilled, one enters the first stage (bhūmi); likewise, up until the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), one enters the tenth stage. Therefore, the ten perfections serve as the feet for the ten stages.

Within the section on the fruition, there is both a general explanation of the fulfillment of the fruition and a specific explanation of the fulfillment of the fruition, which can be understood from the text.
"The radiance of merit" refers to the two kinds of adornments belonging to the fruition.
"Causing sentient beings to cross the ocean" refers to the turning of the wheel of Dharma upon the fruition.
From the passage beginning with "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones" for twenty and a half lines below, it clarifies the practice of self-cultivation through repentance.
The text consists of two parts:
first, one line requesting the Buddha; second, nineteen and a half lines clarifying the repentance.
This latter part is divided into five sections:
The first four and a half lines repent for the obstacle of retribution;
the next one and a half lines repent for the obstacle of afflictions;
the following six lines repent for the obstacle of karma.
Next, two lines clarify the dedication of merit;
next, five and a half lines repent of the two difficulties of good and evil.
Regarding the obstacle of retribution, the text is further divided into two parts:
The first two and a half lines present the characteristics of the obstacle of retribution; the subsequent two lines request its eradication.
"A hundred kalpas" refers to the time when the retribution is experienced.
Within that time, one receives a body, and the body itself is the retribution.
Retribution for one's actions constitutes an obstruction; such action itself is an impediment.
Poverty and suffering are instances where the "retributive environment" (依報) is incomplete, which is likewise an obstruction of retribution.
As for sorrow, feverish distress, and fear, these arise because external poverty oppresses one, causing internal anxiety and burning; all of these are obstructions of retribution.
The various evils one has committed are the suffering of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Poverty and hardship are the suffering of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Sorrow, feverish distress, alarm, fear, and a mind that is constantly timid and inferior are the suffering of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
"Temporarily lacking joy" refers to the suffering of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
All of these are, in essence, obstacles of retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*).
Next, regarding the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*), the text is divided into two parts:
The first two lines present the characteristics; the next line requests purity.
Next is the section on karmic obstructions, which consists of three parts:

the first two lines discuss vertically the karma created throughout the three periods of time; the next two lines clarify horizontally the manifestation of the ten non-virtuous actions in the present; and the final two lines seek repentance for past karma.

Now, that which is currently being experienced is called a "retributive obstacle" (*vipākāvaraṇa*); that which has not yet been experienced is bound to the practitioner, and if one cultivates the path of goodness, it can act as an obstruction.
Question:
Past and present [obstacles] must be repented of, but the future does not yet exist; why then do you speak of repenting for it?
Answer:
The Sāṃkhya school calls it "future existence" (*anāgatabhava*), while the Abhidharma masters call it "destined existence" (*bhavyabhava*).
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Because it obstructs the future, it is termed 'killing'."
"Since the present moment perishes from instant to instant, what is there that can be killed?
It is merely the cessation of the future that is called 'killing.
Since both the sutras and the śāstras regard the future as existent, it is necessary to perform repentance."
To provide a contemporary illustration:

suppose a layperson, while engaged in worldly affairs during the day, gives rise to immeasurable evil thoughts; although the actual events have not yet occurred, their sequence will inevitably unfold accordingly.
Suddenly, he resolved to leave home and cultivate the Way; thus, all the matters he had previously contemplated were simultaneously set aside as conditions changed.
Future karma should be understood in this same way: although it does not yet exist in the present, when its time arrives, it is inevitable.
If one now repents, one becomes utterly pure and serene.
It can be understood that the three karmas of the present life are arbitrarily expanded into the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*).
"To distance oneself" means to sever evil.
The practitioner is one who is well-born.
The ten abodes are the causal stage of the initial resolve.
Reaching the ten powers is the fulfillment of the final fruition.
Next, to clarify dedication (*pariṇāmanā*): because sentient beings are stubborn, they are attached to existence and cannot ascend beyond it.
Now, by repenting these transgressions, it is called "dedication."
He uses this land and other worlds as the text for rejoicing; however, his current intention is not thus:
whatever merit is performed in this land or other directions, he dedicates it all to sentient beings so that they may together proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
Just as a sound enters a horn and can be heard from afar, the power of skillful means is vast and equal to space.
Furthermore, regarding the concluding phrase "this dedication," one must not treat it as mere sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); the explanation of sympathetic joy is provided in the subsequent text.

Regarding the explanation of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*): this refers to the eight difficulties discussed within the context of good and evil, rather than the eight difficulties concerning being born before or after a Buddha.
The text is divided into two parts:
the first four lines point to evil as the difficulty.
The next one and a half lines refer to evil obstructing the good as an obstacle, or to goodness obstructing the Path as an obstacle.
The first four lines concern the obstacles of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
"All that exists" refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
To commit various evils with a body obtained as retribution—is this not an obstacle of retribution?
Regarding the perils of birth and death, there are two interpretations:
if one takes its cause, it is an obstacle of karma; if one takes its fruit, it is an obstacle of retribution.
Various forms of lustful desire constitute the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
A mind that is flighty and restless further constitutes the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
This flightiness and restlessness are *vitarka* and *vicāra* (applied and sustained thought), and *vitarka* and *vicāra* belong to the category of retributive phenomena (*vipākadharma*).

Just as an Arhat, though having severed all afflictions, still possesses discursive thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) and a distracted mind upon emerging from meditative absorption,
one should know that such restlessness is an obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), not an affliction (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, when people of the world turn their studies and change their course of action without creating karmic obstructions, this is entirely due to the fault of frivolity; is this not itself an obstruction?
As for the difficulty posed by evil associates, since evil associates can defile a person’s three karmas, this belongs to the category of karmic obstructions.

It is like relocating a stable to the edge of a slaughterhouse, or like Mencius’s mother moving her neighbor to a place where goods were being sold amidst wailing; the colors red, black, and dark blue are precisely what they signify.
The three poisons constitute the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "encountering the difficulty of no difficulties," there are two meanings:
first, if one does not cultivate goodness, obstacles and difficulties will not arise;
however, if one wishes to cultivate goodness, evil obstacles will immediately emerge.
Goodness itself is not an obstacle; rather, when evil comes to obstruct goodness, goodness is termed an "obstacle" (nāna).
This meaning is easy to understand, as ordinary people all interpret it in this way.
Second, various forms of goodness are obstacles: since goodness can obstruct the Path, how could it not be an obstacle?
This meaning shall now be explained.
Regarding those who encounter no obstacles yet are themselves hindered: they consider themselves free from evil and are unwilling to cultivate goodness.
This refers to the same principle as when followers of the Two Vehicles enter emptiness and give rise to the notion of nirvana and the notion of security, thereby ceasing further pursuit of Bodhi.

Regarding the difficulty of cultivating merit: if one performs many conditioned acts while seeking only agreeable fruits, it is like the case of a certain bhikṣu who practiced exclusively for merit but did not cultivate the precepts;
he fell among white elephants, his body draped with the seven treasures, yet he had to receive excrement in a golden bowl.
Furthermore, as in the *Sūtra of the Former Deeds of King Suśobhana* and others, is it not difficult to cultivate merit?

Regarding the difficulty of encountering a favorable time: during the beginning of the kalpa, when people lived in Uttarakuru, they experienced nothing but pleasure and did not cultivate the Path at all; is this not indeed the difficulty of encountering a favorable time?
"Even meeting a Buddha is difficult" means that those such as the Brahmin woman Ciñcā, Sunakṣatra, and Devadatta all experienced difficulties despite having met a Buddha.
By this analogy, it should be said:
hearing the Dharma and giving rise to slander, or encountering the Saṅgha and causing schism, are both difficulties.
If it is read as the "difficulty" found in the phrase "difficult and easy," this carries the meaning of evil coming to obstruct the good, thereby making the good difficult to accomplish;
if it is read as the "obstacle" found in the phrase "obstacle and difficulty," this means that goodness itself is inherently difficult, yet it can also act as an obstacle to the Way.
Furthermore, according to the scriptural text which says, "All such difficulties as these,
I now repent," one should know that the scripture intends the meaning of "difficulties" as obstacles.
The twenty-one verses beginning from "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are my refuge" constitute the third section of praise.

If we discuss the sequence, the preceding offerings of material wealth and Dharma were those of body and mind; as these had not yet been fully expressed or completed, they are now further supplemented by verbal praise.
If we consider them as Dharma-gates, the former was the Dharma-gate of making offerings, while the present is the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
The text consists of three parts:
first, one line that introduces the chapter and offers praise; second, nineteen lines that provide the formal praise; and third, one line that concludes the praise.

Regarding the "various Buddhas," in terms of horizontal extent they span the ten directions, and in terms of vertical extent they span the three periods of time; in terms of phenomena, they are the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, and in terms of principle, they are the *dharmakāya*.
The words are concise while the meaning is vast; this is the ingenuity of the headings.
"That upon which I rely" refers to the single essence of the three Buddhas within the *dharmatā*.

As for the "ocean of Buddhas," the four eyes enter the Buddha-eye and the ten knowledges enter the knowledge of suchness (*yathābhūtajñāna*); all lose their original names and are simply called the Buddha-eye and Buddha-knowledge. It is like objects cast into rock sugar or streams converging into the sea—there is nothing that is not sweet or salty [respectively].
The Dharma-nature of the three Buddhas encompasses all phenomena; therefore, it is called the "Ocean of Buddhas.
This is further divided into two parts for formal praise:
first, sixteen lines of praise expressed through words; second, three lines of praise that transcend words.
The address consists of two parts:
first, one line briefly praises and briefly illustrates; second, fifteen lines extensively praise and extensively illustrate.
Regarding the brief praise, it briefly praises the golden hue among all the marks and signs of excellence.

The *Śāstra* compares immediate iron to immediate gold; immediate gold to ocean gold; ocean gold to dragon gold; dragon gold to Jambudvīpa gold; Jambudvīpa gold to the gold of the Four Heavenly Kings; and so on, successively comparing each to the gold of the sixth heaven; finally, the gold of the sixth heaven is compared to the golden hue of the Buddha’s body, such that the gold of the sixth heaven is like iron by comparison.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s golden light shines through so completely that no shadows are cast upon the walls or barriers.

When the Buddha enters the city, he emits a light that illuminates the ground; a woman bows her head in prostration, and her gold hairpin falls to the earth. Seeing only a dazzling radiance, she does not know what is actually the ground.
What is the hairpin?
When the Buddha has passed by and his radiance has subsided, one then sees the golden hairpin.

Since the golden-colored body is the locus upon which all the marks (lakṣaṇas) rely, and yet only the "golden color" is mentioned, we know that this is a general praise of all the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjanas).

Gold has four meanings: its hardness and indestructibility are likened to permanence; the wealth of one who possesses it is likened to bliss; its substance being free from blemish or impurity is likened to purity; and its exquisite, brilliant luster is likened to selfhood.
Among all virtues, the four virtues constitute the totality.

As for the analogy of Mount Sumeru: since Mount Sumeru is composed of four precious substances, how much more so the Buddha’s body, which is fully endowed with the four virtues; thus, we know this is a comprehensive illustration.
The extensive praise and extensive illustration consist of two parts:
first, twelve and a half lines of extensive praise; second, two and a half lines of extensive illustration.
The extensive praise, in turn, has four sections:
From the line "Its color is unsurpassed" down to the second line, there is a detailed praise of the unsurpassed golden hue.
"Unsurpassed" refers to the virtue of the Self (ātman).
From the line "Pure and stainless" down to the third line, there is a detailed praise of the Buddha’s stainless physical form.
"Stainless" (*vimala*) refers to pure virtue (*śubha-guṇa*).
From the line "His merit is towering high" for three and a half lines below, there is an extensive praise of the Buddha’s physical form as being securely established (*pratiṣṭhita*).
"Securely established" refers to the virtue of permanence (*nitya-guṇa*).

From "Within the three realms of existence" down to four lines, there is a broad eulogy of the Buddha’s physical form as being able to eliminate suffering and poison; this refers to the quality of bliss (*sukha-guṇa*).
From "Like the waters of the great ocean" down to two and a half lines, there is a broad analogy.
The text consists of two parts:
the first two lines provide a broad illustration, and the following half-line provides a synthesis with the metaphor.

The ocean of the Buddha’s merit is that which thought cannot know and speech cannot exhaust; it is where the sphere of mental activity ceases and the path of language is cut off—this is precisely the meaning.
The waters of the ocean are difficult to know; how much more so the virtue of constancy.
The dust of the earth is difficult to know; how much more so the virtue of purity.
The weight of Mount Sumeru is difficult to know; how much more so my own virtue.
The limits of emptiness are difficult to know, how much more so its joyful virtues!
The passage beginning with "The Buddhas are also like this" serves as the application of the analogy.
The three lines beginning from "All who possess a mind" express a transcendence of words through praise.
The text consists of two parts:
first, one and a half lines that directly negate speech to express praise; second, one and a half lines that cite the analogy and apply it to the point at hand.
That "all who possess a mind cannot know" is precisely the negation of thought.
Since thought has already ceased, what could the mouth proclaim?
This means that speech is cut off.
To further cite the analogy and apply it, it can be seen in the text.
The line beginning with "adorned with the marks and secondary characteristics" serves as a summary.
"Marks" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the synthesis of all primary marks;
"secondary characteristics" (anuvyañjana) refers to the synthesis of all secondary characteristics.
Regarding "adornment," it means that within each individual mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and each individual minor sign (*anuvyañjana*), one possesses a multitude of virtues as adornments.
From the passage beginning with "By virtue of the various causes and conditions of my wholesome karma," there are fifty-one and a half verses; this constitutes the fourth aspiration.
If practice is without aspiration, it is like an ox without a driver—it cannot reach its destination.
It is like a painting without glue, like unbaked clay, or like the moon reflected in water; therefore, one sustains practice with aspiration.
This is also the repentance for the offense of regressing.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, forty-seven and a half lines clarify the making of vows; second, four lines concern rejoicing in accordance with those vows.
The first vow also has two parts:
first, nine lines of self-vows; second, thirty-eight and a half lines of vows for others.
The self-vows also have two parts:
The first four vows fulfill the fruition, while the subsequent five vows perfect the cause. Regarding the fulfillment of the fruition, there are four aspects:

the first vow, attaining the Buddha-way, fulfills the wheel of the will; the second vow, preaching the Dharma, fulfills the wheel of speech; the third vow, subduing Māra, fulfills the wheel of the body; and the fourth vow, remaining for a long duration to benefit others, fulfills compassion.
The fulfillment of causes and vows further consists of four parts:

first, one verse on the fulfillment of conditioned merit through the vow of the six perfections; second, one verse on the fulfillment of unconditioned merit; third, two verses on the fulfillment of mindfulness of the Buddha through recollection of past lives; and fourth, one verse on the fulfillment of meeting the Buddhas.
The text for making vows for others consists of two parts:

the first eight and a half lines are a vow to manifest as the King of Medicine Trees to extract suffering through great compassion; the subsequent thirty lines are a vow to manifest as the King of Precious Jewels to bestow happiness through great kindness.
The eradication of suffering is further divided into four parts:

first, one verse generally eradicates all sufferings; next, one verse eradicates the suffering of impaired faculties; next, two verses eradicate the suffering of illness; and finally, four and a half verses eradicate the suffering of royal calamities.
Bestowing happiness is further divided into three parts:
first, sixteen lines and a half bestow the happiness of worldly fruits; next, nine lines and a half bestow the happiness of supramundane causes; and finally, four lines provide the conclusion.
In the preceding passage, Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) extracted suffering, causing those with deficient faculties to become complete;
now, Great Benevolence (mahāmaitrī) bestows happiness, so that their sight and hearing become keen, clear, and joyful.
While the various faculties are described in the same way, there is a slight difference between "bestowing" and "extracting."
From the passage beginning "May all sentient beings always receive offerings" for nine and a half lines, [the text] provides the joy of the causes for transcending the world.
The text is divided into two parts:
the first three and a half lines cause the practitioner to possess external conditions for cultivation; the subsequent six lines cause the practitioner to possess internal causes for cultivation.
Furthermore, there are two types of external conditions:
the first two practices involve encountering the Triple Gem, while the latter one and a half practices involve being free from the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).

Since human conditions differ—some encounter the Buddha but do not escape their difficulties, while others escape their difficulties but do not encounter the Buddha—I now pray that they may both escape their difficulties and encounter the Buddha.
Internal causes are also twofold:
first, half of the five practices lead to birth in a noble family; second, the other five and a half practices result in great abundance of wealth and treasures.

Because human causes differ, some may possess great wealth yet be lowly and base, while others may be noble yet impoverished. Since their causes were incomplete, [the Buddha] now causes them to be both noble and wealthy.
Women have five obstacles; may they be free from the suffering of these five obstacles.
From the line "If I, in the present... onwards, four lines conclude the vows for both oneself and others.
The first two lines conclude [the discussion of] oneself, while the latter two lines conclude [the discussion of] others.
From "If in this Jambudvīpa... onwards, there are four lines concerning sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Sympathetic joy means rejoicing in the cultivation of virtue by others.
This is also the repentance for the sin of envy.
The text is divided into two parts:
the first two lines concern rejoicing in others, while the latter two lines concern rejoicing in oneself.
From the verse beginning with "If there is one who pays homage," there are nine lines of verse; this constitutes the fifth summary.
The text is divided into three parts:
the first two lines summarize the severing of evil, hence it says that one transcends the sins of sixty kalpas.
The next four and a half lines conclude by establishing the production of wholesome roots; therefore, it says they are "revered by kings and great ministers.

The following two and a half lines conclude by establishing the frequency of encountering Buddhas; although spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are not mentioned separately, the Buddha naturally encompasses them.
Commentary on the Chapter on Praise. Regarding the praise in this chapter, there are generally four intentions:
first, from the person who praises; second, from the production of goodness; third, from the cessation of evil; and fourth, from the person being praised. First, concerning the person who praises:

In the preceding chapter, he clearly explained the marks and signs of a Buddha and expressed his doubts regarding the Buddha’s lifespan; subsequently, the four honored ones all descended into his chamber.
With single-minded faith and understanding, he dreamed at night that a golden drum emitted a sound, and upon waking at dawn, he went to Mount Qi to recount his dream.

In this chapter, the Buddha recounts how [the Dragon King] was formerly a venerable nāga who praised the Dharma King face-to-face, vowing that he would speak of it during the day as he had dreamed it in the night.
Because he speaks of this person’s fundamental history, it is called the "Chapter on Praise."
Second, regarding naming based on the arising of goodness: for goodness does not operate in isolation; its arising must rely upon conditions (*pratyaya*).

Among all conditions, none is superior to the Buddha. Since the Dragon King’s praise of the Buddha can give rise to sublime goodness, it is named after this condition that gives rise to goodness; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Praise" (*Stutiparivarta*).

Third, regarding those named after the eradication of evil: among all transgressions, none is more heinous than slandering the Buddha; therefore, to overturn and eradicate this sin, one must offer praise.
Since praise serves as the remedy for slander, it is named according to that which acts as the remedy; thus, it is called the "Chapter on Praise" (*Stutiparivarta*).

Fourth, as for naming it after the person being praised: this refers to the Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present. Since these Buddhas are most honored and profound, and because they are extolled and proclaimed immeasurably, it is therefore named the "Chapter on Praise."

If one wishes to distinguish them: to describe [virtues] is called "praise" (*praśaṃsā*), while to employ metaphors is called "extolling" (*udīraṇā*); they may also be distinguished from one another in this way.
The *Śāstra* (Treatise), fascicle thirty, states: "To celebrate its merits is called 'praise'; when praise is insufficient, to further proclaim and extol it is called 'extolling'."
In this chapter, "reverence" refers to bodily action (*kāyakarman*), "respect" refers to mental action (*manaskarman*), and "praise" refers to verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Without the arousal of verbal action, the body and mind cannot function freely.

To bring forth clarity for body and mind, sound serves as the Buddha-work; therefore, by extolling and proclaiming, one praises and lauds the Tathāgata’s true merits, which is why it is called the "Chapter on Praise."

To summarize these four meanings, they all constitute the causes and conditions for the four *siddhāntas*; it is for this reason that the title of this chapter is established as the "Chapter on Praise.
Although this chapter is titled according to the four *siddhāntas*, its primary function is precisely to engender wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*).
The text consists of two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verses.

As for the address to the Earth Goddess, she is the mistress of this great earth; all the practices of the Bodhisattvas are entrusted to her, and because her lifespan is long and she perceives the events of the past, future, and present, her testimony regarding the meaning of the matter is authoritative.
As the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra*) states: "When one has accumulated merit and virtue, who shall bear witness?
The Buddha then pointed to the earth, saying, 'It is she who knows me.
The present account of the past deeds of the Honored One Golden Dragon (Suvarṇa-nāga) is likewise for the purpose of addressing the Earth Deity.

Furthermore, regarding the pairing with the goddess Śrī (Good Woman): the male deity represents the yang, signifying expedient means (*upāya*), while the female deity represents the yin, signifying reality (*tattva*).

Since true wisdom can give rise to all manner of virtues, she is appropriately paired with "Good Woman" because she gives birth to goodness; and since she serves as a witness to the past, she is appropriately paired with "Firmness" (*Dṛḍhā*), and so forth.
Since this discourse now treats the function of generating goodness, it is addressed to a virtuous woman.

As for the Venerable Golden Dragon: because this king cultivated the Dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* in the past, in accordance with the principle of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he is called "Golden";
and because he can praise the Buddhas of the three periods with wisdom, his eloquence being like clouds and rain, he is called "Dragon."
Because he is able to bring great benefit to sentient beings and is looked up to by all things, he is called "Venerable" (Zun).
Since he derives his name from his practice, he is called the Venerable Golden Dragon (Jinlong Zun).
In total, there are sixty-two and a half verses, which are divided into three parts:

first, thirty-five verses praising the Buddhas of the three periods; second, twenty-five and a half verses making vows for future lives; and third, two verses concluding by correlating the events of the two periods.
Regarding the praise of the Buddha, the text consists of five parts:

first, one and a half lines of general praise; second, twenty-three lines of specific praise; third, three lines of universal praise by analogy; fourth, five and a half lines of praise beyond words; and fifth, two lines of dedication.
Regarding the general praise: vertically, it encompasses the three periods of time; horizontally, it encompasses the ten directions.
"Time and direction" constitute the general aspect of phenomena (dharmas), while "subtle, wondrous, and quiescent extinction" constitutes the general principle.
This general principle is the general Dharma-body (dharmakāya); this general phenomenon is the general of the two bodies—the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) and the response body (nirmāṇakāya).
This general praise of the three bodies is also a general praise of the three virtues, the Three Jewels, and various other sets of three dharmas.
In this way, all Buddhas are universally and entirely pure.
"Purified" (*viśuddha*) is a term of general praise.
It is not only purified, but also eternal (*nitya*), blissful (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and so forth.
From the line "the supreme among forms" (*rūpāṇāṃ rūpam uttamam*) downward, for twenty-three lines, there is a specific praise according to each characteristic.
The text appears intermittently, divided into six thematic sections:
first, six and a half lines praise the ocean of the seven major marks and also praise the excellence of the deep-blue hair;
next, two lines praise the ocean of the two minor marks.
The next two lines universally praise the ocean of the major marks;
the next thirteen lines further praise the ocean of the four major marks;
and the final two lines praise the ocean of the minor marks.
The next two lines praise the softness of the hands and feet; this, too, constitutes a great ocean of marks. Why is this so?
Because the major and minor marks alternate with one another, together adorning the Buddha’s body.

The Dragon Honored One possesses skillful wisdom and understands according to the characteristics of the Dharma; he praises according to those characteristics, and thus he praises by alternating between the major and minor marks.

Now, the marks and signs are fundamentally for the purpose of adorning the Buddha’s body. The Buddha’s bodies are of many kinds: the body born of parents, the *sambhogakāya* (body of sublime manifestation), and the *dharmatākāya* (dharma-nature body). Since these bodies are not the same, their marks and signs also differ. Since the substance of the marks differs, their functions also differ. Since their functions differ, their karmic activities also differ.

Regarding the differences among the three bodies: when [the Buddha] raised his hand to grasp a tree in the Lumbinī Garden and was born from the right side of his transformation-body, heaven and earth shook violently. Ārāḍa was greatly startled; he uncovered the infant with a fine cotton cloth and examined his marks. Every mark was radiant and clear, certifying that he would surely attain Buddhahood, yet he could not utter a word for grief.
This is the mark of the Buddha’s birth-body (*janmakāya*), as explained in the *Śāstra*.

The Buddha’s body of sublime excellence (*vairocana-kāya*) is majestic and awe-inspiring, like Mount Sumeru towering over the great ocean; all its major and minor marks are likewise majestic and awe-inspiring, distinct from the ordinary body, ordinary radiance, and ordinary marks—this is precisely the mark of the Buddha’s body of sublime excellence.

The Buddha of the Dharma-nature body cannot be seen by ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or those on the lower stages; it is only those who are ready for deliverance who are enabled to see him. This is the body that is bodiless and the mark that is markless.

All-knowledge is his head; the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is his topknot; the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates are his hair; great compassion is his eyes; the Middle Way is his white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa); the untainted (anāsrava) is his nose; the eighteen emptinesses are his tongue; the forty unique qualities are his teeth; the four great vows are his shoulders; the three samādhis are his waist; the Tathāgatagarbha is his abdomen; and the wisdom of means and reality are his hands, while meditative concentration and wisdom are his feet. Thus, these marks adorn the Buddha of the Dharmatā-body.

Regarding the karma of the marks and signs: as stated in the *Śāstra*, one hundred merits produce one mark, and three thousand two hundred merits produce the thirty-two marks; this is the meaning of the Buddha’s birth-body (janmakāya) possessing the marks and signs.

If one guides all activities of the marks with the wisdom of emptiness, then each and every activity will be in accord with emptiness; among all forms of accord, accord with emptiness is the foremost. This is the meaning of the characteristics of the Buddha’s special, exalted body (*viśeṣa-kāya*).

If one brings all karmic actions to fulfillment by guiding them with the wisdom of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), then every single action is none other than the dharma-realm of the true mark; this is the meaning of the characteristics of the seed of the Dharma-nature body Buddha (dharmatā-kāya-buddha).

The three bodies, the three kinds of characteristics, and the three kinds of karmic characteristics of those characteristics cannot be treated as either identical or distinct, nor as simultaneous or separate.
If they were either one or different, they would not be pure; they would not be subtle and quiescent.
Because it is neither sequential nor simultaneous, neither unified nor distinct, it is beyond words; even the most eloquent praise cannot reach it.

Now, this sutra specifically extols the marks and signs of the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of sovereign radiance), which encompasses the *dharmatā-kāya* (the body of reality) above and includes the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (the manifested body) below, clarifying them from the central perspective. This is truly the skillful expression of one who praises [the Buddha]. . . . and so forth.

Each and every mark clearly manifests its function; for instance, as with the mark of the level soles of the feet, no demonic or heterodox forces can cause it to waver, no phenomena of existence or non-existence can move it, and no extremes can shake it.

Regarding the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head: it is not worshipped by dharmas, nor by persons, nor by noble ones; for within its own category, there are specific instances where it is excluded, and so forth.
From the passage "The Buddhas of the past and future" onwards, this is the third round of eulogy by analogy.
The Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are equal; their single mind and single wisdom, as well as their responsive transformations, are likewise so.
To specifically cite one Buddha and one mark serves as the basis for praise, yet this applies universally to all Buddhas in the same way.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, "The merit of recollecting a single Buddha is equal to that of all Buddhas of the ten directions"; this is precisely its meaning.
Regarding the purity of body and speech, there are two interpretations.
One interpretation says:
"That which is praised is the purity of the three karmas; I now prostrate to them all.
Another interpretation says:

The one who is able to praise is pure: with beautiful flowers and incense, this is purity of body; by making offerings, this is purity of mind; by singing hymns, this is purity of speech, and so forth.

From the verse beginning "Even if one had a hundred tongues" onwards is the fourth section, the Praise Beyond Words (*anabhilāpya-stuti*). Of these, the first three and a half lines constitute the Praise Beyond Words, while the subsequent two lines constitute the Praise Beyond Mind (*citta-stuti*).
As for the three sections, they may be intended to represent the ineffability of the Three Bodies (trikāya).

Suppose there were a person with a hundred heads, each head having a hundred mouths, and each mouth having a hundred tongues; even if such a being were to live for a thousand kalpas, they could not exhaustively praise the merits of the physical marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) of the Buddha’s birth-body (janma-kāya).

Suppose there were a person with a thousand heads, each head having a thousand mouths, and each mouth having a thousand tongues; even if such a person were to live for ten thousand kalpas, they would be unable to exhaustively praise the merits of the Buddha’s extraordinary body and his marks and signs of excellence.

Even if the waters of the great earth and heavens were dropped one by one like hairs, all sentient beings would be unable to know the marks, signs, and meritorious virtues of the Dharmatā-kāya Buddha; therefore, one must transcend both speech and mind in order to praise them.
The two lines beginning with "From this moment on" constitute the general dedication.
The twenty-five and a half lines beginning with "Such a king of men" constitute the second section: the extensive aspiration for future vows.
The text consists of two parts:
the first one line is the Buddha’s exposition, and the subsequent twenty-four and a half lines are the Veneration of the Dragon King’s (Nāgarāja) vow.
This section is further divided into five distinct parts:

The first five lines are the vow to preach during the day what was dreamed at night; the next two lines are the vow to take a pure land for the sake of others; the next two and a half lines are the vow to seek together with others the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); the next three lines are the vow to transform those below; and the final twelve lines are the vow to seek [enlightenment] above.
The detailed explanations within this section may be sought there.
Question:
Since all vows are fulfilled, why is no prediction (vyākaraṇa) granted here?
Answer:
"The Dharma-companion will arrive in the future; his arrival is not far off," and so forth.
From the line "One should know through faith" onwards, the two lines constitute the third section, which reconciles the ancient and the modern, as per the text.
The Wenshu (Textual Commentary) on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Three;
*Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* Wenshu, Fascicle Four;
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty.

The Disciple Guanding’s Record of the Explanation of the Chapter on Emptiness. Regarding emptiness, there are four kinds: namely, entering emptiness by extinguishing form; form itself being emptiness; entering emptiness by extinguishing extremes; and extremes themselves being emptiness.

This sutra encompasses the repentance practices of all vehicles and requires four kinds of emptiness; yet, since this chapter specifically designates "emptiness," it refers exclusively to emptiness as being identical with the extremes.
Why is this so? A sūtra states:
"The emptiness [of all things] has already been explained at length in countless other sūtras"; therefore, it is explained here only briefly.
Furthermore, as for emptiness, it is the emptiness of existence and the emptiness of non-existence.
"Emptiness of existence" refers to the emptiness of the twenty-five aggregates of existence.
"Emptiness of non-existence" refers to the emptiness of the ashes of the two vehicles.
When both sides are pure, it is called emptiness.
To state this directly would cause those who are deluded to become confused by terminology and muddled regarding the principle, such that they could not achieve transcendental awakening.
Now, I shall provide a sixfold analysis: emptiness negates neither-existence-nor-non-existence;

neither-existence-nor-non-existence negates emptiness; emptiness cultivates neither-existence-nor-non-existence; neither-existence-nor-non-existence cultivates emptiness; emptiness is identical to neither-existence-nor-non-existence; and neither-existence-nor-non-existence is identical to emptiness.

Regarding "emptiness refutes that which is neither existent nor non-existent": this refers to the views of ordinary people and heterodox teachers concerning neither existence nor non-existence; the realization of the Two Vehicles who dwell one-sidedly in neither existence nor non-existence; and the adherence to the gate of neither existence nor non-existence within the teaching-path of the Distinct Teaching—all of these are refuted by the emptiness of the "Emptiness" category.
The views of all heterodoxies are of many kinds: first, the four single views; second, the four compound views; and third, the four complete views.
The four single views can be understood.

The fourfold compound views refer to: existence and non-existence, non-existence and non-non-existence, both existence and non-existence as well as both existence and non-non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence as well as neither existence nor non-non-existence; these are the fourfold compound views.
Regarding "possessing the four views": within a single phrase there are four phrases; with four sets of four, there are sixteen phrases, hence it is called "complete.
Although they appear as single or multiple, whether complete or incomplete, all are vast and pervasive suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
Although it is reckoned as being neither existent nor non-existent, this is in fact a false view; therefore, it is sublated by the emptiness of the "Chapter on Emptiness.

As for those of the Two Vehicles who dwell one-sidedly in the realization of neither existence nor non-existence, they say "not existent" because they have severed the view of eternalism, and they say "not non-existent" because they have severed the view of nihilism.

The two views of existence and non-existence are extinguished without remainder; the views and afflictions of the three realms are forever exhausted. One gives rise to the thought of passing into extinction and the thought of peace and security: "The holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
One merely preserves this and does not further seek toward *sambodhi*.
However, when those of the two vehicles give rise to true realization, they sever the views of permanence and annihilation; thus, their approaches differ.
Some enter through the gate of existence, as in the *Abhidharma*;
some enter through the gate of non-existence, as in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*;
and some enter through the gate of both existence and non-existence, as in the *Kun-le*.
Alternatively, one may enter through the gate of "neither being nor non-being," as in the *Nata-Kātāyana Sūtra*.
To be free from annihilationism and eternalism is called the Noble Middle Way.

Although all four gates equally eliminate the extremes of annihilation and permanence, they are nominally identical to the Middle Way; in reality, however, they preserve partiality and grasp at realization, and are therefore sublated by the "Emptiness" chapter.

Regarding those who adhere to the gate of "neither existence nor non-existence" within the teaching path of the Separate Teaching (*prthaktva-śāsana*), the Buddha employs skillful means for bodhisattvas of dull faculties to explain the Middle Way through these four gates, just like the analogy of the raft.
Those who do not grasp the essential meaning will give rise to disputes regarding the four gates.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The true, good, wondrous, and great parinirvāṇa is empty; the Buddha-nature is likewise form, non-form, and neither form nor non-form."
"If one adheres to each gate individually, then one harbors a contentious mind regarding the Tathāgata and fails to see the Middle Way.
To cling to these teaching gates is still to be refuted by the emptiness discussed in the "Chapter on Emptiness."
The new edition states, "A Bodhisattva of the first stage wishes to practice the path with signs"; this is the meaning of one gate, for within the text there are explanations of all four gates.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Prior to this, we were all called people of false views.

The "neither existence nor non-existence" that refutes emptiness refers to the empty-view of ordinary delusions, the realization of emptiness by the Two Vehicles, and the gate of emptiness in the path of teaching; because these fall into the two extremes, they are what is refuted by the Middle Way of neither existence nor non-existence.

Regarding the cultivation of characteristics: one who perceives emptiness, realizes emptiness, and teaches the path of emptiness should cultivate the Middle Way that is neither existent nor non-existent.

One who perceives that which is neither existent nor non-existent, realizes that which is neither existent nor non-existent, and employs the teaching-gate of that which is neither existent nor non-existent should cultivate the emptiness of the Middle Way.
Regarding "identity" (*xiāngjí*): the emptiness that destroys the two extremes is itself the Middle Way, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
This Middle Way, being neither existent nor non-existent, is itself the emptiness that destroys the two extremes; they are non-dual and without distinction.

Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha has spoken of it by various names. Emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent; however, it is not designated by the name "neither existent nor non-existent" because that would be a brief description. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Emptiness."

Regarding the purpose of this chapter: the "Chapter on Repentance" destroys evil, the "Chapter on Praise" generates goodness, and the "Chapter on Emptiness" leads to the accomplishment of destroying evil and generating goodness.
Furthermore, because it guides and establishes the function, the essence, and so forth [of the treatise], the *Vyākhyā* states: "If this emptiness did not exist, nothing at all could be accomplished.
Since it guides and establishes the superior category [of the treatise], the "Chapter on Emptiness" is elucidated.

Furthermore, while the constant fruit reveals the essence, it is not that the cessation of evil and the production of good do not clarify emptiness; those of sharp faculties have already understood this. However, for the sake of those with dull faculties, the Great Compassionate One gives rise to a mind of great pity and further clarifies that the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates and all produced phenomena is empty and quiescent. This chapter consists of forty-five lines of verse, divided into two parts:
the first four and a half lines introduce the intent to expound emptiness, and the subsequent forty and a half lines constitute the actual exposition of emptiness.
Regarding "other immeasurable sūtras," this refers to the detailed to clarify the concise, and likewise indicates the concise to reveal the extensive.
If it refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, then this sūtra would not be included within the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-vaipulya) category;
yet if it does not refer to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, other sūtras do not extensively clarify the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, what does this mean?
The answer is:
regarding the various sūtras, the compilers should establish the sequence for the preceding sections, while all subsequent sections are subsumed under the examples of the preceding ones.
Moreover, let us cite one instance by way of analogy.
As the *Āgama Sūtras* state: "When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Śāriputra could not bear to witness the Buddha's passing, so he went before him and departed."
"Jūntóu came to the Buddha's dwelling carrying his robe and bowl.
This is an event that occurred after the [Buddha's] passing.
Yet it is collected within the *Āgamas* from twelve years prior; one should know that the latter portion of the *Āgamas* extends even to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Furthermore, since the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings are positioned in sequence before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, yet it is stated therein that "he had already bestowed predictions upon the śrāvakas at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa," does this not imply that the Vaipulya teachings extend as far as the *Nirvāṇa*?

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) precedes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Fahua) in sequence; the *Śāstra* states: "Since Subhūti received his prediction within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, are all bodhisattvas thereby fixed in their destiny?"
"Is it not definitively fixed?
One should know that the *Prajñāpāramitā* also extends to the *Nirvāṇa*.
Inferring from this, those that speak of a sequential order refer to the earlier sections, while those that refer back and forth to one another refer to the later sections.
The compilers subsequently organized the material according to the clarity of its meaning and the similarity of its categories, bringing related sections together;
some may not realize that the arrangement appears to deviate from the original sequence, yet in truth, it does not.
This sutra belongs to the latter portion of the Vaipulya (fangděng) class; it is not contradictory in meaning to refer to the *Prajñāpāramitā* as its "extensive exposition.
Regarding the "concise exposition," the Buddha employs both concise and extensive methods, which should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuskoṭi*):

first, there are cases where both name and meaning are extensive, such as the eighteen emptinesses, the twenty emptinesses, and the twenty-four emptinesses; [the other permutations follow accordingly].
In some cases, both name and meaning are abbreviated, as in the case of "solitary emptiness" (*ekākī-śūnyatā*);

in other cases, the name is extensive while the meaning is abbreviated, as when various names such as *dharmatā*, *bhūtalakṣaṇa*, *bhūtakoṭi*, *tathatā*, and *dharmadhātu* all refer to a single meaning;

and in yet other cases, the name is abbreviated while the meaning is extensive, as with the names "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), whose meanings are vast and wide-ranging.
From the stage of ordinary beings up to the ultimate state of Buddhahood, all are termed "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
The *Śāstra* states: "The unsurpassed among sentient beings is the Buddha.

From the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of an ordinary person up to the stage of Buddhahood, these are also referred to as the liberation of form (*rūpa-vimukti*) and the liberation of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-vimukti*).
The *Śāstra* states: "Among all dharmas, that which is unsurpassed is nirvāṇa.

What is now said is a brief exposition on the two kinds of emptiness regarding arising and dharmas; as the subsequent text says: "The house of the five aggregates, when contemplated, is entirely empty and quiescent."
"Good daughter, you should observe where there are persons and sentient beings"—
this is precisely its meaning.

Because the faculties and conditions of sentient beings differ, those who attain awakening through an extensive explanation are termed "sharp-facultied," while those who attain awakening through a concise explanation are termed "dull-facultied."
Does this statement seem contradictory?
Śāriputra attained awakening upon hearing it once; this indicates he was of sharp capacity and that the teaching was concise.
Maudgalyāyana attained awakening upon hearing it a second time; this indicates he was of dull capacity and that the teaching was extensive.
The intent of this sutra is not to clarify the sharpness or dullness of realization, but rather to discuss the sharpness or dullness in terms of hearing and retaining [the teachings].
Those of sharp faculties can retain them through extensive hearing, whereas those of dull faculties can only retain them through concise hearing.
Now, these faculties possess only the capacity for awakening, but lack the capacity for extensive retention; therefore, it is said that they cannot know extensively.

Regarding the meaning of immeasurable emptiness: the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the two vehicles is the meaning of measurable emptiness, whereas the Middle Way of the bodhisattvas is the meaning of immeasurable emptiness.
This sutra elucidates the true mark of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which is precisely the meaning of immeasurable emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"Various wondrous skillful means" refers to the *siddhānta* (established tenets) skillfully employed, such as the aforementioned various distinctions made to clarify the cause by way of the result, and to extinguish evil while generating goodness.
Regarding the arousal of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): because sentient beings are afflicted by the heavy illness of clinging to existence, great compassion is likewise profound.
As for my current exposition: "exposition" (*yan*) means "extensive," which is the opposite of "concise."

The previous discussion on the two types of emptiness regarding arising phenomena was called "concise" (*lue*); the present discussion concerns the two meanings of arising phenomena, and is therefore said to be "elaborate" (*yan*).

To "know the intentions of sentient beings" means to know that this particular capacity delights in conciseness and finds it appropriate to be concise, and that through conciseness they awaken to conciseness; hence, it is said that he knows their intentions.
The introductory section explaining the intent of teaching emptiness is concluded.
From the verse beginning with "This body is false and deceptive" for forty and a half stanzas below, this is the second part, which correctly elucidates emptiness.
This is further divided into two sections:
First, from "The falsity of the body" downward for nineteen and a half lines, it clarifies the objects of the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena;
second, from "Good daughter, you should contemplate" downward for twenty-one lines, it clarifies the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena.

Without an object, contemplation is not correct; without contemplation, the object is not manifest. One should therefore cite the tenfold examination of object and wisdom from the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) to clarify their inconceivability.

The subsequent passage states, "the realm of inconceivable wisdom, the illumination of inconceivable wisdom"; the new edition reads, "suchness-dharma, suchness-wisdom," which conveys precisely this same meaning.
The visualization of the object of emptiness also has two parts:

first, from "This body is false and deceptive" downward for seventeen and a half lines, the visualization of the actual phenomena (*dharmas*) is explained; second, from "The elements of water, fire, and wind" downward for two lines, the visualization of the conceptualized (*parikalpita*) object is explained.
Regarding "real phenomena" (*bhūta-dharma*): one contemplates the five aggregates as non-existent and contemplates the sixteen aspects as being without a person.
Because this contemplation of emptiness accords with ultimate principle, it is called "real phenomena";
because the body, though not yet dead, is a deceptive, foul, and impure thing, it is called a "conceptual construction."
It is also called the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) and the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*).
Direct entry by taking emptiness as the object is termed the practice of wisdom;
practicing while concurrently engaging with phenomenal phenomena is termed the practice of conduct.
It is also called the Right Path and the Aids to the Path.
Contemplation of emptiness that accords with principle is termed the Right Path;
the contemplation of impurity that destroys greed is termed the Aids to the Path.
In the Hīnayāna, one who cultivates the primary path (*maula-mārga*) to sever the fetters is called a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*);
one who cultivates the auxiliary path (*sambhāra-mārga*) to sever the fetters is called a person doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that for a bodhisattva, generating the resolve that accords with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) constitutes cultivating the primary path, while sporting with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) and purifying buddha-fields constitutes cultivating the auxiliary path.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to the great carriage and its retinue; this is precisely that meaning.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that through right wisdom one becomes detached, detaching from the ten marks and abiding in Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, by clearly contemplating white bones, one shatters the twenty-five realms of existence and achieves the King Samādhi.
Various sūtras discuss these two meanings, each varying in its degree of detail.
This sutra briefly clarifies the meaning of the primary and auxiliary practices.
Furthermore, there are two aspects to the objective realm of the true dharma:

first, from "The body is false" downward for ten and a half lines, the objective realm is discussed in terms of the fruit of suffering; second, from "From various causes and conditions" downward for seven lines of verse, the objective realm is discussed in terms of the cause of accumulation.
Contemplating this suffering and its origination, one gives rise to the Path and Cessation; if one can perceive the Four Truths, then one attains the severance of birth and death.
Once existence in birth is exhausted, one will no longer undergo further existences, and so forth.
The state of suffering is further divided into three parts:

first, the two lines beginning with "the falsity of the body" clarify the realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); second, the nine verses beginning with "the village of the six sense bases" clarify the realm of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); and third, the single line beginning with "the body is empty and false" concludes the aforementioned realms of the emptiness of persons and phenomena.
Regarding the statement that "this body is false and deceptive, serving as the objective realm for the emptiness of arising": the body is formed by gathering the aggregates (*skandhas*).
By calculating the existence of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) arises.

If one realizes that this arising is false and deceptive, then the body cannot be found upon investigation; the view of a self does not arise, and other cognitions and views likewise become quiescent. Therefore, with respect to this conventional arising, it is established as the objective realm of the emptiness of arising.

Furthermore, upon examining the origin of this body: a single thought of deluded imagination relies upon the physical form bequeathed by one's parents; this is the beginning of what is given a provisional name.
These two drops of red and white are the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
The discernment of suffering and pleasure is the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
The conceptualization of this suffering and pleasure is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
The possession of the three natures is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Consciousness abiding therein is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Furthermore, the semen and blood are the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*); moisture is the water element (*ap-dhātu*); warmth is the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*); and vital breath is the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). The space enclosed by these four great elements is the seed of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*), and the mind that dwells in dependence upon this is the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*); this is the beginning of the primary dharmas.
Contemplate this body and its name as dependent upon false and deceptive phenomena; how could they possibly be real?
Therefore, they are called "false and deceptive.
As for the "empty village," it refers to the accumulation of the body and its name, which arises like a bubble on water that encloses space; with the bubble arising, the name also arises.
As soon as it arises, it is subject to cessation; even the name "bubble" ceases.
Through the power of ignorance and karma, one takes recourse in the physical bodies of the parents, and thus the bubble of the aggregates (*skandha*) arises.
When the bubble of the aggregates arises, the designation of a "body" arises; when the bubble of the aggregates ceases, the designation of a "body" ceases. Therefore, it is called an "empty village."
From the "village of the six sense bases" onwards, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is elucidated.
How is this known?
