Because this passage merely scrutinizes the sense organs and their objects without discussing the self or persons (*pudgala*), we know it refers to the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena.
The text consists of three parts:
first, one line clarifies the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*); second, three lines clarify the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*); and third, five lines clarify the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).
As for the "six bases," they are the six sense organs.
That which is capable of producing consciousness is called a faculty (*indriya*).
That which is the destination of the objects (*viṣaya*) is called an entrance (*āyatana*).
Furthermore, because they are the points where consciousness enters, they are termed the six entrances (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Examining its primordial origin, there are but three things: namely, life-force (*jīvitendriya*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Like solidified butter or thin curd, it undergoes a transformation every seven days; blown by the subtle wind (*kauśalya-vāyu*), the five *kalala* (embryonic stages) unfold, and having gathered the pure matter of the four great elements, they coalesce to form the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body.
When the sense faculties (indriya) are established, they possess the function of producing consciousness (vijñāna).
This constitutes the opening up of form (rūpa) into five [aggregates], while mind (citta) is treated as one.
Because consciousness dwells in dependence upon the faculties, it is termed a "village" (grāma).
Dust enters through these [senses], and thus they are said to be the dwelling place of the thieves of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

When the eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the body touches, and the mind conditions, each has its own object of observation; they cannot be confused with one another, and thus it is said that "they do not know one another."
From the phrase "the eye-faculty receives form" (*cakṣurindriyaṃ rūpaṃ paśyati*) onwards, the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are clarified;
by further dividing "form" (*rūpa*) into ten and including a portion of one base, and by dividing "mind" (*citta*) into two, the twelve bases are established.
When the dust enters the sense organ, and the sense organ likewise enters the dust, they interpenetrate one another; this is collectively termed "entry" (*praveśa*).
When the sense organ gives rise to consciousness with particular intensity, it is specifically termed a "root" (*indriya*).
The meaning of "defilement" (rajas) is predominant here, so it is specifically termed "defilement.
When the defilements of a single sense-faculty mutually interpenetrate, it is said that each takes its own respective object.

Since the objects of other faculties do not enter this [particular] defilement, and this defilement does not enter the faculties of others, it is said that they do not function as objects for one another.
From the section "The Mind is Like an Illusion," the eighteen *dhātus* (realms) are clarified.
Here, the mind is further expanded into eight and form into ten.
As for the term *dhātu*, it refers to that which is demarcated and distinct without confusion; thus it is called a "realm."
The text consists of three parts.
First, from "The mind is like an illusion" onwards, it clarifies that consciousness pervades all sense faculties.
Even if the eyes and ears do not encounter their respective objects, the mind still pursues them with anticipatory thoughts; therefore, it is said to be "galloping about."
It is like a person who sits while racing across the world; because of ignorance, they do not know that the sense bases and objects are empty and treacherous, and thus they are harmed by bandits.
As it says in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, and so forth.
Second, from "The mind always relies upon" onwards, it clarifies that consciousness is constantly present in the faculties; therefore, the six faculties are mentioned.
Consciousness is also constantly present in the objects; therefore, the spheres of experience are mentioned.
If one were to claim that consciousness does not reside in either the faculties or the objects, why would there be immediate response and immediate cognition?
Because it is immediate awakening, it is always present within the faculties and their objects.
The *Śāstra* states: "When the faculty is unimpaired, the mind desires to hear, and there is also a sound—through the harmony of these various conditions, hearing occurs."
This is precisely that meaning.
Third, the passage beginning with "The mind resides within the six sense organs" clarifies how consciousness repeatedly emerges from and enters into the faculties.
It is like a bird in a net, flitting in and out, pecking at one thing and abandoning it for another in a continuous cycle, never resting for even a moment.
Consciousness within the network of the sense organs is likewise: it may reside in the ear or in the eye, its coming and going being without fixed location.
Although it is without fixed location, one can still discuss it as being "constantly present," and so forth.
The line beginning with "The body is empty and illusory" constitutes the third section, which summarizes the two types of emptiness regarding the phenomena of arising.
The emptiness of the body cannot be nourished or sustained; this summarizes the objective realm of the emptiness of arising.
Nourishment is one of these sixteen;
since nourishment is empty, the remaining fifteen are also empty, which constitutes the establishment of the objective realm of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, "there is no presiding master" establishes the objective realm of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The *Śālistamba-sūtra* (or *Upadeśa*) states: "Regarding these five faculties, the mind is their sovereign.
This clarifies that at the very beginning of conception, the mind resides prior to all other faculties and is therefore designated as the sovereign.
In fact, one cannot control the sense faculties; when the faculties become greatly disordered, the mind suffers affliction.
When the body is ill, the mind likewise follows suit.
How, then, can it be considered the master?
At times, the proponent and opponent may argue with one another as follows: "Earth possesses four subtle elements and is therefore dull, being constrained by water;
water possesses only three subtle elements and is therefore constrained by fire."
Fire consists of only two atoms and is constrained by wind;
wind consists of one atom and is constrained by the mind;
the mind has no atoms, and therefore it attains sovereignty.
Furthermore, because one is afflicted by the four great elements, the principle of a master cannot be established; therefore, it is said that there is no true master.
As for "there being no disputes," if one calculates that the four great elements exist, then contradictions will arise.
Just as four snakes might contend with one another or four nations might resist each other, there could be disputes and litigation.
Now, observing that the four great elements are empty, they cannot find an opening within emptiness; therefore, it is said that there is no dispute or litigation.
This concludes the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*).

From the seven lines of verse beginning with "Arising through the conjunction of various causes and conditions" onwards, the section explains the object by way of the accumulation of causes; this is the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).
The text consists of three parts:

first, two lines clarify the characteristic of collective origination; second, three and a half lines clarify the characteristic of the collection devouring one another; third, one and a half lines clarify the characteristic of the collection of wholesome and unwholesome objects.
The first three are the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), while the last one is the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*).
The first three are the objects of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana-viṣaya*), whereas the last one is the object of contemplation that assists the path (*mārga-sahāya-darśana-viṣaya*).
The former arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), while the latter arises from the cessation of ignorance.
If one were to discuss arising and ceasing directly, it would not differ from the Lesser Vehicle.
Ignorance is originally unarisen yet arises, and unceasing yet ceases; though arising and ceasing are non-dual, they appear as two.

Regarding "arising from various causes and conditions": both suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origination (*samudaya*) arise from causes and conditions; however, since one intends to clarify the meaning of origination, it is necessary to provide an explanation of the causes and conditions for origination.

Of these, the first three phrases refer to the causes and conditions for the arising of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), while the latter five phrases refer to the causes and conditions for the arising of substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*).

In the Hīnayāna, the four great elements are analyzed down to the subtle particles known as *paramāṇus*. From these subtle particles arise coarse particles; these are used as the causal conditions for establishing the provisional and the real.

Now it is clarified that while coarse matter can be analyzed away until it is exhausted, the subtle particles are likewise exhausted. When both the coarse and the subtle are entirely exhausted, what thing remains to serve as a causal condition?
Regarding "causes and conditions": ignorance, as an internal delusion, acts as the cause because one does not understand the two kinds of emptiness regarding phenomena and persons;
craving and attachment, directed toward the external, act as the condition because of defiled clinging to the spheres of contact.
Ignorance moistens craving, and through the accumulation of karma, birth arises; therefore, it is said that [birth] arises from the conjunction of various causes and conditions.
Because karma arises, there occurs a single moment of entering the womb, which invites the fruit of suffering.

This single thought-moment of entering the womb arises from ignorance and craving; since the mind that produces is already illusory, the mind that is produced is likewise illusory. When one investigates its beginning and end, both the agent and the object are entirely empty; therefore, it is said that there is no solidity or substance.
The five propositions arising from false conceptualization clarify the causes and conditions for the arising of real dharmas.
Due to the failure to comprehend through false conceptualization, in a single thought-moment one takes up residence in the womb, and the five aggregates arise.

Regarding the "mechanism of karmic power": wholesome and unwholesome karma is the master of the mechanism; the aggregate of form is the apparatus of the mechanism; the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations operate within it, moving to and fro and advancing or halting for its own amusement.
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) relies upon the six [senses] for its entry and abiding; therefore, it is called an "empty village.
Because it is produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta), it is said to be "established.

Regarding the phrase "increasing and decreasing according to time and mutually harming one another," as for the vertical discussion of increase and decrease, it is like the ten distinct stages described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
From the stage of the kalala, it is called "increasing"; at the stage of youth, it is called "flourishing"; and at the stage of old age, it is called "decreasing.
Regarding increase and decrease discussed crosswise: when fire increases, water decreases; when water increases, fire decreases; and the same applies to wind and earth.
Furthermore, there is arising and ceasing in every thought-moment; arising is increase, and ceasing is decrease.
Moreover, because new sense-faculties arise, there is increase; because the sense-faculties cease, there is decrease. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states:
"According to the seasons, they mutually harm one another; the wind of spring, the fire of summer, the earth of autumn, and the water of winter undergo increase and decrease," and so forth.
For example, when four snakes are first in their basket, it is called "birth";
when the strength of the four snakes is equal, it is called "vigour";
when they contend with one another over who is stronger or weaker, it is called "sickness."
When two snakes fight and become exhausted, they pause briefly and remain motionless; this is called "being well-adjusted. Once they have rested, they fight again.
When a snake becomes weak, it is like being old.
When a snake is severed, it is death.
Such increase and decrease constitute the fruit-body (*phala-kāya*), which arises from the accumulation of karma.
These four factors—attachment being like earth, hatred like fire, desire like water, and delusion like wind—are mutually contradictory.
The *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Śrīvyākarana-sūtra*) states: "Greed leads to old age; hatred leads to illness; delusion leads to death.
By extension, it says that the equal distribution [of the three poisons] leads to birth.
When accumulated karma devours one another, it causes the four great elements to increase or diminish, and so forth.
"Being in the same casket" clarifies that while the caskets are identical in nature, they differ in substance.
The snake possesses venomous stings, and the four great elements possess eighty-four thousand afflictions; in terms of causing harm, their significance is the same.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* uses the metaphor of a casket for the provisional body; the body depends upon the four great elements as a casket holds snakes. When the casket breaks, the snakes depart; when the body perishes, the great elements vanish—just as with a bird in a cage, and so forth.

Furthermore, the power of karma acts as a casket; karma sustains the four great elements, and when karma ceases, the elements disperse. Just as a bird within a cage seeks an exit everywhere, so too is the bird of the mind:
not for a single thought has it been bound within the casket of the body, but constantly rushes outward.
This is to seek death in every thought-moment; it is not the Way for securing the person.
As for their differing natures: the two that ascend are Yang, and the two that sink below are Yin.
Why are they contradictory?
It is because their natures are distinct.
How can things of distinct natures combine to form a body?

Regarding "the various directions also consist of two": the four great elements correspond to the four cardinal directions—wind in the east, fire in the south, earth in the west, and water in the north.
Furthermore, they correspond to the four seasons—wind in spring, fire in summer, earth in autumn, and water in winter.
The east and south belong to Yang and ascend; the west and north belong to Yin and descend; hence it is said that "two ascend and two descend.
The same applies to all directions.
If one speaks in terms of relative positions, the east rises while the west sinks, and the south ascends while the north descends.
If one discusses the four intermediate directions, the eastern direction encompasses two dimensions:
one dimension of yang above and one dimension of yin below.
The same applies to the other three directions.
Some say that within a single root all four great elements are present, with two above and two below, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "all extinguished without remainder": first one observes their dispersal and extinction, saying that wind and fire move upward while earth and water move downward. When one subsequently searches upward for wind and fire and examines downward for earth and water, they cannot be found; hence it is said they are "all extinguished without remainder."
The vast differences in the rising and sinking of karmic fruits arise from the accumulation of good and evil deeds, which diverge like the heavens, and so forth.

Regarding the fact that the two natures of mind and consciousness are restless and never still, the *Śāstra* states: "Mind, thought, and consciousness are one dharma with different names; it is called 'mind' (*citta*) in relation to enumeration, 'thought' (*manas*) when it is capable of generating [subsequent moments], and 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*) when it performs discrimination."

He further said: "There is a distinction: that which arises first is called mind (citta); that which arises next is called intellect (manas); and that which subsequently discerns is called consciousness (vijñāna). Just as with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), they cannot be considered one."

Regarding the "two natures": the mind (*citta*) possesses distinct natures of good and evil, and the mental faculty (*manas*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) likewise possess distinct natures of good and evil; therefore, they are said to have two natures. Regarding "restlessness" (*caukṣa*):

when the mind arises first, it is accompanied by mental factors (*caitasika*), and when the mental consciousness arises subsequently, it is also accompanied by mental factors; therefore, it is called restless.

Furthermore, when the four great elements are disintegrating, one is pulled in different directions by good and evil karma, not knowing from which side one will emerge; thus it is said to be "restless.

Since even this state involves the mind constantly engaged in vitarka and vicāra before the karma has yet expired, how much more so must there be restlessness when one is being dragged about by such karma?
There is "pulling by ripening" and "pulling by force.

Although one may practice wholesome deeds in this life, if the evil karma of a previous life has ripened, it will coincide with the present moment and one will immediately receive its retribution; therefore, it is called "pulling by ripening."

Regarding "forcible dragging": although a person may have committed evil deeds, at the moment of death, if their wholesome mind becomes intensely powerful, they will immediately ascend in accordance with that goodness.

Both "mature dragging" and "forcible dragging" clearly manifest the nature of agitation; they likewise involve falling into the various realms of existence in accordance with what is produced by karma, and so forth.
The two lines beginning with "When the elements of water, fire, and wind disperse, perish, and are destroyed" clarify that karma has ceased and the vessel of suffering is abandoned.
When the vital breath and life-force are exhausted, this is the departure of the wind; therefore, it is said to "disperse."
When heat is exhausted, this fire departs; therefore, it is said to "extinguish.
When water is exhausted, the body decomposes; therefore, it is said that "great and small impurities overflow externally.
When earth disperses and ceases, the bones and flesh fall apart; therefore, it is said to be "like rotten, decayed wood."

Regarding "the large and small impurities": the body is the large, while the four limbs are the small; the feet are the large, while the hands are the small; the hands are the large, while the fingers are the small. In this manner, they are successively categorized as large and small, all of which are filled with and flow forth from foul, putrid, and impure substances.
This is called the "Aids to the Path" (*bodhipakṣa*).

If one correctly contemplates and subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*), yet the afflictions are not subdued, one should practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an aid to breaking the mind of desire.

The *Śāstra* states: "The three gates of liberation are the doors to nirvāṇa; the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the methods for opening these doors; and the nine notions of impurity and so forth are the auxiliary methods for opening the doors."

Impurity is the primary gateway for breaking attachment to desire. If one advances in the cultivation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the great impurity (*mahā-aśubha*), then one's own body and the bodies of others, a single body and many bodies, a single land and many lands, mountains, forests, rocks, and walls—all bases of existence and all that they support—are entirely impure.
Although this may not yet be the case, if the power of visualization is perfected, a sense of dread will arise; this can greatly assist the Path and bring forth right wisdom.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The contemplation of impurity is both real and unreal. It is called 'real' because it can destroy afflictions; it is called 'unreal' because it designates what is pure as impure."
This contemplation of impurity also possesses both the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The *Mahā-sūtra* states: "Contemplate the white bones with discernment; among each of these joints and members, which one is 'I'?"
The eight-colored radiant light is likewise without self; since a self cannot be apprehended, this is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
The eight-colored light of the person of refined bone is not seen, and the four great elements lack substantiality; this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This concludes the explanation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) regarding the arising of phenomena, which ultimately results in the perfection of the Path.

From the passage beginning with "Good daughter, you should contemplate" down to the twenty-one lines, this is the second section, clarifying the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness regarding both arising and phenomena.
The text is divided into two parts:

first, eight and a half lines clarify the cultivation of the two types of emptiness—the emptiness of phenomena and the emptiness of persons—arising from causes; second, twelve and a half lines clarify the arising of function once the fruit is perfected.
Within the section on causes, there are further two sub-sections:

The first three and a half lines clarify the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness regarding arising phenomena (*utpattidharma*) in relation to suffering and its origin; next, from "The essence and characteristics of ignorance" downward, five lines clarify the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness regarding arising phenomena in relation to the twelve links of dependent origination.
Regarding the suffering and its origin, there are again two parts:

first, from "O virtuous daughter" down to one and a half lines, it clarifies the emptiness of sentient beings; second, from "In this way, these great [elements]" down to two lines, it clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Question:
The Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are teachings of the Two Vehicles; how can they be the contemplative gateways of a Bodhisattva?
Answer:

The Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are the objects of contemplation common to all three vehicles; they are like a great highway upon which both the noble and the humble travel together, such that one cannot claim it belongs exclusively to the common people simply because lowly folk walk upon it.
What is the general meaning? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the past, I and you all did not see the Four Noble Truths," and so forth.

It further states: "Ordinary beings have suffering but no truth; Śrāvakas have both suffering and the truth of suffering; Bodhisattvas understand suffering and, being free from suffering, possess the true truth; and the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess the true and the real."
Why is this so? Because the followers of the Two Vehicles contemplate the four truths as finite, whereas Bodhisattvas contemplate the four truths as both finite and infinite.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There are four kinds of twelvefold dependent origination:..."

By contemplating with inferior wisdom, one attains the state of a śrāvaka; by contemplating with middling wisdom, one attains the state of a pratyekabuddha; by contemplating with superior wisdom, one attains the state of a bodhisattva; and by contemplating with the most superior wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a Buddha.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that "the twelve links of dependent origination are the unique teaching of the Bodhisattvas.
For example, when the Buddha was formerly the youth Māṇava, although he practiced various deeds, they were not yet *pāramitās*."

Upon seeing Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; in a single thought-moment, he became harmoniously attuned to the practice of suffering as empty, up to the practice of cessation as empty; he became harmoniously attuned to the practice of ignorance as empty, up to old age and death as empty.
Among all forms of association, association with emptiness is the foremost; because practice guided by emptiness is called a *pāramitā*.
Because he had attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the Buddha immediately bestowed a prediction upon him.
One should know that do Bodhisattvas not contemplate the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination?
Although the Two Vehicles likewise contemplate them, there is a difference in their mode of contemplation.
The Śrāvakas contemplate all the fruits [of suffering] collectively as a single contemplation of the Truth of Suffering.
One contemplates all afflictions and karmic actions collectively as the Truth of Origination.
Furthermore, since both suffering and origination pertain entirely to the present, this is called the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The Pratyekabuddha contemplates suffering as sevenfold: five in the present and two in the future.
He contemplates origination as fivefold: two in the past and three in the present.

Because he contemplates the three periods of time separately and distinguishes between suffering and origination individually, this is called the "distinctive contemplation" (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*) of the Pratyekabuddha.

Although there are differences between the general and the specific, they are alike in being self-discipline and self-deliverance; they are alike in being the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness—the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena—yet they differ from those of the Bodhisattvas.

The Bodhisattva cultivates the four immeasurables and the six perfections for the sake of sentient beings; he contemplates the four truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, realizing the two kinds of emptiness regarding phenomena and persons.
To illustrate this now, I shall provide a simile.
It is like grasping five fingers to form a fist: if one finger were a fist, there should be five fists;
if one finger has no fist, how could there be five?
The self and persons are likewise: by gathering the five aggregates, one forms a sentient being.
If there were a sentient being within a single aggregate (skandha), there would have to be five sentient beings;
if there is no sentient being within a single aggregate, then even though there are five, there is still none.
One cannot find a sentient being by seeking it within the aggregates, nor can one find a sentient being by seeking it apart from the aggregates.
Although one may seek a fist and not find a fist, it does not preclude the existence of fingers with skin and bone;
although one may seek a person and not find a person, it does not preclude the existence of the phenomena of the five aggregates.

When those of the two vehicles attain the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they are not yet able to know the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). They must further analyze and seek the finger joint by joint—through the skin, flesh, bone, and marrow—and find that no finger can be obtained. By exhaustively pursuing earth, water, fire, and wind down to the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), they find that no form (*rūpa*) can be obtained. Since there is no perception or sensation (*saṃjñā-vedanā*) in either the preceding or succeeding moments of thought, when they seek the finger and cannot find it, they finally realize that the finger does not exist;
when they seek phenomena and cannot find them, they only then realize that phenomena are empty.

Since one cannot attain the objects of the two emptinesses—of persons and of phenomena—nor can one attain the wisdom of the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena, the same applies to the universal contemplation of the Bodhisattva.

This constitutes the Bodhisattva’s and the Two Vehicles’ analysis of the characteristics of the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena; it is as stated [in the text] regarding the distinction between merely practicing for oneself and acting for the sake of others.
If one discusses the emptiness of the individual substance of the bodhisattva, it is fundamentally different from that [previous case].
It is like seeing a fist in a mirror: since the substance suspended therein is already empty, there is no need for further investigation.
Since the fist in the mirror is illusory, the finger in the mirror is not real.
Since the clenched fingers within the mirror are illusory, the clenched fingers outside the mirror are likewise not real.
Sentient beings are also like this; they exist only as names, which we call "sentient beings."
These names are originally empty from the very beginning; they are not made empty through subsequent investigation.
Since names are merely provisional designations, phenomena (dharmas) are likewise not phenomena.

The essence of the name is itself the essence of the phenomenon, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The nature of the self is like the nature of form; the nature of form is like the nature of the self."
"In this world, the phenomena of birth arise from ignorance and volitional formations; since the five fruits are empty, how could the two causes be real?
As the subsequent text states: 'Their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent; they exist only because of ignorance.'"
Since ignorance has already been stilled, how could that which arises from ignorance not be stilled?
Although one does not apprehend the two objects—phenomena and dharmas—one can clearly and thoroughly penetrate these two objects without being defiled by them;

although one does not apprehend the two wisdoms regarding the emptiness of phenomena and dharmas, one can clearly and thoroughly penetrate these two wisdoms of emptiness without being purified by them.

Neither defiled nor pure, it transcends both extremes and correctly enters the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while simultaneously illuminating the two truths. The three truths are vividly clear;

they are realized as a single great awakening, neither before nor after. In accord with this profound *dharmatā*, one fully attains the treasury of the vajra jewel; this is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness—of self and phenomena—which arises from within the essence.
Although the various masters of the Hīnayāna speak of "analytical emptiness" (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*), their meaning is the same as that of the non-Buddhists. Why?
Because they analyze form down to its ultimate limit, the *paramāṇu* (atom), either leaving a residue of particles unbroken or breaking those particles until they are exhausted.
If it exists without being destroyed, it is merely the view of permanence;
if it is destroyed until all traces are exhausted, it is merely the view of annihilation.
Since the views of annihilation and permanence remain distinct and clear, what could this be other than heterodoxy?
Although various Mahāyāna masters speak of the emptiness of essence (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), they are the same as those of the Lesser Vehicle. Why?

Because by employing wisdom regarding essence alone, one cannot in a single thought-moment empty the mind, sport in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), purify Buddha-lands, or fully explain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; how then could one attain the three knowledges within a single thought-moment, or perfect the five eyes to achieve Bodhi?

He resembles a person in the Lesser Vehicle who has destroyed the Dharma; lacking the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, the knowledge resulting from vows, the *uṣṇīṣa*, and so forth, he is merely one liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*). How can this not be called the Lesser Vehicle?

Now, the opening fascicle of this sutra explores the profound and reaches the vast; the "Preface Chapter" speaks of "wandering within the immeasurable and most profound *dharmatā*," the "Emptiness Chapter" speaks of "seeking the Tathāgata’s true *dharmakāya*," and the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body" speaks of "seeking the quiescent, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. How could these be interpreted according to the heterodox views of worldly people?
How could one employ the analytical method of the Hīnayāna?
How could one employ the realization of essence by a Mahāyāna master to understand this meaning of emptiness?

The line beginning with "Good daughter, you should contemplate" (善女當觀) and the subsequent one and a half lines clarify the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*): the first phrase addresses the listener and exhorts them to practice; the next phrase points to the aforementioned object; and the final four phrases constitute the actual contemplation.
The "Virtuous Woman" is the tree deity of the Bodhi tree.

When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, there must always be one who responds and proclaims it; thus, by entrusting the teaching to a single individual, they instruct the multitude, and for this reason, they address that person.

Furthermore, at that time, the karmic conditions of the assembly were such that they were suited to a virtuous woman; if she heard this addressed to her, their past roots of goodness would be awakened.

Moreover, the male deity represents skillful means (*upāya*) and the female deity represents the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Since he wished to expound the perfection of wisdom to shatter ignorance and attachment, he addressed the female deity.
Furthermore, the Buddha attained the Way at the Bodhi tree; wishing to expound this Way, he addressed the tree deity.
This represents the four *siddhāntas*, and his addressing [the deity] was not without cause or condition.
"Regarding 'should be contemplated' (*dṛṣṭavya*): this encourages one person by taking them as an example for all.
All Bodhisattvas must cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); there is no Bodhisattva who does not do so through this. Therefore, it says 'should be contemplated.'"

"All phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) refers to the objects of the two types of emptiness—whether provisional or real—pertaining to the aforementioned Four Noble Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Although the terminology is brief, its inclusion of all phenomena is exhaustive; hence, it is called "all phenomena."
This explains, correctly and clearly, the general contemplation.
This "as it is" (yathābhūta) has three meanings: namely, as things (yathāvastu), as principle (yathātattva), and as neither thing nor principle.
"As things" refers, for example, to the provisional conceptualization of impurity used as an aid on the path, which may be applied diffusely.
"Suchness as principle" refers to the non-existence of the two types of emptiness regarding phenomena and their arising.
"Suchness that is neither phenomenon nor principle" refers to the *dharmatā* and the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, the phenomenon itself is suchness as principle, and suchness is that which is neither phenomenon nor principle.
That which is neither phenomenon nor principle is precisely as it is with respect to principle, and precisely as it is with respect to phenomena.
Principle is precisely as it is with respect to phenomena, and precisely as it is with respect to that which is neither phenomenon nor principle.
Because these three dharmas are neither identical nor different, they are called "thus" (tathatā).
Since the three dharmas are both identical and distinct, they are called "all dharmas.
The phrase "where is there a person? points toward the contemplation of principle (*li*).

As for "where": if a person were present in the sphere of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), the other four aggregates would not be required; yet if there is no person in the sphere of form, there is likewise no person in the other four spheres.
Since there is no person in any of the five locations, it is asked: "Where is there a person?
Furthermore, since there is no person in the location of the fruit, there is likewise no person in the location of the causes—ignorance and formations.
There is no person in the combination of cause and fruit, nor is there a person apart from cause and fruit; therefore, it is said: "Where is there a person?"
Since the person does not exist, the sixteen views regarding sentient beings and so forth are all non-existent; therefore, it says "as well as sentient beings.
The phrase "the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent" points out that this is neither a contemplation of phenomena nor a contemplation of principles.
The fundamental nature is without phenomena, nor is it empty.
Since emptiness is fundamentally empty of phenomena, and since there are no phenomena, what is there for emptiness to empty?

Because there are no phenomena, phenomena are quiescent; because there is no emptiness, emptiness is quiescent. Such is the fundamental nature; it has not been so only now. Therefore, it is said that the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent.
"Because of ignorance there is existence" points out the observation of phenomena.
If things were empty and yet further empty, how could these phenomena exist?
Since phenomena exist, emptiness exists; since emptiness exists, there exists that which is neither phenomenon nor principle. These three types all exist because of ignorance.

Because there is ignorance and delusion, there are formative forces (*saṃskāra*); because there are formative forces, there is the dharma of birth; since there is the dharma of birth, there is the contemplation that aids [the realization]; when the aid comes to assist the primary, there is the contemplation of the principle of emptiness; when the primary and the aid manifest the fundamental, there is the contemplation of that which is neither phenomenon nor principle.
Not knowing this matter is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "From delusion comes craving, and thus my illness arises; because the illness arises, medicine is produced."
This is precisely that meaning.

If one knows that the intrinsic nature of ignorance is empty and quiescent, such that ignorance itself does not even exist, how could there be phenomena or principles, or that which is neither phenomenon nor principle?
Because it is ultimately pure, it is called the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).
However, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is deeply ingrained and constitutes a great obstacle to the study of the Path.

Whatever an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) does is always accompanied by the notion of "I": when I walk, when I stand, when I sit, when I lie down, and when I speak, I am never apart from this "I"; likewise, when I practice giving and precepts, even up to practicing wisdom, I do so thinking, "I am practicing."
If one grasps at another’s physical remains and conceives of them as the self, this self is coarse and dull;
if one clings to sensory objects (*dharmas*) and conceives of them as the self, this self is subtle and sharp.

For instance, if one clings to a single phenomenon, thinking "I know" or "I understand," and gives rise to the notion of a self regarding that phenomenon, asserting that this one phrase alone is true while all else is false, this constitutes an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
To call what is not the Path "the Path" is the clinging to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
To call what is irrational "reason" is the clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
To call what is improper "proper" is false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
To disparage others from this point on is pride (*māna*). To repudiate [the truth] is anger (*pratigha*);

to praise is craving (*rāga*); to destroy is doubt (*vicikitsā*); and not to understand is delusion (*moha*). These ten underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*) take the self as their root; unaware of this, they increase day and night. Even if one possesses worldly wisdom and eloquence such that one could—as the long-nailed ascetic did—split rocks with stones, break trees with trees, exhaust water with water, or extinguish fire with fire, one will only move further away from the Path.

"Even if I were to follow the dhyānas up to the Brahma-world and reach the limit of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, my mind would remain constant; even as I emerge, it would return [to its former state].
Since such a vulgar heretic lacks even the 'warmth' of the Dharma, how could he possibly destroy me?"

To explain this self in detail, it consists of twenty types of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a real body): namely, five based on identifying the self with the aggregates, five based on identifying the self as separate from the aggregates, five based on the aggregates being within the self, and five based on the self being within the aggregates; these constitute the twenty.
If one aggregate were the self, the remaining aggregates would be without a self; if all were the self, there would be five selves.
This interpretation is not tenable.
If the self exists apart from the aggregates, since it is separate from the aggregates, whose self would it be?
This argument is not tenable.
If the self were contained within the aggregates, then the aggregates would be superior to the self, like a vessel containing fruit or a house housing a person.
This argument is not tenable.
If the aggregates were within the self, then the aggregates would be inside the self;
this meaning is not tenable.
This serves to refute the thirty types of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-identity), speaking thus with reference to external objects.

Yet, if the inner mind still conceives of a self, one should further reflect: does the self exist within wisdom, does it exist apart from wisdom, does wisdom exist within the self, or does the self exist within wisdom?
These arguments are all untenable; furthermore, they refute twenty kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-identity).
When the internal and external factors are combined, there are forty kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi; this is called the emptiness of persons (*pudgalaśūnyatā*).
The *Abhidharma* states: "The view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is a common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*).
When the view of self arises, it does not yet move the body or speech; it is only when volition (*cetanā*) subsequently arises following the view of self that the body and speech are moved."
Having severed the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one realizes the emptiness of sentient beings.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* clarifies that the mind of the view of self is precisely volition (*cetanā*), which is capable of moving body and speech.
Once the view of self is severed, one realizes the emptiness of sentient beings and also realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
In the Mahāyāna, it is held that the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) itself encompasses all phenomena; thus, one need not separately cultivate the contemplation [of their emptiness].
To realize the emptiness of sentient beings is precisely to realize the emptiness of real dharmas.
The refutation of the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* applies universally to all three preceding statements.
If principle is identical with phenomena, where is there a person?

Whether one identifies with the aggregates or is separate from them, there is no person within the aggregates, nor are the aggregates within the person. Since these twenty kinds of views have been refuted, it is said: "Where is there a person?"
The wisdom that is capable of observing is itself the person; there is a person apart from wisdom; the person exists within wisdom, and wisdom exists within the person.
This conception is also refuted; therefore, it is said: "Where is there a person?"

If one practices the contemplation of the fundamental emptiness and quiescence of what is neither an action nor a principle, then because of this fundamental emptiness and quiescence, there is fundamentally no self that is either identical to or separate from the aggregates (*skandhas*).
Since both the aggregates and the person who possesses the aggregates are non-existent, such conceptualizations are shattered; therefore, it is said: "Where is there a person?"
The nature of the wisdom that is capable of such observation is also quiescent; therefore, it is said, "Where is there a person?
When one practices the contemplation of impurity as an aid to the Path, if one observes with a defiled mind grasping at objects, this is precisely the defilement of the five aggregates.
If the wholesome mind possesses shame and remorse, this is precisely the skillful means for the concealment of the five aggregates.
This view all relies upon form; form is itself impure. Because it is impure, there is no person and no self; therefore, it is said, "Where is there a person?"
The observing wisdom that is capable of such observation is likewise so; therefore, it is said, "Where is there a person?

If one attains awakening through this discourse, the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) are destroyed; thus, one attains the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and no longer possesses the delusions of view.

As for those who practice the twenty kinds of contemplation, they eliminate the actual delusions; once the actual delusions are eliminated, one enters the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), at which point one should state where phenomena exist.

If one has not yet awakened to this and treats it as a formal treatise, although they may perform twenty kinds of contemplation, their views and delusions will not be eliminated; instead, while suppressing craving toward conventional designations, they will cross over into the true dharmas and conceive a self.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Sentient beings are attached everywhere; they abandon one thing only to grasp another, like the centipede that falters when asked to walk.
One must further apply twenty kinds of contemplation upon the true Dharma so that the wisdom of emptiness becomes clear, ensuring there is no fault in any circumstance.
The two lines beginning from "Thus, these great [elements]" clarify the contemplation of real dharmas (*dharmasatya*).
Since those who have previously attained the realization of emptiness already understand the dharmas,
this is further explained for the sake of those who have not yet realized it.
The text is also divided into three parts:

the first two lines show that phenomena are empty; the next line and phrase show that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is neither empty nor provisional; and the final line shows that phenomena are provisional—these correspond, for example, to the three aspects of the emptiness of persons.
"These great elements" refers to the four great elemental dharmas.
"Each is not real" precisely clarifies the contemplation of emptiness.
If the four great elements each maintained their own nature, then earth, maintaining its nature of solidity, should neither move nor be warm.
Water maintains its nature of moisture; it should not freeze, nor should it ripple.
Fire maintains its nature of heat; it should not solidify, nor should it flame.
Wind maintains its nature of motion; it should not be sustained, nor should it stop upon striking a wall.

Since the one great [element] possesses three natures, it is neither entirely solid, nor entirely moist, nor entirely hot, nor entirely mobile; because it loses its original nature, it is unreal, and being unreal, it is empty.

The *Sutra on Invoking Avalokiteśvara* states: "Earth has no solid nature; the nature of water does not abide; fire arises from conditions; and the nature of wind is unimpeded—each and every one enters the limit of reality as it is."
This is precisely its meaning.
Previously, one examined the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), hence it was said, "Where is there a person?
Now, one examines the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), hence it is said, "Each and every thing is not real."
That which is unreal is precisely emptiness.

That which is fundamentally unborn refers to the fact that the nature of dharmas is inherently neither born nor extinguished; it is neither the contemplation of emptiness nor the contemplation of the provisional.
Realizing that its essence is fundamentally unborn, there is no combination in the middle, and even at the end it is not empty.
Since the essence lacks the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), how could these elements arise? If the essence is fundamentally unborn, how could there be a combination in the middle?
If the four great elements are not in harmonious combination, how can the five aggregates be in harmonious combination?
If the great aggregates are not in harmonious combination, how can there be the emptiness of dharmas?
They are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; it is not through the wisdom of contemplation that they are made to be neither born nor extinguished.
"This is what is meant by 'the principle is identical with the phenomenon.
"By these causes and conditions" refers to the contemplative understanding of dependent origination.
When contemplation merges with the principle, one realizes that it is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "There are also causes and conditions; by extinguishing ignorance, one immediately attains the blazing lamp of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This is precisely the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That which exists through combination is merely a provisional designation based on phenomena.
Since its fundamental substance is not real, how could there be the great aggregates?
These arise from the causal karma of ignorance, which relies upon the fruit of the physical body remaining in this life; thus, there are the four great elements and the five aggregates.
This is precisely that which exists through the delusive conjunction of cause and effect.

Because this dharma exists, its essence is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent; it is simultaneously emptiness, provisionality, and neither emptiness nor provisionality.
The clear exposition of the Three Contemplations exists within the sūtras;

how could one not believe them? Yet, for those of dull faculties, they further create delusive appearances regarding real dharmas, such as claiming that the four great elements and the five aggregates are existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent.
Once the four attachments have arisen, this arising is called "existence" (*bhava*).
This view relies upon form; relying upon form, it gives rise to the notion of a self. From this self arise the five sharp [afflictions].
Through attachment to dharmas, one becomes angry, further giving rise to the five dull [afflictions].
The ten fetters (*daśa-āsrava*) are the origin (*samudaya*), which brings forth future suffering.

If one does not comprehend them in future lives, they will recur endlessly; within the great ocean of birth and death, amidst turbulent floods and billowing waves, one is perpetually deluded by the great darkness life after life.

These deluded material phenomena are the aggregate of form; sorrow and joy are the aggregate of feeling; grasping at signs is the aggregate of perception; the arising of good and evil is the aggregate of formations; and discrimination is the aggregate of consciousness.
Because the latent mind arises, it is called "existent phenomena," not that phenomena are empty.

When the mind does not rely on form, nor does it rely on sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, it becomes tranquil, extinguishing all evils and eliminating immeasurable transgressions.
Such a noble and sublime person is able to perceive Prajñā; they also perceive this most profound dharmatā within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, wherein they behold me, Śākyamuni.

If a practitioner can contemplate the two kinds of emptiness regarding arising and phenomena in this way, they are like one carrying jade to return to its source; within one or two lifetimes they will be able to accomplish their purpose, and it can be guaranteed that they will not be left alone.

The five lines beginning from "The essence and characteristics of ignorance" clarify the contemplation of the two emptinesses regarding the dharmas produced by the twelve links of dependent origination.
The text is divided into two parts:
the first three lines present the characteristics of the objects transcended, and the latter two lines present the characteristics of the contemplation itself.
The first section also has two parts:

the first two lines clarify the objective realm of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā). Thus, the text says, "it is called ignorance," and the *Śāstra* asks, "Who is old and dies? From this, we know it refers to the objective realm of the emptiness of persons.

The last line presents the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); the text says, "old age, death, sorrow, and affliction," and the *Śāstra* says, "this is old age and death. Therefore, we know this is the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena.

However, the sūtras and śāstras on the twelve links of dependent origination differ: some present them across the three periods of time, some as karmic retribution, some as a single moment, and some as ten types.

The "three periods" interpretation—wherein the two causes of the past refute the view of an eternal self, the five effects of the present refute the view of a substantial self, and the three causes of the present and two effects of the future refute the view of annihilation—is the one commonly employed in general practice.

Regarding "fruition" (*vipāka*): when first entering the womb at the stage of *kalala*, it constitutes ignorance; this refers to the twelve links throughout the beginning and end of a single lifetime.

Regarding "a single thought-moment": the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "The twelve causes and conditions exist within a single thought-moment of the mind," and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states, "The twelve causes and conditions are fully present in every person, in every single thought-moment."

When the eye sees forms, the failure to discern them is ignorance (*avidyā*); the arising of attachment and aversion is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); that which is the mental faculty therein is consciousness (*vijñāna*); form together with consciousness and formations is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the arising of craving through the six sense bases is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the encounter between form and the eye is contact (*sparśa*); the experiencing [of it] is feeling (*vedanā*); being entangled in form is clinging (*upādāna*); having perceived the characteristics of form, the arising of the mind is becoming (*bhava*); the arising of the mind is birth (*jāti*), and the cessation of the mind is death (*maraṇa*).
It is the same for mental volition and mental phenomena as well.
In one day and one night, how many times does one’s consciousness circle and entangle itself within the net of the twelve links of dependent origination?
Now, I shall further explain the characteristics of their causal arising.

If one contemplates that name-and-form arise from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and volitional formations arise from ignorance (*avidyā*), then any failure to understand this ignorance—whether asserting it as existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent—and thereby grasping at these four positions, all constitutes ignorance.

This reality is the formations (*saṃskāra*); that which is the mental faculty therein is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness together with the formations of form is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), each as previously explained.

Furthermore, observing a single moment of entering the womb is name-and-form; the unfolding of the five stages of the embryo is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the encounter of the six sense bases with their objects is called contact (*sparśa*); the experiencing thereof is called feeling (*vedanā*). Within this feeling, one makes a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi-vibhaṅga*): there is feeling, there is no feeling, there is both feeling and no feeling, and there is neither feeling nor no feeling.

As the eye perceives forms, the lack of clear understanding regarding those forms is ignorance (*avidyā*); the mind of attachment and aversion toward them is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); consciousness together with the formations of form is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the arising of craving through the six sense bases is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the rest is as explained above.

Up to the point where the mental volition regarding phenomena is not clearly understood, this is ignorance; craving for likes and dislikes constitutes the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); the rest is as explained above.
When one thus examines the great tree of the twelve links of dependent origination, its branches and twigs spread far and wide, covering the three realms entirely—who is able to fully comprehend it?
Who is it that destroys and fells?

Since this sutra is now a brief exposition, it does not discuss the three periods of time, a single thought-moment, and so forth; it merely cites the arising of phenomena as the objects for the two contemplations.
It should be illustrated by analogy: it is like grasping a firebrand and whirling it in the dark; a continuous circle of light appears, revolving incessantly.
The fire is the real dharma.
The "wheel" is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

Sentient beings, throughout the long night, are attached to these provisional designations, dancing with their burning embers without ceasing; they are deluded by the fuel of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), with their fires never extinguished. How, then, can the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) ever be brought to an end?
If one knows that the wheel depends upon the fire, then by stopping the hand, the wheel ceases;
the fire relies upon the fuel, so by removing the fuel, the fire ceases.
When both the wheel and the fire are absent, this is the twofold emptiness of arising and dharmas.
The section on the objective realm of the emptiness of arising consists of three textual examples.
The two phrases concerning the essence and characteristics of ignorance clarify that its fundamental nature is neither existent nor non-existent; this is the objective realm of the Middle Way.
The two phrases stating that it exists through the combination of deluded thoughts and causes and conditions constitute the perspective of the Provisional (Prajñapti).
The two phrases concerning the non-existence of objects constitute the sphere of the contemplation of emptiness.
Therefore, I have spoken of these two phrases to bring this to completion.

Regarding the single practice of consciousness and name-and-form, which clarifies the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena, there should likewise be three [phrases]; however, the text is abbreviated here, and the full meaning can be understood by grasping the underlying principle.
Below the section on "the karma of manifold sufferings," the contemplation of the two emptinesses regarding birth and phenomena (*dharmas*) is clarified.
This passage also contains three points:
the first point, concerning the inconceivability of the karma of manifold sufferings, clarifies the contemplation that is neither empty nor existent.

The two phrases, "fundamentally there is no arising" and "nor is there any combination," clarify the contemplation of emptiness: the former phrase, "fundamentally there is no arising," refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while the latter phrase, "nor is there any combination," refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The two phrases concerning "unwholesome reflection" clarify the contemplation of the conventional (parikalpita): unwholesome reflection in the past led to name-and-form in the present, and unwholesome reflection in the present will lead again to old age and death in the future, and so forth.
Although it is called the "contemplation of the two emptinesses of phenomena and persons," it is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle; the text is brilliantly clear.
When the explanation accords with the meaning, what cause for doubt could there be?
Furthermore, for those of duller faculties, I shall explain the characteristics of the contemplation of emptiness.
If conventional designations were produced inherently, they would not require real dharmas as their basis.
If they were produced by way of real dharmas, they would not be produced as conventional designations.
If [the designation] were produced through the conjunction of the provisional and the real, there would have to be two provisional [designations].
If it were apart from the provisional and the real, such a thing would be impossible.
These present provisional names exist only as words; these words do not abide within, without, or in between the two, nor do they possess self-existence eternally.
Because they cannot be apprehended, this is called contemplating the emptiness of conventional designations.
As for contemplating the emptiness of substantial dharmas: if name-and-form were produced spontaneously, it would not depend upon karma.
If karma were capable of producing [rebirth], why would the karma possessed by an Arhat not produce it?

If karma and its fruit were produced simultaneously, they would each have their own distinct names; yet if they are individually non-existent, how could they be simultaneous? If something were produced without causes and conditions, such a thing is impossible.
One cannot apprehend arising, nor can one apprehend non-arising; one cannot apprehend both arising and non-arising, nor can one apprehend neither arising nor non-arising.
One cannot apprehend cessation, nor can one apprehend non-cessation; one cannot apprehend both cessation and non-cessation, nor can one apprehend neither cessation nor non-cessation.

The absence of cessation and the absence of arising is called "non-arising. Because there is no arising, it is conventionally termed "destruction. Because it is conventionally destroyed, the sixty-two views are destroyed; because the views are destroyed, reality itself is also destroyed.
Since fire has not been kindled, there is no smoke;
since one dances over ashes at midday, there is likewise no wheel.
This is a brief demonstration of the characteristics of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Regarding the "Middle Way Contemplation" and "Provisional Contemplation," it is stated in the *Separate Record* (*Bieji*) and so forth.

The twelve and a half verses beginning with “I have severed all fetters of views” constitute the second section: the function of the two emptinesses arising from the fruit, clarifying the realization of the fruit through the perfection of contemplation.
The text consists of two parts:

the first three and a half lines concern the accomplishment of one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*), and the subsequent nine lines concern the accomplishment of transforming others (*para-parāvṛtti*).
Within the section on one's own practice, there are further two parts:
The first two lines describe the fulfillment of the virtue of wisdom; the subsequent one and a half lines describe the fulfillment of the virtue of abandonment.
Regarding "all views," this refers to the sixty-two views, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), and so forth; therefore, it is called "all."
This refers to the accomplishment of the contemplation of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

"With the sword of wisdom" is a metaphor for the utility of wisdom; the upper part of the metaphor represents the severing of [wrong] views, while the lower part represents the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Envelopments" (paryavasthāna) specifically clarifies the ten envelopments;
"the net of afflictions" (kleśajāla) generally clarifies the ten proclivities (anuśaya).
A net has the fault of ensnaring and confining, while a house has the defect of covering and darkening.
Reaching the profound emptiness and stillness of the aggregates (*skandha*), darkness and obstructions cannot cover it;
tearing asunder the net and destroying the snare, no trap can hinder it.
This is the accomplishment of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
What the followers of the Two Vehicles sever are the general fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), while what the Bodhisattvas sever are the specific fetters of views.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "If the habit-energies of the fetters are not yet exhausted, flowers will cling to the body."
"Because he had not yet severed his distinct views, he was caught by the flower.
As for saying that the Buddha has severed the fetters of views—whether generally or specifically—the ultimate exhaustion of these lies solely in the Buddha."
The *Śāstra* states: "Among sentient beings, the unsurpassed is the Buddha; among phenomena, the unsurpassed is Nirvana.

Whether these [categories of] the unsurpassed are conventional or ultimate is something that the stage of Buddhahood does not confuse; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] has severed [all delusions].

The sūtras and śāstras differ in their explanations; some state that the Buddha’s supreme wisdom cuts off the lowest grade of delusions. Because the power of ignorance is great, it is only the Buddha’s wisdom that can sever it, such that in a single moment of corresponding insight, both the active afflictions and their latent tendencies are exhausted without remainder.
Some say that for those who are superior beings, it is called "severance," while for those who are unsurpassed beings, it is called "having nothing to sever.
This is because, according to the country, the time, the person, and the awakening, there is benefit in all cases, and so forth.
The realization of the unsurpassed path signifies the fulfillment of the right path of the two emptinesses of birth and phenomena (*dharmas*).
Subtle and wondrous merit signifies the fulfillment of the auxiliary paths of the two emptinesses of birth and phenomena.
The line and a half following "Opening the Gate of Ambrosia" clarifies the perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the divine medicine of immortality for the gods; those who consume it enjoy long life, physical well-being, great strength, and a radiant body.

It is like the Buddhas’ virtue of cessation abiding in Great Nirvāṇa; when the functions of true permanence, bliss, self, and purity are realized, one knows that this virtue of cessation is fulfilled.
However, the underlying meaning of this principle further intends to correspond to the various stages described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
"Opening the gate of ambrosia" corresponds to the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*); because it first opens the noble path to obstruct the two extremes, it is called "opening.
"Showing" corresponds to the ten practices (*daśacaryā*); it refers to the detailed and sequential manifestation [of the path].
"Entering the 'Ten Dedications' (daśapariṇāmanā) corresponds to turning back from phenomena to enter into principle.
Abiding in the 'Ten Stages' (daśabhūmi) corresponds to dwelling in the chamber of the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Consuming the flavor corresponds to wondrous enlightenment; one partakes of this flavor oneself while simultaneously bestowing it upon others."
It is not that those on the lower stages do not transform others; however, because their own practice is not yet perfected, their transformation of others is likewise not extensive.

At the stage of Buddhahood, the fruit is perfected: the virtue of cessation is already fulfilled, and the power of compassion is great. Thus, one is able to open the way for sentient beings through the ten abodes (*vihāra*), demonstrate the ten practices (*caryā*), lead them into the ten directions (*pratiṣaṇna*), and establish them in the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Having partaken of the flavor of nectar (*amṛta*) and being fully endowed with all merits, both the purpose of the virtue of cessation and the purpose of transforming others are accomplished.

Furthermore, these correspond respectively to the four wisdoms of prajñā: "opening" corresponds to the wisdom of the path (mārgajñatā), "showing" corresponds to the wisdom of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), "entering" corresponds to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), and "abiding" corresponds to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); "tasting the flavor" corresponds to the Buddha’s dwelling in great parinirvāṇa.
Out of great compassion, he causes sentient beings to attain these four wisdoms; thus, there is no contradiction in the meaning that they are severed at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, this corresponds to the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*), leading beings to enter it.

This is truly because the Buddha’s virtues are perfect and complete; he appears in the world for the sake of great causal conditions to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby also manifesting the meaning of his perfection in cessation.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of "permanence, bliss, self, and purity," which is most convenient for the fruit of cessation (*phala-prahāṇa*), as explained previously and so forth.
The nine lines beginning with "blowing the great dharma-conch" clarify the fulfillment of transforming others at the stage of fruition.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, two lines on turning the wheel of Dharma to transform others; second, seven lines on the four great vows to transform others.
Within the exposition of the Dharma, there are again two sections:
The first line expounds the Dharma, while the second line displays supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

In other sutras, the initial display of supernatural powers startles beings to open the way for the subsequent exposition of the Dharma; in this present sutra, however, the final display of supernatural powers serves to fulfill the preceding exposition of the Dharma.

When cultivating the cause, one gives rise to the correct wisdom of the two emptinesses of phenomena and persons; when attaining the fruit, the perfection of knowledge and virtue is achieved, whereby one is able to teach the Dharma and transform others.

When cultivating the cause, one gives rise to the auxiliary path of the two emptinesses of phenomena and persons; when attaining the fruit, the perfection of the abandonment of defilements is achieved, whereby one is able to employ supernatural powers to transform others.

Regarding the four analogies presented in the exposition of the Dharma: the benefits of hearing the Dharma are indeed immeasurable; yet these four are cited in brief, each intended to correspond to a specific point.

Blowing the conch shell signifies a change of designation; it is an analogy for the Buddha’s teaching of the *Hīnayāna* (Lesser Vehicle) Dharma, which transforms the ordinary nature of suffering-endurance characteristic of worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and leads them into the true nature of the sages (*ārya*).
The Mahāyāna teachings explain how one transforms the biased natures of both ordinary beings and sages to enter the perfect nature of the Middle Way.

The seventh stage of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the first stage of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), and the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) are all positions of changing one's designation; they represent the transition from the biased toward the Middle.

"Beating the great Dharma drum" refers to beating the drum to urge progress and lead the assembly forward; this is a metaphor for the Buddha preaching the Dharma to supervise and encourage deep practice. The stage of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) is at the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*) is at the eighth stage (*aṣṭamabhūmi*); the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*) is at the ten practices (*daśaprayoga*); and the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇayāna*) is at the first dwelling (*prathamavihāra*). In all these stages, through the power of hearing the Dharma, one collectively advances toward the true path of cultivation.

Regarding "kindling the great torch of the Dharma": a torch can illuminate itself and also illuminate others; this is a metaphor for how the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma brings benefit to both oneself and others simultaneously. It is like a single lamp being able to dispel the darkness of a thousand-year-old room, or like one lamp igniting hundreds of thousands of other lamps.
The power of hearing the Dharma to benefit both oneself and others is likewise so.

This refers to the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the ten stages of the Dedication of Merit in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), and also the first dwelling (Chuzhu) of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); these are all positions where the path and contemplation flow together, benefiting both self and others.
Regarding "the rain of the supreme Dharma-rain": while ordinary rain can bring maturity, it requires the labor of farmers to make the growth lush and abundant.

When the seasonal moisture descends once, flowers and fruits flourish; this is analogous to how, although one may diligently cultivate various practices, the momentum for entering the path remains weak.

Hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, they increase their progress on the Path and diminish their births, maturing spontaneously until they naturally flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
It is like a ship upon the great Ganges: without exerting physical strength, it swiftly reaches its destination.
These all pertain to the stage of the "two streams," as explained above.

If one grasps this meaning, then the four stages of the *Avataṃsaka*, the four wisdoms of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the four types of knowledge and vision of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the four virtues of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* can all be understood by analogy.

This single Dharma stands vertically as the locus for all sutras and extends horizontally across all stages; upon hearing the sound of the Dharma, each according to their kind understands it accordingly, and so forth.
Regarding the four similes herein, the term "great" is used because they expound the Great Dharma.
The general explanation clarifies that the Great [Vehicle] is not the stage of the Small [Vehicle].
The passage beginning with "I now subdue" refers to the transformation of others through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
As for "enmity-knots," the fourth dwelling-place (*vihāra*) constitutes the enmity-knot of the Two Vehicles, while the fifth dwelling-place constitutes the enmity-knot of the Bodhisattvas.

Māra is the lord of the afflictions (*kleśa*). To fell a tree, one must remove its roots; to transform sentient beings, one must first subdue their lord. If Māra is not subdued, the path of transformation will not flourish.

The method for subduing Māra requires the employment of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); just as one can only be called brave after defeating an enemy, the King of Dharma cannot be destroyed otherwise.
The Victorious Dharma King: at this time, the path of transformation is thus established.
"Raising the Dharma Banner" refers to the Samādhi of the Dharma Banner.
It rises loftily above all practices and serves as the point of reference for all practices, just as soldiers look toward a military standard.
The three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal; therefore, they are called "subtle and wondrous.
From the phrase "delivering all sentient beings" downward for seven lines, these constitute the four great vows for transforming others.

Although they have already attained fruition, their original vows do not cease; therefore, it is said that the Four Great Vows benefit sentient beings, which is also called benefiting sentient beings through the Four Noble Truths.
The Four Great Vows are the mind of aspiration, while the Four Noble Truths are the objects of that focus.
To deliver all sentient beings is the first great vow; it is also to cause those who have not yet crossed over the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) to cross over that truth of suffering.

From the line beginning with "The afflictions burn fiercely" is the second great vow; it is also to cause those who have not yet severed the truth of origination (samudayasatya) to sever that truth of origination.

The line beginning with "I shall [attain] the ambrosia" constitutes the fourth great vow; it is also the act of causing those who have not yet realized the Truth of Cessation to realize the Truth of Cessation.

The four lines beginning with "Throughout immeasurable kalpas" constitute the third great vow; it is also the act of causing those who have not yet established themselves in the Truth of the Path to establish themselves in the Truth of the Path.
In this context, giving (*dāna*) is identified as the Four Noble Truths.

Giving stands in opposition to stinginess (*mātsarya*); stinginess and greed that obscure oneself constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). The karma of origination that summons its fruit constitutes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Giving, which can destroy stinginess, is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), and the cessation of stinginess is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
"Innumerable kalpas" refers to the high accumulation of merit.
"Diligently practicing all deeds" refers to the broad integration of the Dharma.
As the Treatise says:
The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses the six [perfections], and so forth.
When one relinquishes body, life, and wealth to become equal with the future limit (*aparānta*), and thereby attains the indestructible and eternally abiding, it is called a *pāramitā*.
Because it is lofty in height and vast in breadth, it is said that one follows the various practices of the branches.
The Words and Phrases of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Four;
*Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* Words and Phrases, Fascicle Five.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty.

The Disciple Guanding’s Record of the Commentary on the Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings. Regarding the Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings: they are the foremost of those ascending and the first heaven of the lower realms, dwelling upon the middle of Mount Sumeru.
On the eastern golden terrace, the king is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, translated as "Holder of the Nation," who leads the gandharvas and pūtanas;
