on the southern lapis lazuli terrace, the king is named Virūḍhaka, translated as "Increasing," who leads the kumbhāṇḍas and preta-spirits;
on the western silver terrace, the king is named Virūpākṣa, translated as "Diverse Speech," who leads the piśācas and venomous nāgas.
In the north is the crystal terrace; its king is named Vaiśravaṇa, which translates as "Much-Hearing" (Duowen). He leads the yakṣas and rākṣasas.

Upon hearing this sutra, these four kings rejoiced and each led five hundred attendants to take a vow to protect the sutra. Because this serves as the introductory chapter from this point onward, it is titled the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings."

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the East represents the Truth of Accumulation, the South the Truth of Suffering, the West the Truth of the Path, and the North the Truth of Cessation; these four truths constitute the four heavens. The wisdom that contemplates the Four Truths constitutes the Four Heavenly Kings. Protecting the realm of the Four Truths is called "Protecting the Nation," and protecting the mental factors is "Protecting Sentient Beings."
"World" (*loka*) refers to others; to preach the Dharma for others is called "protecting other sentient beings.

Regarding the "eight classes" (*aṣṭa-nikāya*): beneath the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there are sharp and dull faculties of both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). The *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) designates these as ghosts and spirits (*bhūta-preta*). Furthermore, beneath the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there are likewise views and afflictions; these constitute the eight classes.

If one does not illuminate the principle of the Four Noble Truths, the two delusions of views and thoughts will assail the sovereign mind-king and ravage the realm of objects. Consequently, the sovereign mind perishes and the kingdom of objects is destroyed; the subjects of mental factors scatter in all directions, and both objects and wisdom are tormented by demons.
If one can contemplate suffering and its origin to control these views and thoughts, then the kingdom will be secure and the people at peace.
To be able to expound the Four Noble Truths for others is to protect their lands; by obstructing their views and afflictions, one enables them to attain peace and happiness.
This constitutes the practice of the Four Heavenly Kings of the World who protect through the contemplation of the mind.
The following thirteen chapters constitute the section on circulation (*pravartana*).

Out of compassion for the final age, the Buddha ensured that evil would not obscure the true and correct, and that this King of Sutras would not be obstructed in future generations; thus, those with the karmic affinity would be able to receive and hear the correct teaching. Therefore, it is called "circulation."
This consists of seven general themes:

from the "Four Heavenly Kings" to "Samantabhadra," these clarify how the Heavenly Kings make vows to encourage and exhort human kings to widely proclaim this sutra; they demonstrate the correct assembly of virtuous discourse; they clarify how human kings propagate the sutra and how the Heavenly Kings provide protection and assistance; and they further illustrate the methods for propagating the sutra during one's lifetime.
The "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" clarifies the merit of listening to the sutra, wherein devas, terrestrial deities, rivers, seas, and bodhisattvas all provide protection for such a person.
The "Chapter on Prophecy" attests to the non-falsity of the merit gained from listening to the sutra.
The "Curing of Illness" and "Flowing Water" chapters cite the merit of listening to the sutra in the past to certify that the present act of upholding it is not erroneous.

The "Sacrificing the Body" chapter cites the practice of not sparing one's life for the sake of the sutra in the past, admonishing both teachers and disciples not to be stingy with the wealth of the Dharma.
The "Chapter on Praising the Buddha" clarifies how the various bodhisattvas extol the Buddha-dharma, proclaiming what has been taught with profound and grave benefit, and so forth.
Furthermore, the King of Devas makes fivefold vows:
first, the Four Heavenly Kings protect the requester through their celestial power.
In the "Chapter on Great Eloquence," he pledges to enrich the speaker with eloquence;
in the "Chapter on Goddess Puṇyavatī," he pledges to provide material wealth to sustain the speaker who requests it;
and in the "Chapter on the Earth Deity," he pledges to provide the essence of the earth's fertility to nourish the place where the teaching is requested and the place where it is taught.

In the "Chapter on Vaiśravaṇa," he vows to use martial prowess to crush external enemies and subdue internal troubles, thereby establishing peace for those who request, preach, and listen [to the Dharma].

Furthermore, the "Deva King" protects the nation; "Mahāprajñā" protects the teacher; "Guṇakara" protects the assembly; "Earth Deity" protects the land; and "Vaiśravaṇa" averts calamities, so that the sutra and the Dharma may spread widely, and so forth.
The "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" consists of six rounds of question and answer, which form six sections:

first, an address to the Buddha describing their capacity to protect the nation; second, an address to the Buddha describing the manner of their protection of the nation; third, an address to the Buddha demonstrating their ritual procedures; fourth, an address to the Buddha requesting the benefits of the Dharma; fifth, an address to the Buddha describing both prosperity and decline; and sixth, an address to the Buddha speaking verses to praise his virtues.
The first section is divided into two parts:
first, the petition to the Buddha; second, the Buddha’s confirmation.
The petition to the Buddha is further divided into two parts:
First is the introduction by the sūtra compiler; second is the formal address to the Buddha.
The expression of reverence follows the text.
The section on the formal address to the Buddha is divided into two parts:
First, there is the praise of the sutra; second, the description of its protectors.
Because the various devas have the power to believe in the Dharma, the sutra is praised.
Desiring that the sutra be widely propagated, its protectors are described.
The praise of the sutra is threefold:

from "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*" onwards, it praises the essence of the sutra; from "Adorning the Bodhisattvas" onwards, it praises the central theme of the sutra; and from "This sutra can illuminate" onwards, it praises the function of the sutra.
The formal exposition is extensive, whereas praising the Three [Treasures] is a concise summary of that vastness.
The principle of *dharmatā* is what the Buddha protects and keeps in mind; because the text elucidates this principle, it is called the "King of Sūtras."
Since it is called the "King of Sutras," we know this is a praise of its essence (*tattva*).
By practicing in accordance with this essence, one enables the bodhisattva to be endowed with the two adornments (*alaṃkāra*) and achieve the ultimate fruit.
Since it speaks of "adornment," we know this is a praise of its central theme (*mūla*).

The worldly devas, the pure devas, and the devas of ultimate meaning all revere and look up to this ground of the ultimate stage; they offer worship through the three karmas—honoring this body with their physical acts, gladdening this mind with their mental intentions, and praising this speech with their verbal expressions.

Furthermore, from the hells below up to the bodhisattvas above, all possess the affliction of feverish distress as long as ignorance has not been exhausted; this sutra can eliminate it, bringing clarity and coolness like the moon—this is a praise of its efficacy, and so forth.
From the passage "The World-Honored One is the Golden Light" onwards is the second section, which describes the protection of the nation.
This text consists of two parts:
first, protecting the nation internally through the Dharma; second, protecting the nation externally through strategic counsel.
There are four further ways of protecting the nation through the Dharma:

first, the reasons for protecting the nation; second, protecting the nation by means of the Dharma; third, protecting the nation by means of celestial allies; and fourth, protecting the nation by means of the divine eye.

As for the reasons for protecting the state: by hearing this sutra, one obtains four benefits—benefit in the body through radiant light, benefit in strength through valor, benefit in the mind through advancement, and benefit in virtue through dignity.
One shall obtain two benefits in principle: namely, that both the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom will increase.
Since it is through the state’s propagation of the sutras that this Dharma-moisture is brought forth, how could one not protect it?

To explain why this is so: this meaning precisely accords with the contemplation of the mind; to protect the objects of the Four Truths by means of the wisdom of the Four Truths is itself the practice of the True Dharma.
By means of the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, one guides all mental factors so that they do not function; therefore, this is called practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is precisely what it means to be able to preach the True Dharma; because there is such internal protection for the state, one is called a World-Protecting King who rightly governs the realm.
That the general leads his faction to protect the state is also in accord with the contemplation of the mind.

The mind-king leads the faction of mental factors (*caitta*) to subdue the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), just as the celestial kings, together with their retinues, ward off all evil spirits; or like a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) who, accompanied by the seven treasures and a thousand sons, is such that wherever he goes, the four quarters submit to his virtue.
When the Four Heavenly Kings together oversee five hundred regions, what evil would not be eliminated?

As for those who protect the nation with the divine eye, because they possess the power of clear vision obtained as a karmic reward, there is no hidden darkness they do not illuminate; by preventing incipient signs and stopping gradual developments, what evil would not be eliminated?

Second, from the passage beginning "If this land suffers various calamities and depletions" onwards, is the protection of the nation through wisdom and strategy, which brings together internal and external causes and conditions.
This section consists of three parts:

first, if the king’s realm has many disasters and various hardships—namely, war, famine, and disease—I shall use my wisdom and strategy to urge the Dharma Master to go; or I shall urge him to go through my majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhi*); or I shall urge him to go by manifesting my form; or I shall urge him to go by appearing in his dreams.
If the Dharma Master goes forth to propagate this sutra extensively, it will be like the sun rising in the morning, where the mists and fogs naturally dissipate.
This is an exhortation regarding external conditions.
Next, if the king’s mind lacks the illumination of wisdom, calamities will follow as darkness enters.
If one possesses clear wisdom, strange portents will not arise.
Since the Master has come forth holding the Dharma, the King must listen with single-minded devotion.

If the King listens diligently, the heavens will likewise provide diligent protection; thus, that which is worthy of being favored shall be favored, and that which is worthy of being protected shall be protected. One person shall have cause for celebration, and its benefits shall extend to the myriad regions; the King’s person and the state shall be secure and free from calamity.
This is the internal cause.
Even if there are those who propagate the Dharma externally, if the king’s inner mind is not earnest and reverent, then they will not be in harmony, and the calamities cannot be averted.
Second, if a king lacks the practice of giving, his fortune and merit will be meager, just as a granary and kitchen will have little grain if one does not diligently cultivate the fields.

[The Buddha] exhorts the king to expend his wealth to provide for the fourfold assembly; when the fourfold assembly attains peace, their merit and sustenance will benefit the king, and the entire nation, along with its kin and dependents, will be free from all suffering.
When these internal and external causes and conditions harmonize, they can bring about abundant harvests and prosperity, and so forth.
Third, if the king’s person lacks the virtuous conduct of former kings, his ministers and subjects will not obey;
if his speech lacks the righteous teachings of former kings, neighboring states will not sing his praises.
I now exhort the King to offer worship through the three karmas: reverence is the karma of the body, honor is the karma of the mind, and praise is the karma of speech.
Indeed, the lofty take the lowly as their foundation, and the eloquent take the reticent as their teacher; to humble oneself and respect the inferior is a merit of no small measure.
By the majestic power of Heaven, neighboring states venerated him from afar; their feathered dispatches offered praise, and their songs expressed admiration and envy.
The three karmic actions were reverent and upright; the superior’s transformation of the subordinates was like the wind bending the grass.
When it was thus in the neighboring states, there were no oxen, horses, grasses, or leaves among the people that did not turn lowly toward [the center].

This is because the causes and conditions of the one who praises and the object praised have harmoniously converged; thus, the sounds of praise overflowed into the neighboring states, as can be clearly seen by examining the scriptural text.
Next, the Buddha provides a summary and confirmation, which consists of two parts:
first, a combined summary and praise of the sutra; second, a summary of its ability to protect the state.
Regarding the four kings' initial praise of the sutra’s exposition as being consistent with reason, the Buddha summarizes and confirms it.
Having completed the three praises concerning its essence, principle, and function, the Buddha joined in exclaiming, "Excellent, excellent!
This initial general praise of the single teaching was then further validated by the Buddha, such that it became a universal eulogy for hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
Since all Buddhas are born from this Dharma, many praises are cited to establish the significance of this single point.
From the passage "In the presence of all Buddhas" onwards, the text describes how [this Dharma] is able to protect the nation.
Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, the account of protecting the nation through the Dharma; second, the account of protecting the nation through the eye of wisdom.
Regarding the four ways of protecting the nation through the Dharma, the Buddha confirms and completes them all.
The preceding section clarified the reasons for protecting the nation, which arise from hearing this sutra and attaining its benefits.
The Buddha now describes these present benefits, noting that they truly stem from seeds planted in the past.

"The initial resolve and the ultimate fulfillment are not two different things; yet between these two states of mind, the former is more difficult. Therefore, I pay homage to the first arising of the bodhicitta."
This passage cites what precedes to establish what follows, and describes what follows to clarify what precedes.
From the section beginning with "preaching the True Dharma" onwards, it describes how he protects the world through the Dharma.

The preceding passage states that they are called "World-Protectors" (Lokapālas) because they are able to teach and practice; the Buddha likewise confirms that they are named World-Protectors for being able to teach and practice, and so forth.
From the words "You all today," the text skips ahead to describe how their divine eye protects the nation; although this is slightly out of sequence, there is no loss of meaning in the doctrine.
The preceding passage states that by means of the pure divine eye, which surpasses the human eye, the Buddha brings benefit throughout the long night.
Now, the divine eye illuminates at night without depending on the light of the sun; therefore, it is called the "long night."
From the passage beginning with "You, the Four Kings and your retinues," the text retrospectively describes how their celestial factions protect the nation.
Previously, this was stated directly as protecting the nation; now, the Buddha further praises it as protecting the True Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
From the passage beginning "You, the Four Kings, and the other hosts of devas," the text describes how their wisdom-eye unites to protect the kingdom.
Whereas the preceding section spoke of requesting a Dharma Master to enter the realm to avert evil, this merit now returns to themselves, enabling them to repel the armies of the asuras.

"You have exhorted the King to listen to the sutras and provide for the fourfold assembly; the Buddha describes how his internal wisdom and external merit truly serve to subdue all sufferings and bring about peace and happiness," as stated at length in the text.
The second section recounts the matter of protecting the state as addressed to the Buddha.
It consists of two parts:
first, the address to the Buddha; second, the Buddha’s confirmation and elaboration.
The white report to the Buddha further consists of two parts:

first, regarding the places where this sutra circulates, if the king there is able to receive it upon his head and provide for the fourfold assembly, I and my retinue vow to remain invisible and thereby manifest its benefits.

Second, when evil neighbors raise armies to invade and displace a virtuous nation, I shall conceal my form and stir up various terrors and manifold calamities, causing their military forces to clearly retreat and scatter.
If they do not even disturb the borders, how much less could they harbor [hostility] within?
Next, the Buddha’s confirmation consists of two parts:
from "At that time, the Buddha praised... down to "...there shall be no disputes," this constitutes the confirmation of the first meaning.

The invisible spirit who protects the state desired to cause this scripture to flourish; the Buddha then explained that this invisibility is the protection of the Three Jewels: "I am the Jewel of the Buddha; the cultivation of bodhi is the Jewel of the Dharma; and the absence of strife and litigation among kings is the Jewel of the Sangha. Thus he described how protecting one [the state] enables the fulfillment of all three.
From the passage "The Four Kings should know that in this Jambudvīpa" onwards, the subsequent intent is being explained and established.
Above, by means of celestial majesty to intimidate them and celestial power to repel them, it appears as though [the deities] loathe evil and cherish goodness.

The Buddha exhorted them to direct a mind of universal compassion toward all; thus, those who do evil become naturally apprehensive, while those who do good become naturally joyful. This is not because he treats the wicked with contempt or the virtuous with favoritism, but rather to fulfill the intent of making the former feel their own remorse and retreat from evil.

Furthermore, he exhorted the various kingdoms to each maintain their original occupations, to dwell peacefully within their own borders, and not to give rise to covetous desires. He taught that if the kings are harmonious, the people will not suffer untimely deaths; and if the Dharma flourishes, its fragrance will permeate the heavens.

The Buddha told Śakra: "The causes and conditions of strife lead to the decline of devas and humans. One who is truly capable of bringing kindness and harmony to the world does not merely make offerings to me; they are making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
Such a person does not merely bring peace to one king, but brings peace to all kings;
they do not merely bring peace to one nation, but brings peace to all."
Therefore, it is through compassion and harmony that the second intention is fulfilled, and so forth.
Third, the white-robed one addresses the Buddha to demonstrate the model for a human king.
The text is divided into two parts:
First, it reveals his aspirations; second, it demonstrates his model of conduct. There are six aspirations:
first, the desire to bring peace to one’s own person;

second, the desire to bring peace to one’s wife and children; third, the desire to bring peace to one’s palace; fourth, the desire for sovereign rule over a preeminent realm; fifth, the desire to gather all merits and virtues; sixth, the desire that the kingdom be free from sorrow and suffering.
The six vows are as stated in the text.
From the passage beginning with “World-Honored One, such a person is a king of men” onwards, this is the second section, which demonstrates their model and pattern.
Although they do not follow a sequential order, the number six is complete.
Formerly, he desired to bring peace to his person; now he shows that one must not be negligent, for by restraining the mind, the body finds peace.

Formerly, he desired to settle his palace; now he shows the solemnity of the Dharma Hall, where banners and canopies reflect above and fragrant flowers flourish below. When the Triple Gem is honored and utilized, even the Bai-liang Pavilion will be free from calamity.

The Sovereign desires to lead his realm toward excellence; now, by demonstrating the washing, bathing, and anointing with incense, he manifests profound reverence and eliminates arrogance. Thus, one body is honored here, while the eight quarters find peace there.
The World-Honored One wishes to gather a mass of merit; therefore, he now demonstrates that one should listen to the sutras with right mindfulness.

Listening to the sutras with right mindfulness can bring about immeasurable merit: the celestial deities will exhaust their strength to shelter one from above, the earth deities will exhaust their strength to support one from below, the spirits and ghosts will exhaust their strength to protect one, and the ministers and subjects will exhaust their strength to love one.

If the sovereign desires to bring peace and security to his wife and children, he now manifests a serene countenance and speaks with them, exhorting them to cultivate merit; thus, through the internal and external cultivation of goodness, the resulting benefits are manifold.

If the sovereign desires that the state be free from sorrow and suffering, he now manifests joy and self-congratulation, encouraging himself to persevere tirelessly and redouble his efforts for the benefit of others.
When one person is thus delighted, the four seas become tranquil; this is what is meant.
Next, the Buddha provides the summary and confirmation, which consists of two parts:
first, the summary and confirmation of the six methods; second, the summary and confirmation of the six vows.
The Four Kings [of Heaven] rely on six matters,
and what they teach is limited, pertaining only to the present life.
The Buddha relies on a single matter yet brings immense benefit, transcending immeasurable lifetimes and explaining it with double the detail for its fulfillment.

From the passage "The Buddha addressed the Four Kings" onwards, the text merely propagates the sutra and encourages its listening; this is precisely the description and fulfillment of the method for securing one's person.

Above, it directly demonstrated that the mind must not be negligent; now, it further demonstrates the ceremonial procession of leaving the palace to welcome [the teaching], such that at every step one encounters *nayuta* Buddhas.
Since the methods have doubled, the state of being is also all the more secure.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, one attains transcendence over so many kalpas of hardship" describes the method for accomplishing the security of the nation.
In the former case, one merely ceases the suffering and grief of a single lifetime; now, however, one transcends the hardships of such cycles of birth and death.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, in a future life, one will encounter and become a Wheel-Turning King," this describes the method for securing the safety of one's wife and children.
A Wheel-Turning King possesses a precious queen and a thousand sons, all of whom are free from enmity; thus, throughout such kalpas, his wife and children remain ever at peace.
The phrase "one also attains such power of mastery in the present life" describes the method for achieving the aforementioned peace within the king's domain.
The passage from "Always obtaining the most excellent palace of the seven treasures" describes the method for abiding peacefully within the palace.
The passage from "In every place of birth, up until being fully endowed with an immeasurable accumulation of merit" describes the method for gathering merit therein.
From "You Four Kings" onwards, the six types of aspirations and desires are described and established.
From "The Four Kings down to those who are non-retrogressive," the aspiration for the peaceful abiding of the body mentioned above is described and established.
From "May I myself encounter [the Buddhas] until the sufferings of the three evil realms are ended," he describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned aspiration for the peace of the nation.
From "I have now planted the causes for becoming a Wheel-Turning King, a Śakra, or a Brahmā," he describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow for the security of his wife and children.
From the passage "having already planted boundless roots of goodness" onwards, the text describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned aspiration to encompass a mass of merit.

From the passage "the inner palace and its dwellings are free from all calamities and decline," the text describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow for the peaceful establishment of the palace.
From the passage "The land shall be free from the enmity and thorns of other regions," the excellence of the king’s sovereignty is established as the first.
From the passage "You, the Four Kings," onwards, the six dharmas and six vows are further summarized and established.
"To cause all to be fully endowed" means that if one can humble oneself to welcome [the teacher] and listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart, this constitutes the six vows and six dharmas.
Furthermore, by dedicating the merit to bestow it upon the heavens, one is likewise able to cause the six vows and six dharmas to be accomplished and fulfilled.
The fourth [section] is the petition to the Buddha, requesting that the human king bestow goodness; this follows from the end of the third section.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the petition to the Buddha; second, the Buddha’s endorsement and fulfillment of it.
The white report to the Buddha further consists of two parts:
first, the human king’s mental application; second, the manifestation of the celestial palace’s signs.
Because the human king’s mind dwelt upon the ultimate scriptures, fragrant smoke transformed into golden light.
Because one will certainly obtain [the fruit] through dedicating [merit], the signs of celestial palaces appear.
This fragrance reaches the palaces of devas, nagas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth, extending throughout all three realms of existence.
Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: one burns the incense of the true mark with the fire of wisdom, giving rise to the smoke of precept, concentration, and wisdom.
Since the true mark is the authentic Dharma, it is called "Golden Light."
"Because precept and wisdom are in profound accord with principle, they penetrate and illuminate all things without obstruction," and so forth.
Next, the Buddha provides a formal endorsement (*anumodana*), which consists of two parts:

first, he describes how the fragrance and light do not merely reach the celestial palaces and so on within the three realms of existence, but pervade the hundreds of millions of various palaces and further reach the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In brief, this extends throughout the ten dharma-realms.

From the passage beginning with "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, hear this fragrance" onwards, it describes how the human kings cultivate goodness and make offerings to the various devas, thereby being praised by all the Buddhas.
First, the cause is praised as being accomplished; next, the fruit is praised as being fulfilled, as in the text.
Fifth, he addresses the Buddha, presenting both prosperity and decline together.
The text is divided into two parts:
There are two parts: first, the petition to the Buddha; second, the Buddha’s confirmation and fulfillment.
The petition to the Buddha is further divided into three sections.
The first, from "Petition to the Buddha" up to "causing all evil calamities to be completely extinguished," constitutes the initial exhortation to undertake the practice.

From the passage, "If a king gives rise to thoughts of renunciation... up to 'the benevolent deities will distance themselves, and such immeasurable evils will arise,'" this is the second exhortation regarding the manifestation of decline.
From the passage "The World-Honored One, as a king of men, desires to protect himself and his kingdom," this is the third exhortation.
The raising of this exhortation is fourfold:
first, when a king of men propagates the sutra, the Four Heavenly Kings will conceal their forms to listen and receive it.
First, it is not only the Four Heavenly Kings who listen and receive [the teaching], but Śakra, Brahmā, and the eight classes of beings all assemble to listen and receive it;
second, this human king serves as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of wholesome dharmas;
third, having obtained the benefit of the Dharma, he becomes even more diligent in protecting the nation.
All is as stated in the text.
Next, the exhortation regarding decline also consists of four points:
first, if the king does not propagate the sutras, the devas will lose the ambrosia, and his majesty and power will diminish.
First, Śakra, Brahmā, and the ancient deities all abandon them from afar;
second, malevolent spirits roam in disorder as calamitous poisons arise in competition; third, successive afflictions form into disasters;
and fourth, these calamities become interconnected and consolidated.
Why do calamities arise?
Because malevolent spirits act in disorder.
Why do the spirits act [in this way]?
The devas abandon them.
Why do the devas abandon them?
Because they do not hear the food of the Dharma.
Why is there no food for the Dharma?
Because the King does not propagate the Sūtras.
As stated in the text.
The three kinds of correct exhortation comprise six points:
first, because they desire to obtain benefits in the present life, they will certainly listen;
second, because the devas delight in the food of the Dharma, they will certainly listen.
One listens with certainty because these three [scriptures] transcend the three treatises.

As for the three treatises: the *Veda* treatise expounds upon the matters of Brahmā; the *Vyākaraṇa* treatise expounds upon the ten wholesome deeds; and the *Sāṃkhya*, *Vaiśeṣika*, and *Lokāyata* treatises expound upon the matters of worldly learning, and so forth.
Fourth, because it brings benefit from beginning to end and accomplishes bodhi, one must certainly listen.
Fifth, because the Teacher is superior to Śakra and Brahmā, one must certainly listen.
Sixth, because it is the root of all dharmas, one must certainly listen.
All is as stated in the text.
Next is the Buddha’s confirmation and completion of the discourse, which consists of two parts.
In the first part, he confirms the teaching by raising an exhortation: if [the Dharma] is not propagated, it will decline; thus, there is no need for further confirmation.
Another interpretation states:

In the former instance, both [the Buddha and the interlocutor] provide a formal confirmation (*anuvāda*) and bestow peace and happiness; this is a formal confirmation that raises up encouragement to eliminate decline and suffering. In the latter instance, it is a formal confirmation that raises up [the state of] decline to provide encouragement.
From the passage, "If there be anyone who can perform great Buddha-work among humans and devas," the text describes the encouragement for accomplishment, and so forth.
The sixth petition to the Buddha consists of three parts:
first, the recitation of verses in praise; second, the Buddha’s response in verse; and third, the joyful making of vows.
The verses of praise consist of eight and a half lines, which are divided into three parts:
first, one line praises the three bodies; second, five and a half lines praise the characteristics of the body; and third, two lines conclude with further praise.

Now, the three bodies (trikāya) have both general and specific meanings. According to the text, they are specific: emptiness is the Dharma-body, the sun is the Reward-body, and the moon is the Response-body.
As for the general meaning: emptiness is the Dharma-body, the sun is the Reward-body, and the water-sun is the Response-body;
or emptiness is the Dharma-body, the moon is the Reward-body, and the water-moon is the Response-body.
The emptiness of space is the Dharma-body; the emptiness within the sun is the Reward-body; the emptiness within the water is the Response-body.
It is the same for the moon.
According to the text of the *Jie* (Exaltation) chapter, the emptiness is the Dharma-body, the moon is the Reward-body, and the moon reflected in the water is the Response-body.
Emptiness is the Dharma-body, the sun is the Reward-body, and the rays are the Transformation-body;
the manifested phenomena are the Dharma-body, the master of manifestation is the Reward-body, and the acts of manifestation are the Transformation-body.
Although these are explained separately, their meaning is comprehensive and integrated; thus, the text states "there is no obstruction," which conveys this general sense.
The praise of the physical marks consists of five parts:
the first line praises the two aforementioned marks, namely the eyes and the teeth.
The next one and a half lines praise the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), namely wisdom and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The following two lines praise the latter two marks, namely the evenness and the web.
The final two phrases are a praise beyond words, namely the inconceivable (*acintya*).

The following two lines provide a concluding eulogy: "Now, the marks and signs do not reside solely in the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); they also pervade the *vipākadharmakāya* (retribution dharma-body).
That which adorns the body born of parents is the response-mark."
Adorning the body of honor and self-confidence refers to the marks and signs of the reward-body (*vipākakāya*).
Adorning the dharma-gates refers to the marks and signs of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Herein, the praise of wisdom and abandonment is precisely the marks and signs of the dharma-body.
The text states that there are "no obstructions"; this does not merely praise the characteristics of a single body.

At the beginning of the verse, the Buddha-moon was designated; now, first, the Buddha-moon is identified as the three bodies (trikāya), and next, the seamless integration of these three bodies is affirmed. Therefore, it is said that there are no obstructions.
Next, one binds the Buddha-sun, and thus it is said to be "like a flame.
Next, one binds the Buddha's transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is the meaning of the four bodies; thus it is said to be "like a transformation.
Since all [bodies] are complete with the three bodies and four bodies, this is non-obstruction.
Having concluded the recitation, one immediately pays homage; to pay homage to the Buddha-moon is likewise to pay homage to the Buddha-sun and the Buddha’s transformation.
At the beginning of the chapter, the sutra is praised, extolling its essence, its primary doctrine, and its function;
at the end of the chapter, the Buddha is praised, where the phrasing differs but the meaning remains the same.
The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is the essence; the purity of the Buddha-moon is the principle; and the manifestation as the moon in water is the function.
Such is the wondrousness of the Heavenly King’s celestial eloquence.
Question:
Space is likened to the Dharma-body and the moon to the Reward-body. Does space create the moon, or does it not?
If space were to create the moon, the moon would not be created by space;
if space does not create the moon, how can the moon depend upon space?
Answer:
Space does not create the moon, nor does it create what is not the moon; yet the moon and that which is not the moon must necessarily depend upon space.
Phenomena do not create retribution, nor do they create what is not retribution; yet retribution and that which is not retribution must necessarily depend upon phenomena.
He asked again:

"If it is said that phenomena do not produce results nor non-results, and that results and non-results must necessarily depend upon phenomena, then it should also follow that the moon does not produce shadows nor non-shadows, and that shadows and non-shadows must necessarily depend upon the moon."
"Is the moon also the Dharma-body?
Answer:
"Wisdom merges with the Dharma; the Dharma is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and wisdom is likewise like the Dharma-realm," and so forth.
Furthermore, reflections do not themselves produce motion or stillness; motion and stillness necessarily depend upon the water. Is water, too, the dharma-realm?
Answer: Motion and stillness are like the mechanism [of a puppet].
Within all dharmas there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss; this is no different from the analogy of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, the *Jingdu sanmei jing* states: "Sentient beings also deliver Buddhas."
If there were no receptive capacity (*indriya*), the Buddha would not appear in the world, nor could he attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The appearance in the world and the attainment of enlightenment both depend upon sentient beings.
Thus, it is established that the receptive capacity constitutes the *dharmadhātu*.
The Buddha answered with twenty-four and a half verses. The reason the Heavenly King praised the Buddha was that the Buddha is able to preach the Dharma;
the reason the Dharma King praised the Dharma was that the Dharma is able to bring about Buddhahood.

The *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "When I first attained the Way, I contemplated whom it would be appropriate to revere and praise; none surpassed the Dharma, for the Dharma is able to establish all ordinary beings and sages."
Therefore, the Buddha praised the Dharma in response to the Heavenly King.
The text is divided into three parts:

first, one line praising the essence of the scripture to answer regarding his Dharmakāya; second, one line praising the core principle of the scripture to answer regarding his Saṃbhogakāya; and third, twenty-two and a half lines praising the function of the scripture to answer regarding his Nirmāṇakāya.
All is as in the text.
The three and four kings joyfully made their vows, as in the text.

Regarding the "Chapter on Great Eloquence" (*Mahāpratibhāna-parivarta*): there are four kinds of eloquence—minor eloquence (*parīttapratibhāna*), immeasurable eloquence (*apramāṇapratibhāna*), paired eloquence (*yuganaddhapratibhāna*), and great eloquence (*mahāpratibhāna*).

The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are called "minor eloquence" (*parīttapratibhāna*); the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are called "immeasurable eloquence" (*apramāṇapratibhāna*); being endowed with both types is called "dual eloquence" (*ubhayapratibhāna*); and that which neither dualizes nor illuminates duality is called "great eloquence" (*mahāpratibhāna*).

This deva dwells in the dharma-gate of the adornment of wisdom; abiding in great eloquence himself, he employs his sovereign power for the sake of gladdening sentient beings by delivering one, two, three, or four types of eloquence as appropriate, and is therefore called "Great Eloquence."
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he may bestow one, two, three, or four forms of eloquence as appropriate and establish them accordingly; therefore, it is called "Great Eloquence.
For the sake of confronting sentient beings, he may confront them with one, two, three, or four forms of eloquence to discipline them; therefore, it is called "Great Eloquence."
For the sake of awakening sentient beings, whether it be one eloquence, two, three, or four, by awakening to one, all are awakened and thereby brought forth; therefore, it is called Great Eloquence.

Having made a vow before the Buddha, he is empowered with great eloquence (*mahāpratibhāna*) for the sake of the speaker; therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Great Eloquence" (*Mahāpratibhānaparivarta*).
The text consists of three parts:
first, from the words "addressed the Buddha" (*bhagavantam etad avocat*) onwards, [the section] wherein the Dharma master is empowered and benefited by the power of great eloquence.
Second, from "If there are sentient beings who, for hundreds of thousands... onwards, he applies the power of response and resonance (*pratyaya-bala*) to the transformative path;
third, from "Furthermore, he causes immeasurable... onwards, he applies the power of practice (*caryā-bala*) to the listeners.

At the beginning of the ritual, the Dharma Master employs eloquence of joyful exposition as the adornment of sequential expression; great wisdom constitutes the analytical power of meaning; and dhāraṇī constitutes the analytical power of dharma.
From the phrase "If there are sentient beings" onwards, it adds that the path of transformation flows and spreads without interruption.

It adds that regarding the capacity for transformation—wherein there is no person and nothing to be transformed, no path and no one who transforms—through the harmony of causes and conditions, the path of transformation continues without end.
From the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he causes immeasurable... onwards, there are two benefits added for the audience:
attaining non-retrogression upon hearing the sutra is the added benefit of the cause;
the certain attainment of bodhi is the added benefit of the fruit.
Although the phrasing is concise, the vow is profoundly deep and its benefit is vast.

This concludes the commentary on the "Chapter on the Goddess of Merit. This goddess dwells in the Dharma-gate of the Adornment of Merit, which encompasses all phenomena; because she takes merit as her primary attribute, she is called the Goddess of Merit.
Furthermore, because she can provide the speaker with all that is required so that there is no lack whatsoever, she is named Guṇakārandavatī.
Moreover, because she causes the speaker to contemplate the profound meaning of this sūtra day and night, she is named Guṇakārandavatī.
Furthermore, it causes listeners to swiftly attain Bodhi.
Because it possesses these manifold meanings, it is titled "The Chapter on the Goddess Puṇyavatī.
This is the third intention of the Heavenly King for protecting this sutra: to provide the merit that supports both those who request its exposition and those who listen to it.
The text consists of six sections:
first, from "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, there are four matters concerning the taking of vows to provide for the Dharma Master.
Second, from "I have, in the past... onwards, the source of his merit is clarified.
Third, from "If there be anyone who can recite... onwards, the practice is exhorted and demonstrated; within this text, there are both brief indications and detailed expositions, and so forth.
Fourth, from "At that time, for the duration of a single thought-moment... onwards, the vow to appear as a responsive influence is set forth.
5. From "If one can dedicate what one has done to me" onwards, there is the request for companionship.
6. From "One should pay homage" onwards, there is the specific demonstration of taking refuge and respect.
All is as stated in the text.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā": while the various devas dwell in the path of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and serve as the Dharma-fathers of sentient beings, this goddess dwells in the path of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of true reality (*bhūtārtha*) and serves as the Dharma-mother of sentient beings; these are one in meaning.
For example, just as yin and yang cover and support all grasses and trees, the Perfection of Wisdom nurtures and gives birth to all manner of virtues; this is the second meaning.

While the other perfections each have their own specific domains and thus remain distinct and unmerged, true wisdom illuminates and realizes that there is neither form nor name; this is the third meaning.
The other perfections have equals and superiors, whereas the Perfection of Wisdom has neither equal nor superior; it is the ultimate perfection—this is the fourth meaning.
The Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom is eternally unchanging; its meaning is described as "firm," which signifies constancy.
To be able to bear [the burden] is joy;
to be able to give birth is purity; this is named "ground" (*bhūmi*).
To have sovereign mastery over the power of virtue is the "self" (*ātman*); this is termed "divine" (*deva*).
Because these dharma-gates arise from this, it is titled the "Chapter on the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā.

This chapter represents the fourth intention of the Heavenly Kings for protecting the Dharma: to cause the essence of the earth to well up, thereby nourishing and benefiting those who request, preach, and listen to [the teachings].
The text consists of three parts:
first, from "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, [the Bodhisattva] vows to bring forth the essence of the earth to benefit practitioners;
second, from "At that time the Buddha said" onwards, the Tathāgata confirms and completes this vow.
Third, from "At that time, the Earth Deity" onwards, there is the making of vows to propagate the sutra.
First, regarding the emergence of the earth-flavor, the text is divided into three parts:
from the initial "addressing the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies the benefits for one's own person, which generally involve eight matters that increase progressively.
Through hearing the Dharma, the flavor of the Dharma increases.
Because the flavor of the Dharma increases, physical vigor increases.
Because physical vigor increases, the essence of the earth increases in turn.
Because the essence of the earth increases, all things increase.
Because all things increase, the five fruits of sentient beings increase.
Because the five fruits increase, spiritual practice increases.
Because practice increases, offerings increase.
Because offerings increase, propagation increases.
All is as stated in the text.
From the passage beginning with "For what reason, World-Honored One," the benefits for the retinue are clarified.
The power of this sutra increases through five successive stages of growth.
By the power of this sutra, my retinue increases.
Because my retinue increases, the essence of the earth increases.
Because the essence of the earth increases, all things increase.
Because all things increase, the happiness of sentient beings increases.
Because happiness increases, the secondary environment (niśraya-vipāka) becomes fully endowed; this full endowment is also termed "increase."

From the passage beginning with “The World-Honored One is for all sentient beings” onwards, it is called the increase of gratitude; in total, there are six matters through which this increase develops successively.
Because they recognize my kindness, their attentive listening increases.
Because attentive listening increases, merit increases.
Because merit increases, teaching others increases.
Because teaching others increases, the essence of the earth (*pṛthivīrasa*) increases.
Because the essence of the earth increases, the increase of experienced pleasure occurs.
Because the increase of experienced pleasure occurs, the increase of faithful giving occurs.
All is as stated in the text.
The second part, the Buddha’s confirmation and fulfillment, consists of two sections:
first, regarding the successive increase of hearing the sutra, from the human world to the celestial world, and from the celestial world to the supramundane world.
Day and night, one immediately experiences inconceivable bliss, which is the bliss of transcendence (*lokottara*).
What the earth deity spoke of merely refers to growth in this present life; although the Tathāgata’s confirmation is brief in wording, its meaning is exceedingly far-reaching.
Second, the description of the fulfillment of offerings and their increase:

from the human world to the celestial worlds, and from the celestial worlds to the supramundane; the meaning of this long-term progression may be understood according to what was previously explained, and so forth.
The third section, "Vowing to Protect the Sūtra," consists of three parts:
first, vowing to protect the preachers of the Dharma; second, vowing to protect the continuity of the transformative path; and third, vowing to protect those who listen to the Dharma.
As stated in the text.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Explanation of the Spirit Vaiśravaṇa": the full Sanskrit term for this chapter is *Vaiśramaṇa*, which should be translated as "Secret" (*Mī*).
"Esoteric" has four meanings, namely: esoteric name, esoteric practice, esoteric wisdom, and esoteric principle.

This refers to the Great General of the Northern Heavenly King; likewise, there is one in each of the other three directions: in the east he is named Rāgarāja, in the south Dandī, and in the west Suprabha. Each has five hundred attendants and governs twenty-eight divisions."
The *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* states: "In each of the four cardinal directions there are four divisions; thus, in the six directions, there are twenty-four divisions.
With one division in each of the four intermediate directions, they total twenty-eight divisions."
Furthermore, another proponent says:
"In one direction there are five divisions, namely earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
In the four directions there are twenty divisions; adding the eight classes presided over by the Four Heavenly Kings, these constitute the twenty-eight divisions."
Wandering through the world to reward the good and punish the evil, all such matters are governed by Vaiśravaṇa.
Having heard this sutra with joy, he vowed to protect both the speaker and the listener; because he received his name from this act of protection, he is called Vaiśravaṇa, and so forth.
The text consists of four parts:
first, from "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, there is the making of a vow to protect and uphold [the teaching].
Second, from "By what causes and conditions" onwards, there is the description of the virtues capable of providing such protection.
Third, from the section on "General Vajrapāṇi" downward, there is a vow to use the power of wisdom to benefit and assist the speaker.
Fourth, there is the taking of refuge and paying homage to the Original Teacher.
In the first section, there is the narrative by the sūtra compiler and the actual formulation of the vow; both are exactly as they appear in the text.
The description of his virtues is further divided into three parts:
first, the heading; second, the description; and third, the conclusion.
The heading is as stated in the text.
The exposition is further divided into three parts:
the first five lines describe wisdom (*jñāna*), the next five lines describe the object (*viṣaya*), and the final five lines describe the correct [practice].
The threefold invocation of "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*) indicates that these refer to these three types of meaning.
Since the "divine" (shen) is named "mystery" (mi), and its manifest virtue is described as being worthy of discourse on the meaning of mystery,
if wisdom were merely shallow or deep according to stages and gradations, it would not be called "mysterious. Rather,
that which is the single wisdom as all wisdom and all wisdom as single wisdom— neither one nor all, yet both one and all— is what constitutes the mystery of wisdom.
If one attains this meaning, five phrases are one phrase and one phrase is five phrases; they are neither one nor five, yet they are both one and five—this is solely numerical and solely esoteric.
If an object could be known by the intellect or expressed by the mouth, then that object would not be esoteric.
It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness; it cannot be designated by names, nor can it be expressed in speech—this is called the inconceivable secret realm.
Regarding the discussion of the "esoteric" (mi) based on the number five, it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

If one clarifies the right path in contrast to heterodox paths, or explains the middle in relation to extremes, then this "right" as opposed to "not right," or this "middle" as opposed to "not middle," is in neither case esoteric.

That which is precisely the heterodox yet correct, and precisely the extreme yet the middle—wherein heterodoxy and correctness, extremes and the middle are neither two nor distinct—is what is called "esoteric" (*mi*).
The *Samparigraha-sūtra* states: "If one discriminates all phenomena with the mind, all phenomena are heterodox."
"If one does not conceptually discriminate all phenomena with the mind, then all phenomena are correct"—this is precisely its meaning.
"I practice the Right Path;
whether it be the object or the wisdom, it is from this that they derive their names. "It is so, World-Honored One; You Yourself shall surely bear witness," and so forth.
Furthermore, these three sections generally constitute the secrets of body, speech, and mind.
The first five phrases speak of "knowing"; knowing is the secret of the mind.
The subsequent five phrases speak of "direct perception"; direct perception pertains to the eye, and the eye pertains to the body; thus, this is the secret of the body.

The final five phrases clarify correct understanding; because it is based on correct understanding, it is called "correct discernment" (*samyak-vikalpa*). This discernment is the secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*).
The reason it is said to be "not manifest" is precisely the meaning of "secret."
Thus, the explanation of the names has revealed the esoteric meaning.
Having relished this inexhaustibly, it shall be briefly explained once more.
From the passage "World-Honored One, I know all dharmas" onwards, the meaning is interpreted through the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
The two phrases, "knowing all dharmas" and "all conditioned dharmas," share the same objective realm: phenomena produced by causes and conditions.

Why is this? That which produces is the cause, corresponding to the first phrase; that which is produced is the condition, corresponding to the second phrase. Because the producer and the produced unite, all dharmas arise.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states, "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions," which refers precisely to this meaning.
To "comprehend all phenomena" means to thoroughly realize their emptiness and non-substantiality.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Those phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare to be empty. This constitutes the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional.

To know the demarcations of phenomena means to know that emptiness is not a mere void; by employing the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*), one discerns that there is no distinction between the conventional designations of ordinary beings and sages.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states, "It is also called a provisional designation"; this refers to the contemplation that enters the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
By abiding in all phenomena according to their true nature through these two contemplations as skillful means, one attains entry into the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states, "It is also called the meaning of the Middle Way," which refers to the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka-paramārtha-satya*).
That which "contains all phenomena" is precisely the correct contemplation of the Middle Way; because it can simultaneously illuminate both truths (*satyadvaya*), it is said to "contain."
If one contemplates the three as either identical or distinct, whether vertically, horizontally, or separately, it is not called "mysterious contemplation" (mi-guan).
Rather, that which is three while being one, and one while being three, is called "mysterious."
If one wishes to know where wisdom resides, it is found in speech; this speech is the secret of the mouth (*vāg-guhya*).
The five phrases beginning with "World-Honored One, I see before my eyes" are explained according to the meaning of the three truths and the three liberations.

Regarding "manifestly perceiving the inconceivable light of wisdom": "light" refers to true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Just as the light of the sun and moon is constantly bright and never ceases, this true wisdom illuminates the inconceivable realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), thereby accomplishing perfectly pure liberation.

The inconceivable torch of wisdom, the practice of wisdom, and the accumulation of wisdom are all expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Just as a person holding a hot torch illuminates objects with winding movements—sometimes raising it and sometimes setting it down, following conditions according to their capacity, now here and now there.
"Practice" (*caryā*) has the meaning of cause, and "accumulation" (*caya*) has the meaning of fruit.

Moving from cause toward fruit, once the fruit arises, the cause is abandoned; all of this is the inconceivable conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) illuminated by provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), thereby accomplishing the liberation of skillful means (*upāya-vimukti*).
The inconceivable realm of wisdom refers to the wisdom of the suchness of dharmas (*dharmatathatā*).
Because this wisdom is in profound accord with the suchness of dharmas, it is called the inconceivable realm of wisdom.
This wisdom illuminates the inconceivable ultimate truth of the Middle Way, thereby accomplishing the liberation of intrinsic purity.
If the three truths and the three liberations were either identical or distinct, or existed in a state of vertical or horizontal separation, they would not be inconceivable.
Because it is neither identical nor different, and because it is distinct from both, it is called "inconceivable"; being inconceivable, it is called "mysterious" (*guhya*).

Regarding the five phrases beginning with "World-Honored One, as for all dharmas," they are explained through the three bodies (*trikāya*), which constitutes the correct understanding and correct contemplation.
Right understanding can manifest the essence; this manifestation of the essence is called right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
Right contemplation is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

To attain right discernment and right understanding regarding conditions means to discern the capacities and circumstances [of sentient beings], responding universally to all without waiting for the proper time or missing it; this is the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

As for that which is truly able to awaken and comprehend: the absence of both awakening and non-awakening is called awakening; the absence of both comprehension and non-comprehension is called comprehension.
This ultimate, pure awakening and comprehension is the Dharmakāya.
If these three bodies were either identical or distinct, whether vertically or horizontally, they would not be called "correct.
Because they are neither one nor different, neither preceding nor following, they are called "correct"; correctness is precisely the esoteric (mystery).
In terms of the true manifestation of the Dharma-body, it carries the meaning of "gold";
in terms of the contemplation that clarifies Prajñā, it carries the meaning of "light";
and in terms of inconceivable liberation, it carries the meaning of "clarity."
The Three Virtues are the subtle and secret treasury, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the subtle and secret teaching.

Because I give rise to subtle understanding from the subtle teaching, abide in the subtle principle, practice the subtle conduct, and benefit others through the subtle, I am named "Mystery" (Guhyaka).
"Indeed, World-Honored One, You Yourself shall bear witness to this.
Furthermore, these fifteen phrases explain and establish one another.
If one correctly understands and correctly contemplates them, then all fifteen phrases are correctly understood and correctly contemplated."
If it is the light of inconceivable wisdom, then all fifteen phrases are the light of inconceivable wisdom.
If I were to know them, I would know all fifteen phrases, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the five kinds of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), the three names—Correct Nature (*samyaktva-dhātu*), Conditioned Nature (*pratyaya-dhātu*), and Realization Nature (*abhisamaya-dhātu*)—are not distinct from one another.
Moreover, according to one school, the five are comprised of the Nature of Attaining the Fruit (*phala-prāpti-dhātu*) and the Nature of the Sphere (*viṣaya-dhātu*).
Furthermore, another school takes the nature of being a fruit (*phalatva*) and the nature of being the fruit of a fruit (*phalaphalatva*) as five [natures].
If one treats it as the nature of being the fruit of a fruit, then its nature as an object (*ālambanatva*) disappears, as it is subsumed under the nature of being a causal condition (*pratyayatva*).
If the nature of the objective realm (*viṣaya*) is opened up, it submerges the nature of the fruit-of-fruits (*phalaphala*), being subsumed within the nature of the fruit (*phala*).
Although there are differences in terms of opening and closing, they ultimately consist of five categories.
Now, the five types of knowledge are correlated with the five Buddha-natures (*buddhadhātu*).
When I say "I know all dharmas," it means that within all dharmas there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss (*anurakṣa-svabhāva*).
This nature of peace and bliss is precisely the true cause of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
All phenomena that serve as conditions consist of the merits of bowing the head and raising the hands; these are the Buddha-nature as the condition-cause (*yuan-yin*).
To fully comprehend all phenomena is the wisdom of *prajñā* and emptiness; this is the Buddha-nature as the cause of comprehension (*liao-yin*).
To know the demarcation of phenomena means that the causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane do not overlap; their objective sphere is the Buddha-nature as the cause.
To abide in accordance with reality (dharmatā) according to suchness (tathatā) means that the nature of the fruit abides ultimately within the center of suchness.
That which encompasses all phenomena is itself the nature of the fruit (*phala-svabhāva*); it is able to simultaneously illuminate and encompass them.

If one were to treat it as the nature of the fruit-of-fruits (*phalaphala-svabhāva*), one would take the discernment of the limits of phenomena as the nature of the fruit, and the clear, distinct illumination of the resulting wisdom as those limits; thus, abiding in the nature of suchness while encompassing is called the nature of the fruit-of-fruits, and so forth.
"If that is so," regarding the two sets of five phrases below, they should likewise correspond to the five Buddha-natures.
Although the Master does not explicitly explain this, such is the logical pattern.
One must, accordingly, elucidate their intended meaning and interpret the text so that it is understood in this way.
The passage beginning with "For this reason, World-Honored One" is the concluding section.
The passage beginning with "World-Honored One, General Vajrapāṇi" constitutes the third vow, wherein he pledges to enrich the speaker with wisdom and eloquence.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, benefiting the transformer; second, benefiting those to be transformed.
Benefiting the transformer is further divided into three sections:
"Adorned speech" below [refers to] benefiting the karma of speech;
"the refined essence of various flavors" below [refers to] benefiting the karma of body;
"a mind that is courageous and sharp" below [refers to] benefiting the karma of mind.
From the passage "For this reason" onwards, the text benefits those who are to be transformed.
This also consists of three parts:
"For this reason, I extensively expound this sutra" refers to causing those who have not yet planted the seeds [of merit] to plant them.
The passage beginning with "If there are sentient beings" refers to causing those who have already planted the seeds [of merit] to ripen;
the passage beginning with "immeasurable sentient beings" refers to liberating those who have already reached maturity.
Everything is according to the text.
This interpretation of the passage is excellent.
From "Namo Ratnakusuma" onwards is the fourth section of the text on taking refuge and paying homage.
In all the various sutras spoken by the Buddha, there is initially a verse of homage and respect, though translators have often omitted it.
The same applies to the initial verses of the various treatises, which likewise begin with homage.
This particular text concludes with a declaration of taking refuge in the Triple Gem; this may be found within the text itself.
The Words and Phrases of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* Words and Phrases, Scroll Six.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty.
Recorded by the disciple Guanding.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Correct Discourse. Regarding the "Correct Discourse" (*Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*), "correct" (*saddharma*) is synonymous with "holy" (*ārya*).
There are two kinds of holy ones:
There are two types of sages: first, those who are holy within the world; second, those who are holy beyond the world.
To investigate names is to verify reality: first, verifying the reality of facts; second, verifying the reality of principles.
This chapter contains the ancient laws of former kings, transmitted from generation to generation.

The former kings transmitted the mark of power and majesty; the mark of power and majesty was transmitted to the mark of faith; the mark of faith, in turn, transmitted it to his son, and his son transmitted it to future generations.

"Righteous and sagely in every generation, and virtuous and true in every generation"—this is the dharma-utterance of the former kings, and it is also a name established according to the worldly *siddhānta*; thus, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on Righteous Discourse."

When a king practices this dharma in accordance with the law, the yin and yang are thereby harmonized, the sun and moon are thereby made to follow their courses, the hundred grains are thereby made abundant, the myriad people are thereby made joyful, the altars of soil and grain are thereby made secure, and the governance and transformation of the realm are thereby made beautiful. Thus, the people live in harmony and there is no resentment between superiors and subordinates; this is also establishing a name for the sake of the *puruṣasiddhānta* (the established truth for beings), and it is named the "Chapter on Righteous Discourse."
By employing this method, the King ensures that external enemies dare not plot against him,
internal traitors dare not cause alarm,
and malevolent stars dare not appear.

Evil rainbows dare not travel, violent winds dare not stir, and torrential rains dare not fall; thus, calamities and rebellions do not arise, and disasters do not occur. This is also established as a name according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic counteraction), and is titled the "Chapter on Right Discourse."

This is the fundamental gold-light of worldly goodness; from this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* emerges this *Nyāya-prakaraṇa*. By skillfully employing this *Nyāya-prakaraṇa*, the radiance of celestial palaces and celestial bodies is thereby enhanced, celestial power and majesty are thereby increased, the minds of the devas are thereby redoubled in joy, and the flavor of the Dharma for the devas is thereby made twice as profound and far-reaching. This is the supreme virtue and essential path of former kings, and it is also established as a name according to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*; thus it is titled the "Chapter on the *Nyāya-prakaraṇa*."

This text constitutes the second intention within the section on circulation, clarifying how a human king who propagates the sutra moves the hidden sages through spiritual resonance, and how celestial kings assist him so that his virtuous governance flourishes.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the prose section explaining the fundamental facts; second, the verse section presenting the formal discourse.
In the prose section, the description of the former marks of the Honored One addressed to the Earth Deity is as in the text.
The verses consist of eighty-two lines and are divided into four parts;
the first two and a half lines assemble the assembly.
Next, three and a half lines pose the questions;
next, one line concludes the questions and introduces the answers;
finally, seventy-five lines constitute the Brahmā’s response, which is the exposition of the correct treatise.
The assembled texts are divided into three parts:
first, one line in which the Buddha describes his venerable appearance and intends to preach the fundamental dharma of former kings for the sake of the celestial son;
second, one line in which the Buddha describes his venerable appearance and exhorts [the audience] to listen.
Next, the second half of the verse clarifies the location where the treatise was spoken.
Following this, the Four Kings pose four questions:
the first asks why a person is called a "deva" (heavenly being).
Second, he asked why those not born of the gods are called "sons of heaven";
third, he asked why those dwelling in royal palaces are called "gods";
fourth, he asked why those who govern the world through human laws are named "gods."
Next, one line establishes what precedes and gives rise to what follows; this can be seen in detail.
Since there are four questions, there are likewise four answers:
first, the answer that because Heaven protects his entry into the womb, although he is the son of a human, he is called the Son of Heaven (*devaputra*).
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three each share their own merit; although they are human, they are called "gods.
Although they dwell in human palaces, they govern the world according to celestial laws; although they are lords of men, they are called "gods."

Although these are human rulers who govern the world and cause sentient beings to perform good deeds so that they are mostly reborn in the heavens, they are called "devas" (heavenly beings) because the effect is spoken of in terms of the cause.
From the passage beginning with "Even though you now... onwards is Brahmā’s response.
The text consists of two parts:
first, a brief response in ten and a half lines; second, an extensive response in sixty-four and a half lines.
Within the brief response, there are four sections:

The first one and a half lines provide the answer; next, the line beginning with "Because of the accumulation of karma" briefly cites past causes and present effects to answer the King's question regarding his own status; next, five lines cite three points to answer his question regarding the nature of the heavens; and finally, three lines cite three points to again answer the King's question regarding his own status.
In response to the question regarding the three meanings of "Heavenly" (*deva*), these are: not yet having entered the womb, the stage of entering the womb, and the empowerment of spiritual power.
Because he protects the fetus, he is called a "Son of Heaven" (*devaputra*); this answers the second question.
Because they share in virtue, they possess celestial virtue; thus they are called "heavenly" (deva). This answers the first question.
Through the empowerment of supernormal power, they cultivate goodness and restrain evil, and will certainly be reborn in heaven hereafter.
Because the fruit is spoken of within the cause, it is called "heaven" (*deva*).
This answers the third and fourth questions regarding those who govern the world through the True Dharma being called "heaven.
The explanation of the three meanings for why "half [of them] are called heaven" is now complete.
From the passage "half a human king" (*bàn mínrénwáng*) onwards, there are three meanings in the response;

thus, he is called "half a king. First, he is called a "musician" (*zhíyuèzhě*): music depends upon the king. The king embraces this music to bring peace and harmony to the world, such that there is wind every five days and rain every ten days. The elderly play *jīrǎng* (clay lumps), while the young ride bamboo horses; who would not submit to his virtue?
Therefore, one who upholds music is called a king.

Second, by restraining evil and eliminating harm for the people, if Heaven does not suffer from drought, the earth does not suffer from floods, the grasses are not broken or damaged, and the people are free from pestilence—who would not turn to him in admiration of his virtue?
Therefore, one who restrains evil is called a king.

As for the three parents: they instruct on fortune and calamity, guide discourse on good and evil, and establish rites and music so that the people know the prohibitions; who would not turn to their virtue?
Therefore, his parents name him "King" (Rāja).
Because he can act as a parent for those beneath him among the people, the various devas protect him, and he is named "Son of Heaven" (Devānām-priya).
Because he wards off evil so that it does not arise, and because the various devas share their merit with him, he is named "Heavenly" (Deva).
Because he delights in music, the effect is spoken of in terms of the cause, and he is further called a "deva.
It is not merely that half [of his nature] is designated as a human king who has achieved his purpose; half is also designated as a deva, and thus the three meanings are likewise made manifest.

From the passage beginning with "If there are evil deeds" down to the thirty-nine lines and three phrases, it is extensively explained that one who acts contrary to the Dharma cannot be called a deva nor can they be called a king.

Having lost all six qualities, each of the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens gives rise to resentment; thus, the devas do not protect him, and because they do not protect him, he is not a son of the devas (*devaputra*).
These various heavenly kings each said to one another: "This person does not share his merit; because he does not share his merit, he cannot be called a 'heavenly being' (*deva*).

One who abandons and distances himself from wholesome dharmas while increasing unwholesome dharmas lacks the cause for heaven; how could one speak of the fruit within the cause and praise such a person as a 'heavenly being'?"
"One who gives rise to great sorrow and suffering has no sense of attachment to pleasure.
When pestilence spreads everywhere, there is no sense of warding off evil.
To indulge in wickedness while disregarding goodness means one has no sense of father or mother," and so forth.
From the passage "One should properly punish offenses" downward, twenty-four lines and three phrases further elaborate upon six meanings.
"One should properly punish offenses" corresponds to the meaning of parents.
That the various devas provide protection and sustenance is the meaning of "Son of Heaven" (devaputra).
That he extinguishes evil dharmas is the meaning of "executioner" (kai-kuei).
The title "executioner" refers to the Commander-in-Chief, who restrains and subdues malevolent spirits.
The spirits fear the military commander and do not dare to act in disorder.
To cultivate wholesome dharmas is the meaning of "holding the music.
One should explain each of these for them; this is the demonstration of the principle of cause and effect.
"O devas, this is the distribution of merit and meaning.
One may further analyze the text according to the six meanings, as can be sought out at length.
Herein, the meaning of contemplation (vipaśyanā) should be clarified; reflect upon this yourself, and so forth."
Question:
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the root of the correct treatise; what is its intended meaning?
"Heaven" (*deva*) is precisely the gold of the *dharmatā*. Because the *dharmatā* serves as the basis of reliance, it is said that "Heaven protects."
The "sharing of merit" (bun-toku) is precisely "light" (kō); that the reward body (hōshin) merges with the dharma-nature (hosshō) is what constitutes the sharing of merit.
That which is empowered by supernatural power (jinriki) is precisely "clarity" (myō), and so forth.
Furthermore, the parents are gold, for the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) constitutes the parents;
the warding off of evil is light;
and the grasping of joy is clarity.
Taking this as the foundation, one is thus able to provide a correct discourse.

For example, half [of what is discussed] is called the correct discourse of worldly kings and half is called the correct discourse of the supramundane; this constitutes the correct discourse of the world, while the other half constitutes the correct discourse that transcends the world.
That the root and the branches are interrelated is precisely this meaning.
[This concludes] the commentary on the "Chapter on the Accumulation of Goodness. This wheel-turning king accumulates all wholesome dharmas, like a navigator of the sea.
The ocean of goodness is boundless, yet it is encompassed by the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
These six perfections are further expanded, but can be briefly subsumed into two: namely, generosity (*dāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
When Indrasena gave up the four great continents, filling them with precious jewels to use for giving, he thereby accumulated the practice of generosity.
Standing with palms joined, he requested the Venerable Ratnākara to proclaim and elucidate this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, which is the accumulation of wisdom and conduct.
Since this is true for generosity and wisdom, it is likewise so for all other dharmas.
It is named according to its practice; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Good Collection" (*Kuśalasaṃgraha-parivarta*).
These six perfections are distinct: practicing them in this manner constitutes the "collection of goodness" for the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint);
cultivating five of these perfections constitutes the "collection of goodness" for the *pudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint of the individual).
Cultivating the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the accumulation of goodness as an antidote;
