all the perfections (*pāramitās*) are the accumulation of goodness in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Because it derives its name from these four types of accumulation, it is called the "Chapter on the Accumulation of Goodness" (*Kuśalasaṃbhāra-parivarta*).
This chapter concerns the second type of king who propagates the sutras.
Whereas the preceding section clarified how mundane right view moves heaven and earth, this section clarifies how supramundane right view moves the worthy and the sages, and so forth.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the address to the Earth Goddess; second, the exposition in verse.
The verses comprise sixty-four and a half lines, which are divided into two sections:
The first four lines are general, clarifying the practice of *dāna* on the stage of the cause;
the subsequent sixty and a half lines are specific, titled "Skillfully Accumulating the Giving of Wealth and the Giving of Dharma.
This section is divided into six parts:

The first sixteen and a half lines clarify the fundamental matter; the twenty-one and a half lines clarify the noble king’s request for the Dharma; the thirty-nine and a half lines clarify the Venerable One’s proclamation; the forty and a half lines clarify the wheel-turning monarch’s practice of giving; the fifty-two lines conclude by correlating the past and present; and the sixty and a half lines cite cause and effect to provide proof and exhortation—all as set forth in the text.
Regarding this chapter on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, "gold" (*suvarṇa*) refers to the excellent accumulation of the *pāramitās*;
"light" (*prabhā*) refers to the accumulation of *prajñā*; and "radiance" (*prabhāsa*) refers to the accumulation of the [other] five *pāramitās*.
Regarding the discourse on the Jewel-Clarity (Ratnāloka): dwelling within a cave is its gold;
a face like the full moon is its light;
and reciting such a sutra as this is its brilliance.
Regarding the two agents: being within the cave refers to the gold;
granting the explanation for the king refers to the light;
and the king holding the *cintāmaṇi* jewel to rain down treasures throughout the four continents refers to the clarity.
Chapter on Explaining Ghosts and Spirits: The character for "ghost" (*gui*) is glossed as "returning" (*gui*), and it is also said to mean "fear.
Because their retribution involves much terror and dread, they are like the *asuras*, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said that "awe" (*wei*) means the ability to cause others to stand in awe of one's majesty.
"Spiritual power" (*shen*) means capability; those with great strength can move mountains and fill the seas, while those with lesser strength can manifest, conceal, and undergo transformations.
This chapter generally lists all the devas, nāgas, oceans, rivers, suns, moons, and various deities.
Since the preceding section has already concluded with the heading "Devas," it would not be appropriate for them to appear again here.

Although it comprehensively lists beings from all realms, the text concerning ghosts and spirits is more extensive; therefore, following the principle of using the predominant subject, this chapter is titled accordingly.

This is the third chapter; all devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, celestial intelligences, and terrestrial deities have together made a vow to propagate and widely disseminate it everywhere, exhorting its circulation.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verses.
Within the prose, there is first the specific enumeration of objects, followed by the comprehensive offering.
Regarding the distinction between the two aspects: when the Buddha arises from compassion to accept offerings, this is the *Nirmāṇakāya* (Response Buddha).
When the Buddha arises from *tathatā* (suchness) to manifest awakened wisdom, and that wisdom merges with suchness, this is the *Sambhogakāya* (Reward Buddha).
That "all dharmas are entirely the sphere of activity of all Buddhas" refers to the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*).
One who understands it in this way perceives the three Buddhas as distinct.
If one practices the offering of material things, the offerings likewise remain distinct.
As for the perfect offering, it is to exhort others to listen to the sutras.
Listening to the sutras is the offering of the Dharma; among all offerings, it is the foremost. To offer this supreme offering is to make an offering to all Buddhas.

The ability to speak through words is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha; that which expresses is the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha; and that which is expressed is the Dharmakāya Buddha. To revere the words is thus to revere these three Buddhas, and it is also to revere the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"All Buddhas are born from this; therefore, to make offerings to written words is to make offerings to all Buddhas," and so forth.
Furthermore, at another time, he heard it again and recorded it.
The prose section cites four aspirations to form a single exhortation:
"If you wish to know the sphere of the Buddha’s activity. This "sphere of activity" is precisely the realm of suchness, which is the Dharma-Buddha.
Those who wish to know [this] should understand that this is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*), which is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* Buddha.
To be able to hear this sutra—this sutra is itself the written word, and the written word is itself the *nirmāṇa-kāya* Buddha.
Those who are able to listen comply with the Buddha’s teaching, which is itself the offering of Dharma; the offering of Dharma is the sublime offering.
Listening to the sutras can give rise to awakening-wisdom, and because awakening-wisdom arises, it constitutes the Buddha receiving an offering.
The single matter of listening to the sutra encompasses all aspirations and desires; the single matter of "only-completeness" (zhīyuán) subsumes all other distinct matters.
The verse consists of one hundred two and a half lines, divided into six sections.

The first section, from "If you wish to make offerings" downward for eleven lines, praises the preceding prose section on being able to listen to the sutra; this is to exhort practice by citing the perfect and wondrous.
Second, from "Wherever one goes" onwards for three and a half lines, it exhorts practice by citing how listening to the sutra can immediately avert calamities.
Third, from "At the place where the Dharma is preached" onwards for six lines, it exhorts practice by citing how listening to the sutra brings about spiritual auspiciousness.
4. From "The majestic appearance" downward, for five lines and a half, it cites the power inherent in merely listening to the sutra to encourage its cultivation.
5. From "Mahābrahmā Devendra" downward, for forty-nine lines and a half, it cites how listening to the sutra can attract devas, nāgas, and spirits to encourage its cultivation.

Sixth, from the passage beginning "Regarding all sentient beings" down to the twenty-seventh line, it is stated that merely listening to this sutra can bring peace and happiness to the land, thereby encouraging its cultivation, and so forth.

Regarding those who practice *gudao* (sorcery with poisonous insects): from the fourth heaven above, a deity named Mili-tou-qian-jia-tuo—translated into Chinese as Shanpin (Good Class)—is dispatched; he presides over poisonous insects and toxins.
Maheśvara is translated in other sutras as Dazizai (Great Sovereign), while in the *Guanding jing* (Consecration Sutra) he is translated as Weilingdi (Deity of Majestic Spirit).
Maṇibhadra is translated as "Majestic Subduing Conduct.
Pūrṇabhadra is translated as "Accumulated Attainment.
Kumbhīra is translated as "Majesty Like a King."
Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja is translated as "Standing Immovable.
Kapphiṇa is translated as "Attaining Liberation through Patience.
Dharmarāja is translated as "King of Study."
Magadhabhara is translated as "removing crookedness of mind.
Śrīmān is translated as "possessing merit and achievement.
Rājāśaya is translated as "harmonious and peaceful."
*Kṣemaśreṣṭhī* is translated as "Subduer of the Multitude of Faculties.
*Śālamati* is translated as "Delight in Solitary Dwelling.
*Haimavata* is translated as "Lord of the Abode."
Sātākī is translated as "Great Powerful Deva.
Pālihara is translated as "Valiant Progress.
Vemacitra is translated as "High and Remote."
Śyāmāvatīputra is translated as "Virtue of Heroism.
Bhāradvājaputra is translated as "Abundant Martial Splendor.
Kharakaṇṭha is translated as "Roaring Like Thunder."
Kauruṣanti is translated as "unconquerable in battle.
"Liberation from causes" refers to liberation from the obstacle of karma.
"Liberation from effects" refers to liberation from the obstacle of retribution.
"Delivering all beings from existence" means liberation from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the "Explanation of the Chapter on Prophecies," there are four kinds of prophecy; the present case refers to two of them, and so forth.
"Bestowing" (授) means to grant; "prediction" (記) refers to recording the events of attaining the Way.
In this context, because it records the matter of the three great bodhisattvas and ten thousand devas attaining Buddhahood in the future, it is called a "prediction" (授記).
It is also called "bestowing prophecy" (vyākaraṇa) and also called "bestowing certainty" (niyāma).
Bestowing the number of eons and realms is termed "prophecy"; being verified as true and not false is termed "certainty.
That which is given by the Buddha is termed "bestowing" (śāsana); that which is received by the recipient is termed "receiving" (pratilambha).
In this context, because it is bestowed by the Buddha, it is called "bestowing a prediction" (vyākaraṇa).

This is the fourth meaning within the section on circulation: by citing the causes of practicing the sutra in the past, one establishes the fruit of ultimate perfection; thus, it serves as proof that the propagation and protection [of the Dharma] are not in vain, thereby encouraging its circulation.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the bestowal of a prediction (vyākaraṇa), and second, the resolution of doubts regarding that prediction.
The bestowal of a prediction consists of two further parts:
First, the bestowing of predictions upon the three great bodhisattvas; second, the bestowing of predictions upon ten thousand devas.
Regarding the bestowing of predictions upon the three great bodhisattvas, there are two parts:
first, the assembly of those with common conditions; second, the actual bestowing of the predictions.
Regarding the world-system being renamed Pure Banner (Vimaladhvaja), one should discuss it through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), of which this is one.
Furthermore, the ten thousand prophecies are twofold:
first, the arising of understanding upon hearing the sutra; second, the actual bestowing of the prophecy, and so forth.
From "At that time, at the site of enlightenment" onwards is the second section on resolving doubts.
This also has two parts:
first, the question; second, the Buddha’s answer.

As for those who harbor doubts: shifting mountains and filling the sea are not accomplished in a single day; the ultimate fruit of Bodhi is achieved only through the accumulation of practice over time.

To descend briefly from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven involves no hardship of long listening, yet they have not heard of the inconceivable deeds of the past. Because their practice is shallow while their records are deep, they consequently fall into doubt.

Regarding "as with other bodhisattvas": for the bodhisattvas of the six perfections, there is no place where they drew a needle to point at the ground that was not a site for sacrificing their bodies and lives; through precept, patience, meditation, and wisdom, they fulfilled three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

If a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching enters emptiness from the conventional, their practice does not span but a single lifetime; yet when they enter the conventional from emptiness, it takes more than as many eons as there are motes of dust.
If even for a Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching, practicing a single path alone takes immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, how much more so for one who practices all paths universally?
Even those whose measure is beyond counting have not yet received their prediction; yet, having heard this sutra for but a short time, they have obtained such a resolution.
At that time, the assembly was filled with doubt, and thus the tree deity posed the question.
The Buddha’s answer is twofold: first, he cites the present manifestation; second, he cites the distant conditions. Regarding the present manifestation:

having abandoned the pleasures of the celestial palace, he came to hear this sutra. Hearing that the three great bodhisattvas had received the prediction of bodhi, [the Buddha recalled] his own original vow to provide them with the "Dharma-food. Because these three factors converged, he granted them their predictions.

This intention establishes that, at the beginning of the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits," one should honor the Buddhas of the three periods with sublime offerings and, desiring to know the sphere of activity of all Buddhas, listen to this wondrous scripture with a resolute and sincere mind.
Although this principle exists, such a person has not yet been seen; now these ten thousand are precisely those people.

Having heard the prediction of their future fruition, there must necessarily be causes for that fruition: through the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light), they give rise to a body of merit by producing a profound and reverent mind; with a mind free from defilement and burden, they give rise to a body of *prajñā*; and like space, they give rise to the Dharma-body. Within a single mind, they listen as the three virtues are perfectly accomplished.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable merits that cannot be fully described; since this [person] has not received a prediction, to whom would the prediction be granted?
It is with this in mind that the merit of witnessing and hearing [the teaching] is established.
"Practicing according to the phenomenal marks" refers to present activity; it means practicing while conforming to the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
"Possessing sublime roots of goodness" refers to distant conditions;
it means planting roots of goodness while [initially] being in opposition to the ultimate reality.
From "Also by means of the past" onwards is the response that cites remote conditions.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the concise; second, the detailed.
Within this, the brief textual passages constitute the summary, while the two chapters, "Curing Illness" (*Vyādhipraśamana*) and "Flowing Water" (*Jalavāhana*), provide the detailed response.

The commentary on the "Curing Illness" chapter explains that it is a detailed response concerning remote conditions; because the King of Physicians saves from disease, it is called the "Curing Illness" chapter.
Taking the subsequent "Flowing Water" chapter as a whole, the text is divided into five sections:
first, the primary condition; second, the distant condition; third, the proximate condition; fourth, the concluding condition; and fifth, the harmonizing condition.
From "The Buddha told the tree deity" onwards, the fundamental conditions are clarified as in the text.
From "During the Semblance Dharma" onwards, the distant conditions are clarified.
There are six types of distant conditions:

First, the father is introduced; second, a son is born; third, the people of the country fall ill; fourth, the son makes a request; fifth, the father explains it for him; sixth, having understood, he treats everyone.
I request that you practice three things:
first, perceiving the faults and illnesses of others; second, contemplation; and third, proper inquiry.
Inquiry consists of four parts:

The first verse asks about the increase and decrease of the four great elements; the second asks about the transgressions regarding food and drink; the third asks about medical prescriptions for treating illnesses; and the fourth asks about the seasonal fluctuations of disease.

Regarding "the fire of the body does not cease": when one has eaten to satiety, the feverish illness subsides; yet once the food is digested, the heat arises again. Therefore, it is said that the fire of the body does not cease.
Regarding "excess of water causes lung disease": an abundance of water harms the lungs, which refers specifically to the disease of phlegm (*kapha*).

The father physician returned with answers to the four questions: first, six lines answer the increase and decrease of the four great elements; second, one and a half lines answer the transgressions and contacts regarding food and drink; third, two lines answer the seasonal movements of illness; and fourth, eight and a half lines answer the methods for treating illness.
Within these six lines, there are two parts:
first, one line in which the Buddha describes how his father, the physician, intended to answer; second, five lines that constitute the actual answer regarding the seasons.
Regarding the seasons, there are two [aspects]:
There are four seasons in the secular calendar, namely spring, summer, autumn, and winter; winter constitutes the end of the year and spring the beginning of the year.
As for the initial mention of "summer," it may have been spoken as a general reference, or perhaps it was stated specifically because the response concerned the current summer season.

Regarding the explanation "three by three," this refers to the three months of each season—namely, the first (mèng), middle (zhòng), and last (jì)—and thus constitutes the four seasons, which comprise twelve months.
According to the Buddhist system for reckoning time, there are three seasons in a year: winter, spring, and summer; of these, summer marks the end of the year and winter marks its beginning.

Why is this so? It is because [the Buddha] sought to destroy the disciples' attachment to permanence and to open the possibility for the *kārttika* month of the rainy season retreat; thus, the autumn period was omitted.
The three seasons of the Buddha-dharma are likewise explained as three sets of three.

If one speaks of two periods each, totaling six periods, this is based on the secular system of four seasons; while the fundamental period consists of two months, the "earth" (terrestrial) system assigns eighteen days to each of the four seasons, such that the fundamental two months are simply the two months of the Yin-Yang calendar.
At one time there were only two months for each of the yin and yang seasons, which together constitute the six periods.

The first and second months are the period when Wood reigns; the fourth and fifth months are the period when Fire reigns; the seventh and eighth months are the period when Metal reigns; the tenth and eleventh months are the period when Water reigns; the twelfth month and the third month are the periods when Yang Earth resides as a guest sovereign; and the sixth and ninth months are the periods when Yin Earth resides as a guest sovereign.

If one discusses the primary months, they are also explained in pairs; if one discusses the seasons based on the kings, they are likewise explained in pairs; thus it is said that there are six full periods.
If one explains these pairs according to the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-dharma has three seasons, each season consisting of four months, and each month having both a first and a second half.
From the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the second month, this is the first part of spring;
from the sixteenth day of the second month to the fifteenth day of the third month, this is the latter part of the second month of spring.
From the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the sixth month, these two months constitute the first part of the summer season;
from the sixteenth day of the sixth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, this constitutes the latter part of the summer season.
From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month, these two months constitute the first division of winter;

from the sixteenth day of the tenth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, these two months constitute the latter division of winter. Thus, it is said that by speaking in pairs, the full six seasons are accounted for.

It is further stated: "The first and third months are yang months; the second and fourth months are yin months; the fifth and seventh months are yang months; the sixth and eighth months are yin months; the ninth and eleventh months are yang months; and the tenth and twelfth months are yin months. Thus, by speaking in pairs, the six seasons are fully accounted for."

Regarding the three groups of three months that follow the secular calendar: the first month is the primary month of spring, encompassing the subsequent two months as all belonging to the spring season;
the fourth month is the primary month of summer, encompassing the subsequent two months as all belonging to the summer season;
and the seventh month is the primary month of autumn, encompassing the subsequent two months as all belonging to the autumn season.
The tenth month is the primary month of winter; it encompasses the following two months, all of which belong to the winter season—these three being the fundamental groupings.
Furthermore, it is said:

the first and second months are precisely the time of spring, during which wood reigns as the dominant element; earth is temporarily assigned to the third month, and thus it is subsumed under the spring season.
The fourth and fifth months are precisely the summer season; fire reigns supreme therein, while earth is temporarily assigned to the sixth month, being subsumed under the summer season.
The seventh and eighth months are precisely the autumn season; metal reigns supreme therein, while earth is temporarily assigned to the ninth month, being subsumed under the autumn season.

The tenth and eleventh months are precisely the winter season; water reigns supreme therein, while earth is temporarily assigned to the twelfth month (the *laba* month), being subsumed under the winter season.

Earth is the fundamental basis for the four seasons; each season of three months is subsumed within earth. Therefore, it is said that "three threes are fundamentally subsumed," meaning the host subsumes the guest, and the guest is earth.

Regarding the statement in the Buddhist teachings that the three triads are fundamentally subsumed: originally each season consisted of three months; since the autumn season has been abolished, the three months of autumn are each distributed among the [remaining] three seasons, whereby each season then consists of four months.

In terms of the fundamental treatise (*śāstra-mūla*), there are three; in terms of what they encompass (*saṃgraha*), there is one. Therefore, it is said that "the three are subsumed within the three fundamentals.

Question: Each of the four seasons consists of three months; these are thus subsumed within the four sets of three fundamentals. Why, then, is it called being "subsumed within the three sets of three fundamentals"?
Answer:
Three are taken as a single unit; because they are counted by threes, it is said that "three times three" constitutes the basis.

Regarding "adapting to the seasonal fluctuations," "time" is as explained above—whether four, three, two, or subsumed [into one]—there are various differences. One should adapt according to the time, using one's own judgment to weigh and decide what to adopt or discard.
If, according to the Buddha’s Dharma, there is no such thing as autumn, yet it is said that one falls ill during autumn,
how is this to be explained?
From the middle of the eighth month onwards, it is designated as "autumn" in accordance with worldly convention, though it is actually subsumed within the summer season.
From the latter half of the eighth month onward, it is called "autumn" according to worldly convention and is subsumed within the winter season.
To "adjust according to the times" means to exercise discretion between these two periods.

Regarding the increase or decrease of the metabolic processes (*metābō*): if the liver disease is activated in spring, it can be treated; if the spleen disease is activated in spring, it is difficult to treat.
If the heart disease is activated in summer, it can be treated; if the lung disease is activated in summer, it is difficult to treat.
At the end of summer and the beginning of winter, if the lung disease is activated during the autumnal equinox, it can be treated; if the liver disease is activated, it is difficult to treat.
At winter, if the kidney disease is activated, it can be treated; if the heart disease is activated, it is difficult to treat.
The general outline of the increase and decrease across the four seasons is as described above.
Question:
Since all four seasons involve the movement of disease, why is the autumn season excluded?
This is explained in two parts:
first, to refute the preservation of permanence.
In autumn, when the myriad things bear fruit, people reckon them to be permanent and joyful.
To destroy this attachment, the Buddha, during the autumn season, established the *kārttika* month for his disciples because they were prone to excessive clinging to permanence.
Second, it was to open the possibility for a subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* (post-retreat) period.

The original name for *an-ju* (the summer retreat) was "sitting through the summer" (*za-xia*). If one returns within the middle of the eighth month, it is during autumn; thus, it would be "sitting through autumn.
For this reason, the practice of sitting through autumn was subsequently abandoned.
From the line "There is a skilled physician" onwards, one and a half lines answer the question regarding the offense of contact (*āpatti-saṃsarga*).
There are six types of such offenses:
first, excessive sitting; second, excessive sleeping. These two lead to an excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*), for which it is appropriate to frequently practice walking and relaxation (*vyāyāma-vikṣepa*).
Third, excessive activity; fourth, excessive physical exertion; fifth, excessive speech—these give rise to wind disorders (vāta), which should be treated by sleeping much.
Sixth, excessive sexual indulgence gives rise to all diseases, namely those of the balanced temperament (sāṃnipātika).
If the fire element is deficient and phlegm is excessive, [the body becomes cold].
If the fire element is excessive, there is intense heat.
If the wind element is excessive, it fans the fire and produces feverish illness.
If wind is predominant, it blows the phlegm and produces cold-related illnesses.
If these three factors are in equilibrium, there is no illness.
There are also six ways in which one may fall ill due to food and drink:
First, eating in excess;
second, stopping before one has eaten enough;
third, eating while excessively hungry.
Fourth, eating at improper times, such as giving food to someone who is not yet hungry;
fifth, obstructing digestion, such as eating meat or drinking raw milk, which causes leprosy;

sixth, eating what one has never eaten before, such as southerners drinking grain-gruel or northerners drinking honey, or mixing vegetables with honey so they do not ferment, or frying egret meat in pig fat, all of which cause leprosy.
If one who suffers from heat-diseases drinks alcohol or eats wheat and raw beef, it will cause blindness, vomiting of blood, and diarrhea with blood.
If one suffering from phlegm-diseases eats sweet, fatty, salty, or sour foods, it will cause nasal congestion, excessive secretions, and furthermore, dysentery.
The "six greats" refer to the six hollow organs: the large intestine, small intestine, gallbladder, stomach, triple burner, and the two bladders.
From the phrase "those with wind disorders" downward, two lines answer the question regarding the timing of the onset of illness.
The fourth and fifth months are the time when wind arises; the sixth and seventh months are the time when wind begins; the eighth and ninth months are the time when wind ceases.
The sixth and seventh months are the time when heat arises; the eighth and ninth months are the time when heat begins; from the tenth month to the first month is the time when heat ceases.

The eighth and ninth months are the time of arising during the period of equilibrium; the tenth and eleventh months are the time of emergence during the period of equilibrium; and the twelfth and first months are the time of cessation during the period of equilibrium.

From the tenth month to the first month is the time when phlegm is generated; from the second month to the third month is the time when phlegm arises; from the fourth month to the seventh month is the time when phlegm is extinguished.
Phlegm is water, and its affliction lies in the lungs.
Regarding wind manifesting in summer: in summer, the pores are open and unobstructed; thus, external wind can enter and stir the internal wind.
Regarding heat diseases manifesting in autumn: the pores are closed and obstructed; the heat remains latent within and cannot circulate, thereby forming a disease.
Regarding those whose [humors] are balanced but move in winter: if they move in spring, the water-based lung disease does not subside;
when summer arrives and wind moves again, the wind disease does not subside;
when autumn arrives and heat moves again, the heat disease does not subside.
This is because all diseases are aggravated in winter.
In the second and third months, phlegm arises and damages the lungs; thus, lung diseases are provoked.
From the passage beginning with "For those who have wind-diseases" (vātika), the following eight and a half lines provide the methods for treating these ailments.
The text consists of three parts:

the first two and a half lines concern preventing illness with medicine before it occurs; the next two lines clarify treating the illness with medicine while it is present; and the final four lines concern replenishing with medicine once the illness has subsided.

Regarding those with wind disorders who consume fatty, salty, sour, and hot foods during the summer: in the summer months, the pores are open and dilated; by thoroughly moistening and obstructing them with these fatty substances, one prevents the wind from entering.
Salts are hot in nature and can dissolve water, making the body firm and solid; they treat wind-weakness (*vāta-śūnya*).
Hot food induces perspiration, drawing the wind out, and furthermore treats cold-weakness (*śīta-śūnya*), preventing the wind from entering.
Cold and sweet substances, such as clarified butter (*sarpis*) and milk, can treat heat disorders.
Sweet and sour substances taken in equal proportions during winter eliminate wind disorders.
For lung diseases, one should consume fatty and greasy foods to block the pores, preventing water from entering.
Heat can parch, while water can moisten and circulate; therefore, [the former] can treat lung diseases.
Overeating triggers lung disease because when food is consumed in excess, the intestines and stomach become distended, thereby provoking the lungs.

Regarding the fever that arises when food is digested: when food is moist and nourishing, the fever-disease remains latent; once the food is digested and lacks such moisture, the fever-disease emerges.
Having been digested, the body becomes depleted and porous, and wind-energy enters the body, thereby giving rise to wind-disease.
Wind is alleviated by sparse [foods], while ghee and richness [alleviate] phlegm; salt removes wind and sweetness removes heat. When the lungs harbor wind and water, vomiting is appropriate.
This interpretation of the text is derived from the commentary of the Tripitaka Master Zhendi.
From the section on "The Goddess of Good Women" (*Śubhavyūhā*) downward is the sixth [section], "Knowing and Universally Treating.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, light illnesses are cured immediately upon hearing the teaching; second, heavy illnesses are eliminated by taking medicine, and so forth.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the three poisons and their equal proportions are internal illnesses.
Counting the breath, impurity, loving-kindness, and dependent origination are the medicinal dharmas.
Those who are suited to hear these medicinal dharmas and thereby attain awakening are practitioners by way of faith whose illnesses have been cured.
One who attains awakening through the practice of contemplation and the refinement of the mind is like a person of the Dharma-practitioner (dharmānusārin) whose illness has been cured.
The eye corresponds to spring, the tongue to summer, the nose to autumn, and the ear to winter; the body corresponds to all four seasons, encompassing and belonging to all times.

Exquisite sensual desires increase the affliction of greed; coarse sensual desires diminish the affliction of greed. Exquisite sensual desires diminish the affliction of hatred; coarse sensual desires increase the affliction of hatred. Neutral sensual desires increase the affliction of delusion; favorable or adverse sensual desires diminish the affliction of delusion. Collectively, all three types of sensual desires increase the affliction of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); individually, the three types of sensual desires diminish the affliction of applied and sustained thought. These are the characteristics of increase and decrease.

Regarding transgressions through contact: when contrary to one's feelings, one commits anger; when conforming to one's feelings, one commits greed; when neither contrary nor conforming, one commits delusion. In total, these three constitute the transgressions of vitarka and vicāra.

Furthermore, at the time of pride, anger arises; at the time of seeking and desiring, greed arises; at the time of perverse understanding, delusion arises; and at the time of heedlessness, vitarka and vicāra arise.

Loving-kindness remedies anger; impurity remedies greed; dependent origination remedies delusion; and counting the breath remedies discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), and so forth.
In the "Explanation of the Flowing Water" chapter, the text of the "Flowing Water" chapter states: "First, it can flow; second, it can provide water."
"To give water" means to bestow the water of peace and happiness: first, the peace and happiness of this world; second, the peace and happiness that transcends the world.
As for the peace and happiness of this world, it is like the elephant carrying water on its back to rescue those parched fish.
Supramundane peace and happiness refers to making a vow such as:
"In future ages, I shall bestow the food of Dharma and grant the prediction of Bodhi.
As for "flowing water," it means flowing to remove the waters of suffering; these are twofold: first, the suffering of karmic retribution, and second, the suffering of karmic causes.
To eliminate the suffering and affliction of karmic retribution is like treating various patients or rescuing thirsty fish.
To eliminate the suffering and affliction of karmic causes is to bestow the Three Refuges, explain the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and praise the Ten Epithets of the Buddha.
He requested his father to seek out methods, desiring to fulfill the meaning of "Flowing Water" (Śrotas).
He borrowed an elephant from the king, desiring to fulfill the meaning of "Giving Water.
Since he possessed both these capabilities, why was the work titled solely "Flowing Water"?
Since the meaning of "flowing water" is already clearly manifested within the text, the title must necessarily include the name "Flowing Water.
Without complicating the prose, both meanings are simultaneously revealed; such is the ingenuity of the one who brought forth this sutra.
"Householder" (長者) refers to the ten meanings of a householder as explained in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
"Son" (字) means the son of the Water-Bearer; thus, he is called a "son."
This text is the third section within the "Dispelling Doubts," concerning the proximate causes for establishing a karmic connection.
There are two parts to these proximate causes:
first, the introductory lead-in; second, the actual proximate cause.
The introductory prelude has two further parts:
first, the distribution of grace and the spreading of virtue; second, the praise of the people of the land—both as written in the text.
The proximate prelude has three further parts:
First, clarifying the retinue; second, the occasion of seeing the fish; third, the actual rescue of the fish, as in the text.
From the passage "In future ages, one shall bestow the food of Dharma" onwards, this is the fourth section: the formal establishment of the karmic connection.
Furthermore, there are four parts:

first, making a vow; second, contemplating the preaching of the Dharma; third, correctly preaching the Dharma; and fourth, the fish transforming its rebirth to be born in heaven to repay his kindness through offerings.
Regarding the fish repaying its debt of gratitude, the text is divided into four parts:

first, the fish transforms its rebirth and ascends to heaven; second, the deva repays the kindness by descending to earth; third, the king sees the light and inquires about the omen; fourth, the elder seeks instruction and provides a definitive answer, as explained in the text.
Requital of gratitude has two meanings:
first, the phenomenal (shi), and second, the principle (li).
Regarding the phenomenal, it refers to the four kinds of benefits: the water that nourishes the four sides of the pearl, food and drink, causal conditions, and the ten titles [of the Buddha].

Regarding the principle, according to the text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "By giving food, one causes others to obtain life, which symbolizes permanence; by causing others to obtain happiness, one thereby attains nirvāṇa; by causing others to attain awakening, one thereby achieves the sovereign self (vaśavartin); by seeking wealth in accordance with the Dharma, one thereby attains purity."
He used forty thousand [gold pieces] to repay the grace of the Buddha’s eternal bliss, selfhood, purity, and permanence.
Fifth, regarding the synthesis of past and present: formerly, the Buddha was uncertain about the number of fish, but the tree deity definitively determined it to be ten thousand.
Now, while the divine [teachings] seem shallow in their application yet profound in their records, the Buddha has expounded the wondrous causes and conditions.
Because the present and the past are interconnected, this chapter is concluded as a synthesis.
Regarding the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body": the meaning of relinquishment is manifold; among wealth, status, and lifespan, why is it that the body alone is given this name?
This receives its name from its primary significance.
For the recipient, the body is essential, whereas other things are not;
for the donor, the primary act is the relinquishing of the body, while the relinquishing of other things is secondary. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body."

The text consists of four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the benefits received by the assembly; and fourth, the conclusion. Regarding the question: having previously heard that the Great Being cures illnesses and saves fish—truly providing vast salvation for small people and small insects so that they obtain benefit in two lifetimes—the questioner asks: The text consists of four parts: first, the question; second, the answer;

third, the benefits received by the assembly; and fourth, the conclusion. Regarding the question: having previously heard that the Great Being cures illnesses and saves fish—truly providing vast salvation for small people and small insects so that they obtain benefit in two lifetimes—the questioner asks:
At that time, the assembly wished to hear of matters concerning the profound resonance and ultimate fulfillment achieved through sacrificing one’s body and casting away one’s life.
"Is it possible to hear how suffering in practice leads to joy in fruition?
For this reason, they made this inquiry.
The Buddha’s response consists of two parts:
first, an account of the causal origin; second, the actual explanation of the relinquishing of the body.
The causal origin comprises ten sections:

1. A stūpa emerges from the earth; 2. the great assembly harbors doubts; 3. the Buddha rises and pays homage; 4. the tree deity asks about the homage; 5. the Buddha explains the reason for the homage; 6. he commands Ānanda to retrieve it; 7. Ānanda describes the state of the bones; 8. he commands that it be shown to the great assembly; 9. following the command, it is retrieved and displayed; 10. the Buddha exhorts the assembly to pay homage—all as described in the text.
From the passage "In the past there was a king" onwards is the actual relinquishing of the body.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the prose (gadya), and second, the verse (śloka).
The long version consists of four parts:

first, clarifying his original retinue; second, the skillful means of relinquishing the body; third, the actual relinquishment of the body; and fourth, the grief and longing following the relinquishment.
Regarding the original retinue, there are five sections:
First, to clarify his original retinue:
Mahārodha is translated here as "Great Faultless One" (Dà Wúzuì).
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchāsūtra* states that "Rodha is translated as 'Middle'."
Mahāprajāpatī is sometimes translated as "Great Deliverer," though this is not yet fully established.
Mahādevī means "Great Goddess.
Mahāsattva is translated as "Great Being" (or "Great Heart").
Second, the journey;
third, each describing their characteristics;
fourth, seeing the tiger that had given birth.
Each of the five [bodhisattvas] sets forth their vision.
From the passage, "He then thought: 'The time has now come for me to relinquish my body,'" onwards, this is the skillful means (*upāya*) of relinquishing the body.
This skillful means is twofold:
First, the exposition of contemplative understanding; second, the arousal of vows. Vow and practice support one another.
Regarding the phrase "just seven days old": seeing that there were seven spots on the head of a tiger cub, one knew it had already been seven days; this is recorded in the *Shanhai jing*.
It is further said:
"After seven days his eyes will open.
Furthermore, it is said that one who does not eat for seven days will surely die; the tiger cub was on the verge of death, and thus he knew it would be seven days.
Some say:
"Spirits manifesting and awakening others is like the tree spirit counting the fish.
There are two ways of truly sacrificing one's body: [the first is through supernatural manifestation; the second is through physical renunciation].
First, he renounced his body; second, he moved heaven and earth.

After he had renounced his body, his kinsmen were filled with grief and suffering. First, his two elder brothers, distressed by sorrow, each spoke a verse as they went together toward the place of renunciation; next, his parents were overcome with grief and suffering.
The ninety-three lines of verse are divided into three parts:
the first two lines generally clarify past practices; the next verses specifically correspond to the prose; and the final part provides a concluding synthesis.
The first part is as the text states.
The section beginning with "I recollect my past lives" is the prose commentary on the subsequent individual verses; the four lines of verse above [this] concern his original retinue.
Above, there was a description of the characteristics and a presentation of the contemplation, which is not versified here; all other parts are versified.
From "The Great Being of Superior Time" (*Kālasuvrata*) downward for two lines, the verse praises the skillful means of relinquishing the body, not the making of the vow.
From "He immediately ascended a high mountain" downward, the verse praises the actual act of relinquishing the body and its resulting spiritual resonance.
From "At that time, the two elder brothers... onwards, the verse describes how the kinsmen were filled with grief and suffering after the prince had abandoned his body.
From "At that time, the prince... onwards, the verse describes the grief and suffering of his parents.
From "The Buddha addressed the tree deity" onwards is the third section, the Conclusion.
This conclusion consists of three parts:
first, the conclusion regarding the person; second, the conclusion regarding the stupa; and third, the conclusion regarding the vow.
The section beginning with "When this sutra was being preached" concerns the benefits conferred upon the great assembly.
The section beginning with "The tree deity [said], 'This is called paying homage to a stūpa'" constitutes the fourth part, which summarizes the intent of the inquiry.

The Chapter on Praising the Buddha: This chapter is named according to both the agent and the object. The agents of praise are the three groups of bodhisattvas, and the object of praise is the one World-Honored Buddha. Since the title indicates both the agent and the object, it is called the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha."

I maintain that the three instances of the Bodhisattva are the praisers and the one Buddha is the praised; alternatively, the one Buddha is the praiser and the three instances are the praised; furthermore, the three instances are the Buddhas-to-be and the one Buddha is the present Buddha.
Speaking generally, all [the preceding chapters] are capable of praising [the Buddha], and all are the Buddha; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha.
As for the sequence, this present chapter exists because of the seventeen preceding chapters.

Why is this? The "Introductory Chapter" (Xùpǐn) describes the general framework: the Tathāgata dwells within immeasurable and profoundly deep dharmatā, exhausting its source and reaching its ultimate limit.
The "Chapter on the Lifespan" (Shòuliàngpǐn) concerns the profound mystery of the ultimate fruit, which, through its vast integration, is able to give rise to great function.
In the "Chapter on Repentance," it is exhorted that if a bodhisattva wishes to practice and study,
they should eliminate evil as taught in the "Chapter on Repentance," generate goodness as taught in the "Chapter on Praise," and achieve completion as guided in the "Chapter on Emptiness."
From the "Four Kings" chapter to the "Samantabhadra" (or "Saṃjñeya") chapter, the vows for the circulation [of the scripture] are established, and the merits of the requester are explained.
From the "Right Discourse" chapter to the "Good Collection" chapter, the merits of the speaker are elucidated.
From the "Devatās" chapter to the "Jalavāhana" chapter, the merits of the listeners are explained;
in the "Sacrificing the Body" chapter, the merits of the practitioner are clarified.
All such benefits that appear in the world are the power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*—the great essence, great wisdom, and great function of the Tathāgata.

Since it is well-conceived at the beginning and brought to completion at the end—from the initial stage through the middle to the final conclusion—all the bodhisattvas and others praise the Buddha and extol both the teaching and the Teacher; therefore, this is called the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha."
This passage consists of two parts:
first, the sūtra-narrator describes and enumerates the assembly of those who offer praise.

From this point until the description of the offering of the three karmas at the realm of the Golden Jewel Canopy (*Suvarṇaratnacchatra*), prostrating on the ground represents the body, and chanting in unison represents the speech; thus, speech and body together express the mental karma (*manaskarma*).
The second part, the actual verses of the teaching, consists of sixty-five and a half lines.
The text is divided into three sections:
first, twenty lines spoken by the various bodhisattvas; second, twenty-seven lines spoken by Śraddhālakṣaṇa; and third, twenty-eight and a half lines spoken by the tree deity, and so forth.
I maintain that this passage consists of four parts:
the first three are the eulogizers, and the last one is the object of praise.

Furthermore, the object of praise is itself an eulogizer, and the eulogizer is also the object of praise; thus the text says: "The Buddha arose from samādhi and, with a voice as subtle as a whisper, spoke in praise, saying:"
"Excellent, excellent, O tree-spirit, virtuous daughter!
On this day you have spoken these words most excellently.
Is this not praising that which is worthy of praise?
Since its meaning is already clear, there is no need for confusion.

Furthermore, this is a threefold seal of the Bodhisattva Praise Teachings; from the "Introductory Chapter" onwards, it eloquently explains the Tathāgata’s fruition-stage: his great essence, great wisdom, and great function, as well as the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of causes.
In the preceding passage, there is the Buddha paying homage to the *śarīra*, which is the fruit-body paying homage to the causal body.

In the present passage, there is the Buddha praising the Great Repentance—the Great Praise, the one who can request and preach, the one who can listen and practice—all of which constitute "joyful preaching. One should know that this joyful preaching is the fruit-body praising the causal Bodhisattva.
If one praises the cause with the mouth while the fruit is present, the meaning is weak;
if one praises the cause with the mind while the fruit is present, it is established by natural extension, and so forth.
Question:
Question: Where did the Buddha enter meditative absorption, such that here it is said he "arises from samādhi"?
Answer:
At the outset, when about to preach the sutra, the Buddha dwelled within the profoundly deep nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Now that this exposition is nearly concluded, he has arisen from samādhi.
From beginning to end, this sutra is spoken entirely within the realm of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and its text is exceedingly clear.

If one considers it as entering into *dharmatā*, then within the sovereign freedom of *dharmatā*, four Buddhas or five Buddhas may occupy the same place or separate places, see together or see differently, and come and go four times; while remaining in one state or abiding in one place, they appear to each person according to their perception, all without any obstruction.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the three karmas of all Bodhisattvas praise the Buddha; these three karmic activities are easily understood.
Regarding the three contemplations of the mind: one contemplates the body and finds no body; the body is empty, existing as nothing more than a name.
Names are immeasurable; sometimes the relinquishing of the body is called "giving" (dāna), and even the emptiness of the body is called "wisdom.
Whether it be the six perfections, the ten perfections, or the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates like grains of sand, their names are themselves empty.
It is taught that emptiness is not fixed as empty and the provisional is not fixed as provisional; that which is neither empty nor existent clearly reveals the Middle Way.
The three contemplations are thus complete, and all six categories of phenomena—both phenomenal and noumenal—are fully present.
If there is no wisdom of contemplation, the matter will likewise not be accomplished.
For example, regarding the three robes and six requisites: if one understands their underlying meaning, both the "three" and the "six" are established;
if one does not understand it, not only are the six absent, but even the three are not established.
Contemplating the mind is likewise so: if one attains contemplation of principle, the six contemplations will all be perfected;
if one does not grasp the meaning, since there is no contemplation of principle, even the contemplation of phenomena will not be accomplished.
This refers to the statement that "there are neither six nor three," and so forth,
describing it as most excellent and exceedingly vast.
*The Words and Phrases of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
